articles.title: Russia Continues to Develop Cheap Cruise Missile Substitutes
articles.body:
An Oct. 5 report by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) says Russia is increasingly turning to cheaper, maneuverable “quasi-cruise” missiles to supplement its conventional strike capabilities, a tactic that is pressuring Ukraine’s already overstretched air defenses.
Building on the relative success of the jet-powered variants of the Iranian-designed Shahed/Geran kamikaze drones, Russia has been introducing the so-called Banderol and Dan-T weapons and is believed to be developing other variants, increasing production and testing new launch platforms.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Mass attacks combining these new weapons with ballistic and conventional cruise missiles and jet-powered drones are exacerbating Ukrainian interceptor missile shortages.
While Ukraine is developing countermeasures including faster interceptors, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence-enhanced automatic gun towers, these will, as President Volodymyr Zelensky has admitted, take time to develop and bring into service. Meanwhile, Kyiv will struggle to protect itself from the onslaught these weapons will unleash.
The Banderol
Russia’s S8000 “Banderol” (meaning a small parcel in Russian) is a jet-powered medium-size cruise missile analog manufactured by the Kronshtadt Group.
It uses the Chinese Swiwin SW800Pro-A95 turbojet engine, giving it a range of up to 500 kilometers (312 miles) at speeds up to 650 kph (400 mph) and a 150-kilogram (330-pound) warhead.
Power Cuts Return After Russian Strikes Damage Grid
The Ukrainian Air Force describes it as a “hybrid of a drone, an aerial bomb, and a missile.”
It first appeared during a strike on the Odesa region in early 2025 before taking part in 40 separate strikes between May and September this year, while Ukraine’s Main Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reported in July that Russia had completed testing and the weapon had entered mass production.
They have been used in attacks targeting ports, logistics hubs, terminals, food warehouses and infrastructure in Kharkiv, Odesa, Zhytomyr and Kyiv.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Kyiv’s presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, said in July that Banderols had been used in 80% of Russian strikes on the Odesa City port.
The Dan-T
Russia unveiled its Dan-T at the El-Alamein airshow in Egypt in September. It is based on the 1990s Dan-M target aircraft, which was designed to simulate US Tomahawk cruise missiles for air-defense training.
According to the ISW report, Russia’s state-owned arms conglomerate Rostec, which makes the missiles, converted Dan-M stockpiles into air-launched loitering munitions by adding 135-kilogram (300-pound) warheads. It has an all-up weight of 270 kilograms (600 pounds) and a 500-kilometer (312-mile) range.
ISW assesses that construction of Dan-Ts has not yet reached scale but is another indication of Moscow’s efforts to repurpose existing technology into strike weapons. As an example, Soviet-era RM-48U missiles – originally designed for S-400 air defense training – have been converted into ballistic missiles for ground attacks on Ukraine.
The extent of Dan-T use is unclear. While Rostec and some Russian milbloggers claim hundreds have been successfully used in strikes on Ukraine, it was not until Sept. 13 that Ukraine began to differentiate between Banderols and Dan-Ts.
Launch platforms
Banderols and Dan-T were initially designed to be air-launched from Orion drones, helicopters and tactical aircraft – which some estimates say would potentially double their range.
HUR has reported ground launches from occupied Crimea, with Ukrainian analysts suggesting Dan-T could eventually launch from ground and naval systems.
Cost versus performance
These “quasi-cruise” missiles have inferior performance to conventional missiles, but their cost allows more to be manufactured and used, while their capabilities are more than sufficient for Russia’s purposes.
Compared to the Kh-101 cruise missile’s 2,500-kilometer (1,560-mile) range, 1,000 kph (625 mph) speed, and 480-kilogram (1,050-pound) warhead, the Banderol has a 500-kilometer (312-mile) range, speed of up to 650 kph (400 mph), and a 150-kilogram (330-pound) warhead.
The cost differential is even more stark. A Ukrainian aviation expert estimates that each Banderol costs less than 10% of the approximately $2million cost of a domestically produced Kh-101 cruise missile.
Banderols present especially difficult targets when used in attacks that combine them with Geran/Shahed drones and conventional missiles. They are maneuverable and have a smaller turning radius, which complicates tracking and interception.
Russian mass production
The report claims that Russia has prioritized production of jet-powered drones and quasi-cruise missiles in order to increase its strike capability at an affordable cost.
In September, Zelensky claimed that Russia would spend $12 billion on the weapons, with Ukrainian defense analyst Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov saying that Russia not only aims to increase the numbers of Banderol, Dan-T, Dan-M and jet-powered drones, but also aims to boost speeds to 750 kph (470 mph) while improving low-altitude flight and maneuverability.
HUR estimated in August that Russia was producing about 80 Banderols a month, with Beskrestnov setting the target at 120 and Ukrainian sources estimating Dan-T production at 14,000 in 2027.
Ukrainian countermeasures
Ukrainian developers recently unveiled upgraded interceptors, such as the LITAVR+ and Sting 2.0, capable of taking on jet-powered Geran/Shaheds flying at speeds over 400 kph (250 mph).
Beskrestnov said up to five such interceptors are in development and still require testing. Ukrainian developers have also reportedly deployed unspecified Banderol countermeasures and are scaling production.
Electronic warfare could reportedly play a role, as both Banderol and Dan-T reportedly rely on satellite and inertial navigation for guidance.

articles.title: Ukraine is fielding Turkey’s Korkut air defense guns, a Turkish cousin of the Gepard. One kind of Russian drone may be too fast for them
articles.body:
- Ukraine has acquired new Korkut air defense guns from Türkiye
- The Korkut is a pair of fast-firing guns on a tracked or wheeled chassis
- Ground-based guns are effective defenses against drones
- But the Russians are launching faster drones, and more of them are getting through
Ukraine has reportedly purchased Korkut self-propelled anti-aircraft guns (SPAAGs) from Türkiye. Effectively a Turkish take on the classic German-made Gepard SPAAG, a mainstay of Ukraine's defense against Russian one-way attack (OWA) drones, the Korkuts could help stiffen Ukrainian air defenses as winter looms and Russia intensifies its terror attacks on Ukrainian cities and power plants.
The problem for Ukrainian air defenders is that the latest jet-propelled Russian drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, are getting through. They fly at around 500 km/h, nearly three times as fast as an older, propeller-driven Geran-2, and in September Ukraine shot down just 55% of them, by Zelenskyy's count, against at least 90% of the slow ones, one analyst calculated. The Korkuts arrive in that gap. Ground-based guns are arguably Ukraine's most cost-effective anti-drone weapons, but they may not work so well against the fastest drones.
That means more Russian munitions are getting through. More Ukrainian homes are burning. More power plants are going dark. It's a crisis now. It'll be an even greater crisis when winter arrives and the temperature drops.
All that is to say, the handful of Korkut systems Ukraine has received from Turkish firm Aselsan are welcome, but they're not silver bullets against Russian drones.
A Korkut battery includes a command vehicle plus three tracked or wheeled vehicles armed with pairs of fast-firing, radar-cued 35-mm autocannons. The exact variant Ukraine received hasn't been disclosed; Middle East Eye's mention of 25-mm ammunition suggests it may be the smaller Korkut 100/25, built mainly to stop frontline drones. The Ukrainian Korkuts join a sizeable fleet of SPAAGs in Ukrainian service, most notably including potentially 90 or more 1960s-vintage Gepards with twin radar-cued 35-mm guns.
Ukraine is running short of its best missiles for hunting Russia’s jet drones. Now MiG-29s are firing 1970s weapons
The tracked Gepards are old but effective. They, like all SPAAGs, can only engage incoming drones and other targets at fairly short range: just a few kilometers. But they're cheap. A SPAAG might fire a few hundred dollars' worth of shells to bring down a $50,000 Geran. A surface-to-air missile can hit a Geran from much farther away, but even the cheapest missiles cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece—and the supply is limited.
Gepards and other gun-based air defenses, along with wide-area strategic radio jamming, were the twin keys to Ukraine's temporary victory over Russian Gerans as recently as late last year. That's when the Russians were still mostly launching propeller-driven Gerans, and the Ukrainians were shooting down most of them.
Slipping interception rates
Vanquishing the slow Gerans didn't solve a separate air defense problem—how to shoot down supersonic ballistic missiles—but it did minimize Ukrainian casualties and mitigate the overall damage to Ukrainian infrastructure. Only the best, priciest, and rarest Ukrainian air defenses such as the Patriot and SAMP/T can hit incoming ballistic missiles. As missiles have run out for those batteries, more Russian ballistic missiles have gotten through.
But now more Gerans are getting through, too. On 26 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 2,730 jet-powered Gerans at Ukraine that month and that Ukrainian air defenses were shooting down 55% of them. Analyst and mapper Clément Molin set that against Air Force totals: of 5,437 drones launched between 1 and 26 September, the remaining 2,707 were slow Geran-2s and Gerbera decoys, and at least 90% of those were downed. The overall interception rate, he calculated, has fallen to close to 70%, from 86% to 90% earlier this year.
Ukrainian forces are scrambling to acquire more inexpensive surface-to-air missiles as well as faster interceptor drones. But they're racing against time and the growing preponderance of jet-propelled OWA drones. The Ukrainians' air defense problem may get worse before it gets better.
"Ballistic missile defense is a serious problem, but the increasing production of Geran-4, Geran-5, Banderol, and Filin jet-powered OWA drones/cheap cruise missiles will also be a growing challenge this fall and winter," Rob Lee, an analyst with the Foreign Policy Research Institute in Philadelphia, warned in August.
Winter weather reduces the effectiveness of interceptor drones and helicopters, Lee noted, and Ukraine will need more high-speed interceptors to counter the jet drones. "The interception rate for OWA drones will likely decrease."
But that doesn't mean the Korkut isn't helping forestall an even worse dip in the overall interception rate for incoming Russian drones. Ukrainian officials are reportedly pleased with the Turkish gun. "Korkut has been pretty much successful in countering the Russian attacks," a Ukrainian official told Middle East Eye. "There were of course some problems but nothing that couldn't be overcome through some small adjustments."
According to Middle East Eye, the Ukrainians are considering acquiring more Korkuts.

- Ukraine’s battlefield gains may be pushing Putin to shift focus to early winter strikes, ISW says
- Russia is out to break Ukraine’s economy this winter, Jetten says—and the Netherlands will help keep Ukraine’s drone-hunting F-16s in the air

articles.title: France's Macron observes test of new nuclear-capable missile without warhead
articles.body:
Macron observes test of new nuclear-capable missile without warhead
French President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday observed the test firing of a new nuclear-capable missile without a warhead, according to the Elysée Palace and the Ministry of Defence.
France on Tuesday test-fired for the first time its new M51.3 nuclear-capable ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine, the defence ministry said. It was not carrying a warhead.
The missile, a variant of France's M51 missile, was fired from the Le Vigilant submarine off Brittany and impacted "in the North Atlantic, hundreds of kilometres from any coastline", it said. President Emmanuel Macron witnessed the firing from a French warship, an official told AFP.
It said the launch was conducted without a payload and in strict compliance with international obligations.
While the announcement made no mention of Russia, the test comes after President Vladimir Putin warned the West last week not to escalate a standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between EU members Poland and Lithuania and which Moscow has made clear it would defend with nuclear weapons if necessary.
Macron hails clear message
NATO has said none of its "exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation". Putin also said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully.
"Today we are stronger. The message has been sent loud and clear for wherever it must be received,” Macron said in a video on X showing him watching the launch.
Macron said in March France would expand its nuclear arsenal and launched an initiative offering European partners joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Since then, the message of being prepared to bear the costs of defending France's values and security has been a constant theme.
France spends roughly €5.6 billion ($6.04 billion) a year to maintain its stockpile of 290 submarine- and air-launched weapons — the world's fourth-largest arsenal. Britain has 225 nuclear warheads. Russia and the United States have more than 5,000 each.
The M51.3 is the latest version of the missile that entered service in October 2025 as part of the modernisation of France's nuclear deterrent.
Paris does not disclose the range of the M51.3. Publicly available estimates for the M51 family generally place its range at around 9,000 km (5,600 miles) or more, while French officials have said the new version can travel further.
France maintains a nuclear arsenal based on air- and sea-launched weapons, with four ballistic missile submarines forming the backbone of its ocean deterrent.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Fresh Intelligence Signals Massive Russian Strike Ahead, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Ukraine has received fresh intelligence indicating that Russia is preparing a massive strike, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday, Oct. 6.
“We received updated intelligence today regarding Russian preparations for a massive strike. We are preparing countermeasures,” Zelensky said after a coordination meeting with government officials, military leaders, and key emergency services.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The warning came as Ukrainian officials worked on additional logistical arrangements in response to what Zelensky described as a Russian operation targeting the country’s logistics. Government officials and regional authorities had prepared those measures together, he said.
Deadlines have been set for a substantial share of the tasks discussed at the meeting, with the most urgent measures already being implemented, according to Zelensky.
Air defense preparations were a central focus of the discussion. The defense minister and Air Force commander briefed Zelensky on the distribution of air defense assets and the organization of defensive coverage around designated key facilities.
Zelensky said Ukraine was securing the necessary ammunition for its F-16 fighter jets, interception capabilities, and interceptor missiles. However, he singled out defenses against ballistic missiles as the most difficult supply challenge.
“The most difficult issue is defending against ballistic missiles, and the availability of these supplies depends entirely on our partners,” he said. “We are working with them daily.”
Russia Continues to Develop Cheap Cruise Missile Substitutes
Zelensky also said Russian forces had attacked several Ukrainian hospitals in Kramatorsk and Kryvyi Rih over the preceding 24 hours.
“The emergency services responded effectively, and it is important that the State Emergency Service of Ukraine responds promptly to every such situation in all of our regions. Thank you for your professional work!”

articles.title: What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say Ukraine brought peace to world? Norwegian professor who nominated Zelenskyy and Ukrainians for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize takes on tough questions
articles.body:
It is rare to hear a European say "I'm sorry" to the Ukrainians. Dag Øistein Endsjø, who nominated the Ukrainian people and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the Nobel Peace Prize 2026, shared it several times during our interview.
Mr. Endsjø is a professor of religious studies at the University of Oslo in Norway. He comes across as courteous and reserved. But when he talks about Europe not helping Ukraine as much as it could, his eyes give away deep personal emotion.
"Just thank you for keeping us safe. Thank you for the extreme sacrifice you've been making for all of us. And I'm sorry that my government and the other governments haven't done enough," he said, speaking to me not as a journalist but as one of the Ukrainians.
These words cut through because tens of millions of us live under daily psychological and physical terror, feeling forgotten and betrayed.
At the same time, Professor Endsjø names things as they are, even when it is uncomfortable. When the full-scale invasion began, he says, he doubted Ukraine would hold. And he admits that Norway has profited from the war: by its own Finance Department's calculation, about €106 billion in additional revenue from higher oil and gas prices.
He was honest with us. Our questions were sharp too, even those about US President Donald Trump's chances to win this year's award, and he answered them the way he answers everything: straight.
Do you think people who fight the war can be nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize?
People who defend themselves, yes! Who defends a free and democratic state against unprovoked aggression, yes, I think so.
Many say Ukraine should stop fighting and negotiate. Wouldn't a peace prize reward the war?
It's not a reward for the war, because the war could stop tomorrow if Russia just realized they didn't want to break international rules and pulled out. This is not about continuing the war. On the other hand, the war would stop the moment Ukraine threw out Russia. That, regrettably, seems to take more time.
This is not, in any way, about rewarding or promoting war as such. This is about standing up against war, because not standing up against war has only provoked more war and aggression from Russia.
Russia is attacking free and democratic countries unprovoked. They started in 2008 with Georgia, and then moved on to Ukraine, and as so many others point out, they have their plans.
"Moldova, if Ukraine hadn't been able to resist this invasion, would also have been under Russian rule now for sure. Poland and the Baltics would have been under extreme pressure, maybe also invaded," Mr. Endsjø says.
If there was a moment when you thought that Ukraine might lose the war?
Yes, in the beginning, when I saw those lines of tanks heading for Kyiv, I was afraid that everything was lost. Also noting the lackluster reaction from the free world and how they only came with condemnations and no ammunition, just a flight out.
If Ukraine is defending peace, why is the war getting closer to Europe's borders?
That is because of Russia. If Ukraine hadn't defended itself and just given up, the war would have been even closer to Europe. We would be even more under threat with probably even more degrees of sabotage and terrorist attacks around in Europe.
Does Ukrainian resistance escalate the risk of direct war between NATO and Russia?
No. The other way around. If Ukraine had given up, it would have been a more direct threat to NATO countries.
But some politicians say that in this case, Russia will just negotiate and sell energy as it did in the past
Yes, while sabotaging and even murdering people around in Europe, and acting like a state of terrorism. So, no, it would remain aggressive. You can listen to various prominent Russians on Russian TV. You know, you're not allowed to say anything on Russian TV unless the government approves it...
People are again and again threatening Finland, Poland, Britain, and the Baltic. Just as they made up these fake republics in Luhansk and Donetsk in 2014, they have tried to do the same in Estonia and Latvia already.
So if it hadn't been for Ukraine and Ukraine's resistance, the risk of direct war between NATO and Russia would have been even greater. Because Ukraine keeps Russia at bay.
If Ukraine agrees to a ceasefire, will you consider this a failure or a victory?
I, as a non-Ukrainian but fellow European, like any other European, have no right whatsoever to tell the Ukrainians what to do.
If the Ukrainians themselves find that this most horrible war is too much, and you want a ceasefire and you want to stop, and it's not for me to criticize. It's not for any European to criticize. We cannot tell the Ukrainians what to do after that horrible sacrifice you've made already.
I only hope that Europe and the rest of the free world will assist Ukraine even more, so that you will be even more successful in throwing out the Russian occupation army of the entire of Ukraine, including Crimea.
What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say that Ukraine brought the world to peace?
They will not use nuclear weapons. If they wanted to do it, they would have done that already. China and India are completely clear that they will not accept any use of nuclear weapons, so that would mean that Russia would be completely isolated and completely devastated economically in weeks. So that's not going to happen.
Putin says the war ends if Ukraine gives up Donbas. Why give a Nobel Peace Prize to a country that refuses?
This is just a proposal from Putin and American so-called negotiators. They're supposed to be negotiating, but this is not a negotiation. This is just about trying to make Ukraine give up without even a fight, which Russia is unable to do, and, incredibly, in some way, try to force Ukraine to give up its rightful ownership of its occupied territories.
This is just appeasement, just as what Chamberlain did in 1938 and what Europe has done again and again in 2008 and 2014. This would be a completely terrible mistake.
"Ukraine deserves the Nobel Prize, no matter how long they keep on fighting against this horrible aggression by this dreadful kleptocracy," Mr. Endsjø says.
Europe says Ukraine keeps the peace for everyone. Can it then demand that Ukrainian refugees go back and fight?
I, as a European, think that other Europeans cannot demand anything of the Ukrainians, whoever they are. This must be up to the Ukrainian people and the Ukrainian government.
Do people in Norway still genuinely believe that Ukraine can win this war, dragging on for so long?
I think so. Very many do believe that. But this depends on whether the West keeps on, and the free world continues to support Ukraine. Here in Norway, we are in a particular situation because, as our own Finance Department calculated last year, we have earned an extra 106 billion euros from the war (additional government revenues generated by high energy prices — ed.) due to higher oil and gas prices.
We don't support you as much as we should. We should have given you those 106 billion euros.
Why should someone in Europe care whether Ukraine wins or loses?
That is the point: that this is a war against the free world from a horrible dictatorship. More or less, you can call it a kleptocracy — that's the most, I guess, the most precise definition of Russia today. It's not a democracy whatsoever. It's most of all a kleptocracy where the top leaders just steal whatever they can get their hands on.
If Ukraine had fallen, it's not just that that would be horrible for Ukraine as such, but that would mean also that Russia would have had its hands on all the immense resources Ukraine has. Also, all the million men and women who probably would have been forced into the Russian army, and made it an even more dangerous enemy to the West.
So this is about the survival of all of us. Ukraine is the free world. We belong together. Ukraine should have been in NATO and the EU a long time ago.
If Russia says it only wants Donbas, why not just give it to them and let the war end?
This is like World War II all over again. They say: "If we only get Donbas, we're going to at least have proper negotiations."
Donbas, that is the Ukrainian Sudetenland. That's just what the West forced Czechoslovakia to do in 1938 and 1939. The Sudetenland wasn't just a nice little border region. It was the defense line of Czechoslovakia. So the moment the Germans got that, they were defenseless against the full-scale invasion that followed in the months afterward.
"Donbas, it's not just a small border region. It's the most important line of defense," Mr. Endsjø says.
Forcing Ukraine to give up anything whatsoever is rewarding the Russian aggression.
But I have to give Putin right in one thing when he says: "We are, you know, continuing World War II." That's true, because you have to remember what Russia did in World War II. They started it together with Nazi Germany in 1939. They occupied the Baltic countries, they occupied Moldova, they occupied half of Poland, they split Poland with Nazi Germany, and they tried to occupy Finland.
When Norway was invaded by Nazi Germany, Russia congratulated Germany. They were on Germany's side. The only thing that made Russia shift sides in World War II was the German invasion. What did they do after World War II? They didn't liberate any country - they occupied. They just changed one occupation for another.
"Eastern Europe wasn't liberated before 1990 and 1991. That's the actual end of World War II, when the Russian occupation of Eastern Europe ended," he stresses.
They even talk about the northern parts of Northern Norway. In 1945, they did have designs. They wanted Svalbard and the northern islands. They had plans to take the regions closest to Norway, which were also part of the Soviet Union. They want everything they have ever had, and they want it back.
Trump has made no secret of his desire for the Nobel Peace Prize. Could the Committee deny Ukraine the award simply to avoid provoking him?
Trump has been nominated for the Peace Prize several times, but I don't think he really has a chance. What I did note is that last year's recipient, Mrs. Machado from Venezuela, was probably chosen partly due to it. I don't criticize the prize, as she is a democratically elected leader, a good candidate, and a good recipient.
"But I believe part of the reason she got it was that the Nobel Committee wanted a recipient who would not provoke President Trump," he says.
I consider that they are going to worry about that again, about whether the recipient is going to provoke Trump or not. You never know what his reaction will be anyway. I don't think they really see him as a serious candidate — someone who just started an immense war in Iran, drawing the whole world economy down.
My nomination has gone viral — there are thousands of posts online. I usually don't get 750,000 views on my Facebook posts, but I did with my post about Ukraine. I really do believe that Zelenskyy and Ukraine are the most worthy recipients at this point in time.
If continuing the war means more Ukrainians will die, why not negotiate to stop the killing? Zelenskyy says Ukraine plans to fight further. Does it bring peace, really?
It does. Look at Norway in 1940. It was peace, but it wasn't peace. It was an occupation. It was killing, it was murder, and even worse in other parts of Europe. What happened in Norway was nothing compared to what happened in Poland, the Baltics, Ukraine, and Belarus.
Thank God the current Western leaders understand this: they are not going to force Ukraine to give up, to let millions of people live under horrible occupation, and give up more land. They stand by Ukraine now, and I hope they will support it even more, especially Norway.

articles.title: Russia is out to break Ukraine’s economy this winter, Jetten says—and the Netherlands will help keep Ukraine’s drone-hunting F-16s in the air
articles.body:
The Netherlands will help Ukraine with maintenance, spare parts, and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten promised in a statement on 5 October. He made this and other statements following a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Russia attacks Ukrainian cities with drones every day, increasingly with jet-powered ones. F-16 fighter jets are one of the effective options for shooting down these UAVs, but Ukraine has far too few of them. The F-16s are used very frequently and therefore require maintenance. About half of the aircraft spend extended periods abroad undergoing repairs and maintenance, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times this month. The process of returning the aircraft has taken too long, and Ukraine has lost time when the jets were most needed to protect Ukrainian airspace, he said.
“A further strengthening of Ukraine’s air defense is literally vital,” the prime minister said.
Russia’s aggression continues to escalate, and F-16 fighter jets can help stop it
Russia is deliberately attacking civilian facilities and energy infrastructure and wants to make Ukrainian cities uninhabitable, Jetten said, adding that “we must not allow this to happen.”
One effective solution is the use of F-16 fighter jets, while Ukraine faces shortages of both these aircraft and the missiles for them.
Ukrainian F-16 pilots lack air-to-air missiles and take off with only the aircraft’s cannon during some daytime missions, the War Zone reported on 2 September. The M61A1 Vulcan 20mm rotary cannon can pose a danger to civilians on the ground, the outlet noted.
Poland promised to provide Ukraine with F-16 missiles back in September, and several partners, including Poland, have already begun the process of transferring ammunition this month. Other partners include Spain and Belgium, which Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha mentioned during a meeting with journalists, Hromadske reported on 1 October.
Ukraine critically needs this ammunition, especially as Russia prepares new strikes, Sybiha said.
“Against the backdrop of the fact that we have not yet built up the capability to repel jet-powered drones, against the backdrop of preparations for new strikes, it was critically important to help our military shoot down these drones. The most effective right now—apart from air defense systems, which are very expensive to use constantly against drones—are F-16 fighter jets,” the minister said.
Zelenskyy held talks with the president of France and the prime ministers of Poland and the Netherlands about means of protecting against Russian strikes, he said in his address on 5 October. In particular, he thanked the Dutch prime minister for his prompt response.
Whether Belgian maintenance delays are the reason for the low number of operational F-16s in Ukraine remains disputed
Fewer than 50% of the F-16s delivered to Ukraine may be operational, Defense Express reports, citing a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) editorial published on 29 September.
The Belgian company that services F-16s for Ukraine takes as long as 40 weeks to complete the work, retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery told the WSJ.
That day, Zelenskyy had already announced that Belgium would send three of its fighter jets to Ukraine this year. Ukraine will receive them under an accelerated procedure, he said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs refutes claims that Ukrainian fighter jets have a catastrophically low operational availability rate and excessively long maintenance times.
“Contrary to these claims, our industrial sustainment partners are not only continuing to deliver overhauled aircraft, but are doing so at an increasing pace. Turnaround times are decreasing, not increasing,” Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on 2 October.
Reports about the condition of Ukraine’s F-16s should not undermine confidence in international funding supporting F-16 maintenance or cast doubt on the need for additional F-16s from the stockpiles of partner countries, Tykhyi warned.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv claims half of Russia’s oil refining capacity destroyed
articles.body:
- Long-range Ukrainian strikes have taken out more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow’s ability to supply its forces during the war, the defence ministry in Kyiv has claimed. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly attacked refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict petrol sales. “Fifty-one per cent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings,” Ukrainian defence minister Yevhenii Khmara said. “Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory.”
- Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country’s oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes’ economic impact, Vladimir Putin said they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. “They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” the Russian president told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts last Thursday.
- Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for high petrol prices, saying the Iran war was no longer responsible. “What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the strait of Hormuz, because Record Numbers of Barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘Refineries,’ where Russia’s are being blown up by Ukraine,” the US president posted on his Truth Social platform.
- Six people were killed and nearly 60 injured when Russian bombs struck a residential area of Ukraine’s north-eastern city of Kharkiv on Monday, officials said. Rescue workers led stunned residents out of badly damaged buildings and flats, guiding them carefully around piles of rubble. Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, lies close to the Russian border and has come under regular shelling and drone attacks since Moscow invaded in February 2022. French president Emmanuel Macron condemned Russia’s decision to scale up strikes on civilian infrastructure, saying Moscow “has made the irresponsible choice to intensify its strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets”.
- Russian drones struck a grain ship in the Black Sea on Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, after Romania reported a ship had caught fire and sunk near its coast with two crew members killed. “A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn,” the Ukrainian president said on X, adding that the ship was Turkish-owned and that Azerbaijani and Indian nationals were onboard. Romanian authorities said two crew members had died and 11 were rescued after the 139-metre-long (455 foot) Royad Mammadov caught fire in the Black Sea, an increasing battlefield for drone attacks in the war. War-related objects found in the Black Sea had more than doubled in six months, maritime risk expert Ambrey said last month in a report. At least a third of them carried live payloads. The objects include unexploded ordnance, drones and other unmanned vehicles found washed ashore or floating at sea, it said.
- Ukrainian drones attacked two facilities at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in south-eastern Ukraine overnight on Monday, but there was no threat to nuclear safety, the head of Russia’s state nuclear corporation said. Alexei Likhachev, director general of Rosatom, said a driver delivering food for plant employees was killed in the drone attack. According to Likhachev, a laboratory building and a radioactive waste processing plant were the targets. Ukraine has not commented on the incident.
- Ukraine has begun using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to take down Russia’s new and fast-moving jet-powered drones. For months, Kyiv has been seeking a way to intercept the new Russian drones pounding the Ukrainian capital, even as it faces a dire lack of suitable ammunition to take them out. Presidential adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said on social media that 12 automated turrets had been installed in Kyiv to counter jet-powered Shahed drones, with more planned. Ukraine’s air force later said it had used the robotic turrets to successfully shoot down Russian jet-powered drones, including the Geran-5, for the first time. “It’s machine vision that is used for the shootdowns,” air force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Ukrainian television. “Artificial intelligence makes it possible to engage even jet-powered drones.”
- Germany’s foreign intelligence chief has warned that the country risks being drawn into a conflict with Russia as hybrid attacks ordered by Moscow increase. Martin Jaeger, head of Germany’s BND spy service, told lawmakers on Monday that Russia’s undeclared “shadow war” against Germany and its allies was escalating further and has “taken on a new, more dangerous character”. Berlin has invested record sums into rebuilding its military to deter Russia, and is among the largest supporters of Ukraine in the war with Moscow. In Brussels, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia was putting lives at risk across Europe with hybrid attacks.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Kharkiv devastated by Russian glide bombs, children among victims
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Kharkiv devastated by Russian glide bombs, children among victims
Key developments on Oct. 5:
- Children among dozens injured as Russian glide bombs hit Kharkiv, 5 dead
- New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
- Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says
- Ukrainian pilots to soon start training on French Rafale jets, Zelensky says

At least five people have been killed, and 53 others, including children, injured after Russian forces struck Kharkiv with glide bombs on Oct. 5.
"The enemy attacked Kharkiv with at least three glide bombs (KABs), with strikes recorded in the Slobidskyi district," Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a post on Telegram.
"As a result of the strikes… warehouse buildings are on fire, and residential buildings have been damaged. There may be people under the rubble of a residential building that was hit in the attack. A search and rescue operation is underway," he added.
Russian glide bombs, often called KABs (Kerovana Aviabomba) in Ukraine, are repurposed aerial bombs equipped with wings and precision guidance systems such as GPS, laser, or infrared targeting.
read also
New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
Automated machine gun turrets using artificial intelligence to aim have downed their first Russian jet-powered drones over Ukraine, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Oct. 5.
A day prior, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that twelve such turrets had been installed where Russian jet-powered drones have been particularly active, including around Kyiv.
"There are already cases of shooting down even jet UAVs, even 'Geran-5' from the those very turrets," Ihnat said on national television.
"The use of innovative technologies — artificial intelligence — has eliminated human error. Machine vision is used in the shooting down. Artificial intelligence allows you to target even jet-powered drones."
Since Russia started using jet-powered drones en masse against Kyiv toward the end of summer this year, they, especially the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, have presented an air defense problem for which Ukraine has not yet found a single solution.
read also
Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says
A cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast on Oct. 5 after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
At the time of the attack, the ship was sailing outside Romania's territorial waters but within the country's exclusive economic zone, about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) from the Romanian coast and roughly 9 nautical miles (16.6 kilometers) southeast of the Pescarus offshore oil platform operated by OMV Petrom, according to Romanian media outlet Digi24.ro. First reports had placed the incident near the Neptun Deep gas development.
read also
Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border amid shift in strategic thinking
Estonia's 1st Brigade, the main combat-ready element of the country's land forces, will be moving to a newly expanded base less than 50 kilometers from the Russian border, placed to better meet a possible Russian attack.
The move, revealed in comments by the unit's commander, Tarmo Kundla, published in the Financial Times on Oct. 5, comes amid increased awareness of Russian military designs on the Baltic country.
The 1st Brigade will relocate from its previous base in Tapa to the town of Johvi, just west of the city of Narva on the Russian border.
Narva is often seen as a potential flashpoint of hybrid or kinetic attacks not only due to its location, but because the majority of its population is Russian-speaking, a common tool of Russian propaganda to justify aggression.
According to Kundla, the brigade's move is connected to a shift in strategic thinking for the Estonian military, which relies on the airpower of NATO forces based in the region — as well as on the deterrent of the alliance's Article 5 — to protect against an attack from its much larger neighbor.
read also
Ukrainian pilots to soon start training on French Rafale jets, Zelensky says
President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed further European assistance in phone calls with the French and Polish leaders on Oct. 5, as Ukraine braces for a new wave of Russian attacks while U.S.-led peace talks fail to make headway.
Zelensky revealed after his call with French President Emmanuel Macron that France is preparing fresh defense assistance for Ukraine amid relentless Russian strikes, with a new support package expected "soon."
"Ukrainian pilots will soon begin training on French Rafale aircraft in France. This is a significant step forward for Ukraine's combat aviation," he added.
Kyiv announced in 2025 that it aims to purchase 100 Rafale jets to bolster its growing fleet of Western-made aircraft. The Rafale is a 4.5-generation multirole fighter, considered one of the most advanced among European jets.
France is Ukraine's staunch ally in its war against Russian aggression and has provided Kyiv with long-range missiles and intelligence support, among other assistance.
Zelensky said that both sides are also "continuing to work on localizing the production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine."

articles.title: Yemen conflict escalating into regional war
articles.body:
Yemen conflict escalating into regional war
Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched a major offensive against the Iranian-backed Houthis, with both sides claiming territorial gains as battles rage around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait connecting the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
The escalation comes after the Houthis took over the key territory around Bab el-Mandeb in September, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints, which has gained particular significance amid disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz caused by the US-Iran war.
On Monday, the Yemeni army claimed to have pushed north along the Red Sea coast toward Mocha, while announcing “a strategic offensive operation on Sanaa,” which serves as the de facto capital of the Houthi movement.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, agreed with Türkiye and Pakistan to rapidly deploy military forces under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, also known as the “Muslim NATO.” The coalition already announced that 100 warplanes are supporting the Yemeni offensive.
The Houthis have denied the government gains, claiming to have made headway around Taiz, some 80km from the Red Sea coast. The group has also retaliated with ballistic missiles and drones against Saudi targets, claiming strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, military bases, and Aramco oil facilities, including the Rabigh refinery. Saudi Arabia has confirmed damage from Houthi attacks on airports at Jizan and Najran.
The Houthis have consistently accused Riyadh of waging an “aggression” and blockade against Yemen, arguing that Saudi military operations serve US and Israeli interests. Their Yemeni opponents, meanwhile, view Houthis – who identify themselves as part of the “Axis of Resistance” – as “terrorists” and insurgents who overthrew the internationally recognized government in 2014.
The conflict in Yemen in its current form began when the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa more than a decade ago, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention. However, fighting largely subsided after a 2022 truce.
Amid the fighting in Yemen and continued US-Iran standoff, US President Donald Trump argued that record gas prices are being driven not by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz but by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
- 06 October 2026 14:38 GMT Pakistan is “fully on board” with military support for Saudi Arabia and has taken Houthi warnings seriously, veteran Pakistani newspaper editor Kaswar Klasra told RT, pointing to repeated visits by Pakistan’s military chief to Riyadh and Istanbul and Islamabad’s pledge to defend the kingdom. “The Saudi conflict is not only between Saudi Arabia and Houthis,” Klasra said, arguing that the Mecca pact makes Pakistan a party to the confrontation and also involves Türkiye.
- 14:13 GMT LU Yemen has become “a kind of Vietnam for Saudi Arabia,” political scientist Dr. Mehmet Rakipoglu told RT, arguing that Riyadh has failed to defeat the Houthis despite a decade of military involvement. He cautioned that activating the Mecca defense pact does not mean automatic deployment, stressing that Türkiye and Pakistan have agreed to send forces to Saudi Arabia, rather than Yemen. Rakipoglu described Ankara’s approach as “strategic patience,” arguing that it wants to determine the timing and form of any confrontation on its own terms.
- 13:29 GMT More than 270 Yemeni government troops and Iran-backed Houthi fighters have been killed over the past 24 hours as hostilities escalate, sources on both sides told AFP on Tuesday. The outlet reported, citing anonymous government officials, that Yemen’s forces lost 115 troops, with dozens more wounded in fighting, as well as Houthi missile and drone attacks.
- 13:12 GMT Senior Houthi political official and spokesperson Mohammed al-Bukhaiti has denied Yemeni government claims of recapturing Mocha and securing Bab el-Mandeb. He told RT that opposing forces briefly advanced near Dhubab airport, north of the strait, but were subsequently driven back. “The enemy never reached the Bab el-Mandeb area,” he said, adding that government forces had not entered Mocha either. He argued that the offensive would prompt the Houthis to expand their control around the strait to establish a buffer zone.
- 13:12 GMT Pakistan and Türkiye should stay out of the conflict or face a Houthi response, senior Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti has told RT following the activation of Islamabad and Ankara’s collective-defense commitments with Saudi Arabia. “We will be forced to defend ourselves against any participation from any other country, whether Islamic or non-Islamic, Arab or non-Arab,” he said, urging both governments to reconsider and arguing that foreign involvement would not shift the military balance in Riyadh’s favor.
- 12:42 GMT The Houthis will “meet escalation with escalation” and could expand attacks to more Saudi airports, al-Bukhaiti has told RT. “The door to escalation remains open to target other airports,” he said, urging international airlines to heed warnings for their safety. He also warned employees of Saudi state oil giant Aramco to stay away from the company’s facilities.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine Securing New Air Defense Contracts, Scouring Globe for F-16 Ammo

Ukraine is moving to strengthen its air defenses as Kyiv races to shield critical infrastructure against intensifying Russian strikes, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday.
“We are preparing new contracts for air defense systems and missiles,” Zelensky said during his evening address, adding that details remain under wraps but “there may be some positive steps.”

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Ukrainian leader, Kyiv is strengthening its defenses daily with additional gun turrets, specialized Shahed-hunting teams and increased production of interceptor systems.
“We expect manufacturers to move quickly on interceptors. The tasks have been defined, and the funding is available,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president also appealed to Kyiv’s international partners for additional anti-ballistic capabilities, describing the protection of critical infrastructure as the country’s most pressing air-defense challenge.
“We need more anti-ballistic capabilities to protect infrastructure specifically. This is the main challenge right now,” he said.
The push comes after Ukraine and Germany signed 15 defense agreements worth more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion) on Sunday, covering air defense missiles, drones, radar systems, Patriot ammunition and protection of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Kyiv has also previously signed contracts for approximately 1,000 Patriot missiles, while Germany pledged additional interceptors from its own military stocks. The effort is aimed at strengthening Ukraine’s missile reserves as Russia continues targeting the country’s energy and civilian infrastructure.

Alongside ground-based air defenses, Ukraine is searching worldwide for ammunition for its F-16 fighter jets.
Zelensky described the US-made aircraft as one of Ukraine’s most effective tools for intercepting Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones.
“We are now sourcing munitions for F-16s virtually all over the world,” Zelensky said. “Packages are already on the way, and there will be more, so that our aircraft have what they need to protect our cities.”

Russia Is Fortifying Key Bridges Against Ukrainian Ballistic Missile Strikes, Partisans Say
Russian authorities have begun urgently reinforcing key road and rail bridges used to supply troops, preparing them for possible Ukrainian ballistic missile strikes, according to the ATESH partisan movement on October 6.
ATESH said its agents in the Rostov region’s road administration learned that civilian agencies and military authorities received instructions from the headquarters of Russia’s Southern Military District to strengthen major logistics nodes and prepare alternative routes if bridges are damaged.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the group, Russia’s federal road agency, Russian Railways, and regional administrations received the orders. The measures focus on crossings considered critical to moving ammunition, fuel, equipment, and personnel toward Russian forces operating against Ukraine.
In the Rostov region, work is reportedly underway to reinforce both highway and railway bridges across the Don River while preparing backup routes that could be used if the main crossings are disabled. Similar measures are being introduced along the Taganrog axis, ATESH said.
Russian forces are also reportedly expecting renewed Ukrainian strikes around Syvash and Armyansk on the route toward occupied Crimea. In the Belgorod region, bridges near Shelayevo and Urazovo are being placed on heightened readiness, with Russian planners reportedly concerned that precision strikes on relatively small crossings could sharply slow logistics and force military traffic onto a limited number of detours.
The planned protection measures include round-the-clock posts staffed by Russia’s National Guard and military commandant units, anti-drone nets, electronic warfare systems, and engineering teams prepared to repair damaged infrastructure. Russian authorities are also reportedly organizing pontoon crossings that could serve as temporary replacements if permanent bridges are knocked out.
“Bridges remain the main supply arteries of the Russian army. Damaging them blocks the delivery of fuel, ammunition, and personnel,” ATESH said.
The reported preparations suggest Russian commanders are increasingly concerned not only about Ukrainian drones and cruise missiles, but also about Kyiv’s expanding ballistic strike capabilities. Bridges are particularly sensitive targets because even localized damage can disrupt large transport networks, force convoys onto predictable alternative routes, and create bottlenecks well behind the front.
ATESH’s claims have not been independently verified, but the measures described by the group would point to a broader Russian effort to make critical logistics infrastructure more resilient as Ukraine expands the range and variety of weapons available for deep strikes.
Previously, Ukrainian forces have marked the first successful operational deployment of the domestically developed FP-7 tactical ballistic missile during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Saudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in Yemen
articles.body:
Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said on Monday.
The officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government have retaken the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait. They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.
The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under an air cover by a Saudi military coalition, aiming to retake all territory held by the Houthis.
However, the offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the south-western part of Yemen, taking the key town of Turbah in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward the strategic provincial capital of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.
The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.
Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, the US secretary of state said that Saudi Arabia and the US had a defense agreement but would not offer more details.
He said the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis had come under attack, and “they have a right to defend themselves”.
The new push sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at the Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in the Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Lithuanian parliament backs removing constitutional ban on nuclear weapons
articles.body:
Lithuania’s parliament voted Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on weapons of mass destruction from the country’s constitution, potentially opening the way for allied nuclear weapons to be stationed in Lithuania.
The amendment passed its first reading with 106 lawmakers voting in favour, 18 against and six abstaining.
A final vote cannot be held until at least three months after Tuesday’s vote. The amendment will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of the Seimas to pass. Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas has said the final vote is scheduled for January 12.
Olekas said before the vote that removing the ban would strengthen Lithuania’s resilience and deterrence capabilities.
He said eliminating the restriction would also remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other European Union and NATO countries.
“We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us,” Olekas said. “By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal.”
Opposition conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas urged lawmakers to support the amendment, saying neighbouring countries do not have similar restrictions. He argued that the existing constitutional provision prevents NATO allies from fully including Lithuania in the alliance’s nuclear deterrence planning.
“With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” Kasčiūnas said. “Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of deterrence as a whole, this decision is strategically important.”
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas also stressed the importance of deterrence, saying politicians should provide the country with every available tool to ensure its security.
Kaunas said Lithuania is surrounded by countries with strategic weapons, pointing to Russia’s Kaliningrad region and Belarus. He described the proposed constitutional change as a response to Moscow’s actions.
“We are responding to Russia’s aggression,” Kaunas said. “If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions we are having today.”
Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution currently states that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment would remove that provision.
Opponents call for referendum
The amendment faced its strongest opposition from lawmakers in the opposition Nemunas Dawn party. Fourteen party members voted against it and two abstained.
Aidas Gedvilas of Nemunas Dawn said he was surprised that parliament considered itself empowered to make such a fundamental change and called for a referendum.
“There are certainly alternatives to this constitutional provision. We could resolve this through a referendum,” Gedvilas said.
Three members of the mixed parliamentary group and one lawmaker from the Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance also voted against the amendment.
The debate comes amid broader discussions in Europe about strengthening nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron presented an idea in March for a new European nuclear deterrence framework under which partner countries could temporarily host France’s nuclear-capable strategic air forces.
The Financial Times reported in June that the United States was considering deploying nuclear weapons in several additional NATO countries in Europe.
Lithuanian military analysts have said Russian media has taken an interest in Lithuania’s plans to remove the constitutional ban.
In early September, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned that Lithuania could become a target for Russia if it allowed allies to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory.
Reactions from Moscow
The Kremlin warned Tuesday that the deployment of nuclear weapons or a permanent US military base in Lithuania would constitute an escalation and force Russia to take measures to protect its security.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian state media.
“A military base is part of military infrastructure. If someone’s military infrastructure – in fact, that of a major NATO member – is approaching our borders, of course, this can only be viewed as a step toward escalation,” Peskov said at a news conference.
“The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighbouring country,” he added.
Peskov was asked how Moscow would respond if Lithuania moved to lift its constitutional ban on deploying nuclear weapons while the United States considered establishing a permanent base there.
“All this will not help ensure stability and predictability on the European continent,” Peskov said. “On the contrary, to our regret, it would be another very significant escalation.”
“As for Russia, of course, Russia will have to take all necessary measures to guarantee its security,” he said.
Lithuanian officials have stressed that there are currently no plans to deploy nuclear weapons in the country. They say removing the constitutional restriction is intended to ensure that Lithuania does not face legal obstacles to participating in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements.

articles.title: Lithuanian PM Warns Europe Against Ukraine War Fatigue
articles.body:
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius warned Europe against growing tired of the war in Ukraine, saying Ukrainians are fighting for peace across the continent, while a Russian victory could push Moscow to seek “other directions.”
“We cannot have war fatigue. We are not the ones at war. They are, and they are fighting for Europe’s peace,” Sinkevičius said, according to Politico.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The rest of Europe is coming to the point of acknowledging that we cannot ignore what is happening in Leipzig, Denmark, and elsewhere,” Sinkevičius told Germany’s WELT in comments on Monday, Oct. 5.
The Lithuanian leader said Russian activities once viewed primarily as a threat to NATO’s eastern members were now spreading across the continent.
“It is not a question of proximity,” he said, pointing to drone incursions, GPS interference, sabotage attacks, and Russia’s weaponization of migration through Belarus.
Concrete NATO response
Sinkevičius argued that political condemnation alone is insufficient as Russia increasingly employs operations that remain below the threshold of conventional war.
“NATO is trying to address it politically. What we need is a concrete plan for how the Alliance reacts,” he said, adding that he hoped such a plan would emerge soon.
He did not publicly specify what should automatically trigger a NATO response or what form retaliation should take.
Lithuania has previously called for greater joint investment in air and missile defenses, cybersecurity, border surveillance, and the protection of critical infrastructure.
Russia Strikes Kryvyi Rih Hospital, 3 Wounded
The government in Vilnius describes Russian hybrid operations as a systematic campaign against NATO rather than a series of unrelated incidents.
Recent cases include the attempted explosive-drone attack at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle Airport, which Berlin formally attributed to Russia, as well as drone incursions and suspected sabotage across Europe.
European intelligence assessments also indicate that Moscow has ordered an intensification of hybrid operations targeting military facilities, transport networks, communications infrastructure, and other strategic sites.
Russia has repeatedly denied conducting sabotage or preparing attacks against NATO members.
Article 5 threshold
Hybrid operations create a particular problem for NATO because they are designed to cause damage while maintaining uncertainty over who was responsible and whether the incident qualifies as an armed attack.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said the alliance deliberately avoids announcing the precise threshold for activating Article 5, its collective-defense clause, so adversaries cannot calculate how far they can escalate without triggering a joint response.
Since 2016, the alliance has maintained that a sufficiently serious hybrid operation could lead NATO members to invoke Article 5, although any decision would be made collectively and depend on the circumstances.
Rutte recently described the term “hybrid attack” as too mild for operations involving drones, sabotage, and cyberattacks. He said NATO possesses both public and undisclosed response options and does not necessarily have to retaliate in kind.
NATO is also developing broader plans to confront a possible Russian attack by combining conventional forces with drones, artificial intelligence, and integrated battlefield systems.
Lithuania’s warning
Sinkevičius warned that a Russian victory in Ukraine could encourage Moscow to search for “other directions” for expansion or pressure.
He urged European governments not to become fatigued by the war, stressing that Ukrainians were fighting not only for their country but also for peace across Europe.
The Lithuanian prime minister also said Russian President Vladimir Putin had successfully subordinated much of Russia’s economy to the war, making the Kremlin more difficult to predict despite its internal economic problems.

articles.title: Ukraine’s battlefield gains may be pushing Putin to shift focus to early winter strikes, ISW says
articles.body:
Ukraine's battlefield successes appear to be forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to reevaluate his theory of victory and shift focus toward long-range strikes to compel Ukraine to surrender, rather than advances on the battlefield, the Institute for the Study of War said on 4 October.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia used more than 800 jet-powered drones during the week of 27 September to 4 October. Ukraine currently intercepts only 50–60% of jet-powered drones, leaving it vulnerable to the large number of new drones Russia is deploying.
The late-September start and the campaign's aim
ISW said Russian forces began their winter 2026–27 strike campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure in late September and that the campaign is aimed at making civilian life unbearable enough to force Ukraine to capitulate.
Russian forces would step up attacks on military facilities, defense industry sites, and related infrastructure in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry said on 4 October, according to Reuters. The announcement followed Zelenskyy's vow to increase attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The ministry also claimed its recent strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions were a response to alleged Ukrainian attacks on civilian targets inside Russia. Among the grievances it named were Ukraine's strikes on Leningrad Oblast during the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in June and alleged strikes on electoral infrastructure in Moscow during the 18–20 September State Duma elections, according to ISW.
ISW called the Russian Defense Ministry's framing of the recent strikes as retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian targets unfounded, saying many of its specific claims are "blatantly false." Russia has provided no evidence that Ukraine targeted electoral infrastructure, and Ukraine's 19–20 September strikes on Moscow targeted oil refineries and warehouses, the think tank said. The Russian strikes "are not an actual response to specific events," it concluded.
The 135 drones, the bridges struck seven times
Overnight on 3–4 October, Russia launched 135 Shahed-type and Gerbera-type drones, while also using decoy drones and Banderol or Dan-T loitering munitions. Ukrainian forces downed 123 drones and two loitering munitions, and strikes hit five locations, according to ISW, which cited the Ukrainian Air Force. Russian forces struck Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges seven times between 1 and 4 October in an effort to disrupt Ukraine's economy and daily civilian life, ISW said.
Ukraine builds new layers of defense against jet drones
More than 12 .50-caliber machine-gun turrets are already working in Kyiv against jet-powered drones, and eight more will be installed in Kyiv Oblast, Zelenskyy said, Suspilne reported. He added that F-16s help a lot against the drones, according to Ukrinform. Ukraine is set to receive 2,000 Bars interceptor drones through joint production with Germany, RBC-Ukraine reported.
Ballistic missiles may be Russia's next wave
Zelenskyy said Ukraine estimates Russia has up to 700 ballistic missiles in reserve and produces 130–140 a month. He made the remarks at a joint media briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv, Ukrinform reported. Russia is likely stockpiling ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles for intense strikes after its jet-powered drones lose their current advantage, ISW assessed. ISW also cited an ongoing shortage of Patriot interceptors.
OHCHR has verified some 15,280 civilian casualties in Ukraine in the first eight months of 2026, 55% more than in the same period of 2025, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said on 2 October.

articles.title: ‘Muslim NATO’ activates force deployment over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
‘Muslim NATO’ activates force deployment over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
A three-nation military alliance dubbed the “Muslim NATO” has activated its collective-defense commitments and ordered the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia amid an escalating confrontation with Yemen’s Houthis.
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan made the decision at an emergency meeting of the Mecca Defense Alliance in Riyadh on Monday after a series of Houthi attacks. In a joint statement they condemned the “attempted targeting” of the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, as well as attacks on Saudi cities and civilian and economic infrastructure.
The group decided to “move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments” and take measures to provide agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their “rapid deployment” in Saudi Arabia. It said the move was intended to boost military readiness and integration and strengthen the three countries’ “collective capacity to confront and counter threats.”
The Emergency Meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee under the Makkah Alliance for Defense reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom and the holy sites. The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the Alliance in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them.
— Khalid bin Salman خالد بن سلمان (@kbsalsaud) October 5, 2026
The alliance was formed in August under an agreement treating an armed attack on any member as an attack on all three, mirroring NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense principle.

Yemen’s civil war has escalated sharply in recent weeks. A Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognized government said on Monday that 100 fighter jets were taking part in Operation Dawn of Yemen, providing air cover for ground forces. Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said 324 “high-value targets” had been destroyed.
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, are a Shiite armed group that has controlled the Yemeni capital of Sanaa and much of northern Yemen for more than a decade. They have accused Riyadh of carrying out extensive airstrikes and hitting civilian targets.
Yemen’s government announced a new campaign on Sunday aimed at retaking all Houthi-held territory. The move followed major gains by the group in September, when it captured swathes of the Red Sea coast and territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route.
Government forces said on Monday that they had retaken several areas around the strait, including the town of Dhubab, which sits strategically along the strait. The Houthis have disputed reports of government advances.
The renewed fighting has killed hundreds of combatants on both sides and forced more than 145,000 people from their homes since September, according to UN figures.
Saudi Arabia first intervened in Yemen in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government after the Houthis had driven it from Sanaa the previous year. Large-scale fighting decreased significantly following a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
Fighting escalated again last month. The Houthis have accused Riyadh of imposing an illegal siege on Yemen, while Saudi Arabia says the group has stepped up missile, drone, and maritime attacks against the kingdom itself and shipping in the Red Sea.
The escalation comes as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed to most shipping and US-Iranian talks on ending the conflict have stalled.
Several Saudi allies have stepped up military support for the kingdom. Britain has agreed to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi warplanes, while France is sending troops, radar, and air-defense systems to help protect the Red Sea oil hub of Yanbu.

articles.title: Ukraine wants to aim Starlink at Russian targets—and build a version Elon Musk can’t switch off
articles.body:
Ukraine is working on a satellite system of its own, something similar to SpaceX's Starlink, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 4 October, Interfax-Ukraine reported. He argued Kyiv should be free to turn Starlink on Russian military targets, warning that China and other states will share comparable satellite technology with Moscow within months. Ukraine's battlefield communications still ride on a network owned by Elon Musk, who has clashed with Kyiv and once limited its wartime use.
Low-orbit satellite internet has turned into a frontline utility that a single company or government can switch on or off, and both armies are now racing to own that link instead of renting it. Control of the network decides whose drones can see the battlefield and fly through the jamming to strike it—leverage Kyiv has gone without while its connection rode on hardware it does not run.
Working on a Starlink of its own
Zelenskyy said there was groundwork in place and that Ukraine was working on a system similar to Starlink. He called it fair for Ukraine to aim Starlink at military sites inside Russia. The timing is the reason, he said: some states will share the technology with Russia late this year or early next, and the Chinese are among them. Moscow is already fielding its own Starlink-style constellation, Rassvet, though for now it reaches Ukraine only in brief passes.
Ukrainian brigades detail Starlink crackdown: Russian terminals “became just bricks,” assaults disrupted
Ukraine's troops and drones lean heavily on Starlink, a network Kyiv neither owns nor controls. Musk has used that control against Kyiv before: in 2022 SpaceX refused a Ukrainian request to extend Starlink over occupied Crimea for a drone strike on Russia's warships, and it has since restricted the network's use for drone operations.
Sanctions, and satellites of its own
Zelenskyy has asked US President Donald Trump several times to sanction the Russian and Chinese companies building Russia's Rassvet network, most recently at the UN General Assembly in New York, he said in a recent Financial Times interview.
The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. Experts call that the gap that matters
Denys Shtilerman, co-founder and chief designer at Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, told the Financial Times in May that the firm had launched two satellites this year and planned dozens more in 2027, aiming to reduce reliance on the US government and Western tech companies. To strike deep inside Russia and gather intelligence, he has said, Ukraine needs its own constellation covering all of Russia.
