articles.title: Ansarallah sets Aramco sites ablaze as mercenaries commit war crimes in Yemen
articles.body:
Ansarallah sets Aramco sites ablaze as mercenaries commit war crimes in Yemen
TEHRAN — Yemeni armed forces fired a coordinated salvo of heavy ballistic missiles and long-range attack drones deep into the Saudi interior on Monday and Sunday, striking major Saudi Aramco installations in Jeddah, Riyadh, and the Khurais oil field.
The precision retaliatory operations ignited massive fires near strategic energy infrastructure, triggered civil defense alerts in Mecca and Taif, and forced flight cancellations across Saudi commercial airports.
Ansarallah official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti warned international airlines that Saudi airspace remains unsafe while the aggression continues.
Footage of burning Aramco sites has been broadcast, and satellite fire-detection data have corroborated blazes in Jeddah and south of Riyadh.
Yemeni military spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Saree confirmed that these strikes answered more than 50 Saudi air raids launched against civilian centers in Sanaa, Saada, Al-Jawf, and Taiz within a single twelve-hour period.
Mercenary war crimes at Dhubab Airport
While Saudi-backed media promoted tactical movements along the western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaked video footage exposed the lawless conduct of foreign-funded proxies.
Verified recordings filmed at Dhubab Airport show members of the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council and UAE-funded Southern Giants Brigades forces committing severe war crimes against captured Ansarallah prisoners of war.
The footage shows heavy military vehicles driving intentionally over bound captives, summary executions of unarmed detainees, and the gross mutilation of corpses. These visual records document grave breaches of international humanitarian law and highlight the total collapse of discipline among Riyadh’s auxiliary troops.
On the ground, claims by Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi regarding gains in Dhubab remain fragile and short-lived.
Historical experience across Taiz, Hodeidah, and Al-Jawf suggests that foreign-backed formations consistently crumble once immediate air support subsides.
Just last month, Yemeni forces demonstrated their tactical agility by liberating Mocha, Dhubab, and Perim Island in an eighteen-hour coastal push. Similar coalition offensives in 2018 stalled completely, and current frontline reports confirm that Ansarallah units have maintained control over essential supply routes while preparing decisive counterattacks to reclaim temporary proxy gains.
Western collusion and strategic failure
This ongoing aggression relies heavily on direct intelligence and logistical support from Washington and Tel Aviv.
American military officials have supplied targeting data for over 200 sites inside Yemen, alongside more than 100 U.S. advisers operating with coalition command.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly offered military backing to support the campaign, following previous Israeli strikes on Sanaa leadership targets.
Yet years of advanced Western weaponry and foreign advice have failed to resolve Saudi Arabia’s core military vulnerabilities or secure its southern border.
The humanitarian cost of the Western-backed campaign continues to climb.
World Health Organization reports confirm over 5,000 casualties since August, alongside a threefold increase in cholera cases across targeted governorates.
Nevertheless, relentless aerial bombardment cannot protect Saudi energy infrastructure from long-range retaliation.
By establishing a direct equation between Saudi aggression and the vulnerability of Aramco facilities in Jeddah and Yanbu, Ansarallah has shattered the coalition’s security guarantees, proving that Riyadh cannot achieve through foreign airpower what it has failed to gain on the battlefield for over a decade.

articles.title: France Prepares First Submarine-Launched Nuclear-Capable Missile Test in Three Years
articles.body:

France Prepares First Submarine-Launched Nuclear-Capable Missile Test in Three Years
France is preparing its first submarine-launched ballistic missile test in three years, with the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Le Vigilant expected to fire the new M51.3 during a long-range trial over the Atlantic, according to French outlet Ouest-France on October 5.
Strategic weapons analyst Étienne Marcuz said the missile is expected to travel roughly 4,700 kilometers, or about 2,920 miles, although that distance is well below the weapon’s estimated maximum range.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The M51.3 will be launched without a nuclear warhead from waters off France’s Finistère coast, where maritime restrictions have already been imposed through October 21.
The test comes after Le Vigilant completed an extensive maintenance period that began in fall 2023 at France’s Île Longue strategic submarine base.
The overhaul included work on the vessel’s nuclear reactor, weapons systems, and other critical equipment. French ballistic missile submarines typically undergo sea trials after such major maintenance, with an M51 launch serving as one of the most important checks that the submarine’s strategic weapons complex is fully operational.
A similar test was carried out by Le Terrible in April 2023 following its own major refit. This time, however, France will be testing the newest operational version of its sea-based deterrent missile.
The M51.3 officially entered operational service in October 2025. Compared with earlier versions, the new variant is reported to offer improved range, greater accuracy, and better ability to penetrate missile defenses. It is also designed to carry France’s new TNO-2 nuclear warhead.
France conducted the first qualification launch of the M51.3 in November 2023 from a land-based test facility at Biscarrosse. That missile was also unarmed and flew toward the Atlantic Ocean.
The M51.3 is a three-stage, solid-fueled submarine-launched ballistic missile developed as the latest evolution of France’s M51 family. Paris does not disclose its exact performance, but earlier M51 versions have been estimated to reach approximately 8,000 to 10,000 kilometers, or roughly 5,000 to 6,200 miles, at speeds of up to Mach 25.
Previous M51.1 and M51.2 missiles could carry multiple thermonuclear warheads with individual yields estimated at roughly 110 to 300 kilotons. The M51.3 is believed to retain broadly similar dimensions to its predecessors, measuring around 12 meters long, 2.3 meters in diameter, and weighing roughly 52 metric tons.
The missile is also expected to become the primary strategic weapon of France’s future SNLE 3G ballistic missile submarines, which are scheduled to begin replacing the current Le Triomphant-class fleet after 2035. ArianeGroup develops and manufactures the M51 family.
Earlier, France’s Air and Space Force has rehearsed one of the country’s most consequential military missions: breaking through hostile defenses and delivering a nuclear-armed missile to a precise launch point using Rafale fighters.

articles.title: Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh airport
articles.body:
Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh airport
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed a direct missile strike on Riyadh’s main international airport as part of a large-scale barrage targeting airports, military bases, and oil infrastructure across Saudi Arabia.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Monday night that the group, officially known as Ansar Allah, carried out three operations using “a large number” of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones in response to intensified Saudi-backed strikes on Yemen.
The first attack targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and achieved a “direct and precise hit,” Saree claimed, saying air traffic was disrupted. The second targeted Saudi Aramco’s refinery in Rabigh, where the group claimed a direct hit started fires. The third operation reportedly targeted Abha Airport, Khamis Mushait air base, the Aqeefah military camp, and other “sensitive sites” in Najran and Jizan.
The Saudi authorities have not addressed the specific claims of direct hits on the airport and refinery or said whether Houthi strikes caused disruption at King Khalid. The Foreign Ministry issued a broader statement condemning continued Houthi attacks on Riyadh and several other Saudi cities and “civilian and economic facilities,” while reiterating the kingdom’s right to respond.
#Statement | The Foreign Ministry expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s strongest condemnation and denunciation of the terrorist Houthi militia’s continued targeting of civilians and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom; its blatant and repeated attacks against the holiest sites on earth—Makkah and Madinah— the capital Riyadh, and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, Najran, Taif, and Yanbu; and its targeting of Saudi vessels in the southern Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
— Foreign Ministry 🇸🇦 (@KSAmofaEN) October 5, 2026
Loud explosions were reportedly heard in northern Riyadh near King Khalid airport. An AFP journalist reported hearing a “powerful explosion,” and residents said blasts shook windows in the area.
Saudi Arabia’s Interior Ministry has renewed a warning that photographing, publishing, or circulating information about missile and drone interception operations or impact sites could result in legal action. The same warning was issued earlier in the war. Saudi media republished it shortly after midnight amid the latest attacks.
The Houthis warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace, declaring it a theater of military operations, while exempting the airspace over Mecca and Medina. King Khalid airport remains operational, but Flightradar24 data shows substantial delays, with average delays reaching 38 minutes.
The group said the barrage was retaliation for 60 Saudi air and missile strikes on Sanaa and the provinces of Al-Jawf, Taiz, Hodeidah, Saada, and Marib over the previous 24 hours, which it said caused civilian casualties. Saree claimed that Saudi forces conducted 1,576 strikes since the latest escalation began.
The exchange comes as Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies intensify a major counteroffensive against the Houthis. The Saudi-led coalition says around 100 fighter jets are providing round-the-clock air support as government forces attempt to retake territory lost along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. The coalition claims it destroyed 324 “high-value” Houthi targets.
Saudi-backed forces said on Monday that they recaptured Dhubab and the nearby towns of Bab and Hadeid, with witnesses telling AP they saw government tanks and troops entering the towns. The Houthis have denied reports of a broader retreat, while fighting has also intensified around Taiz.
The US is also assisting the Saudi campaign with intelligence sharing, target identification, and operational planning, American and regional officials told AP. The US Embassy in Riyadh has warned Americans to remain vigilant for missile and drone attacks.

articles.title: Ukraine Claims Record Barrage on Russia With 1,750 Drones, 17 Flamingo Missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine launched a record-breaking number of drones and missiles at targets across Russia over the past 24 hours on Tuesday, according to Russia’s defense ministry.
Russian air defenses claimed to have intercepted and destroyed 1,750 fixed-wing drones and 17 Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles, as well as two guided aerial bombs and a US-made HIMARS rocket.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The reported drone total exceeds the previous record of 1,671 Ukrainian drones claimed by Russia on Aug. 18, when attacks were reported across 15 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
The number of Flamingo missiles reported over the 24-hour period is also unprecedented. Russia had previously claimed to intercept no more than three to six Flamingos in a single day.
The figures have not been independently verified.
Moscow among the main targets
The record-breaking barrage included repeated attacks on Moscow and the surrounding region.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones were heading toward the capital early on Oct. 6, with 105 destroyed as they approached the city. He later reported another 68 drones intercepted by air defenses.
Moscow Region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 drones were destroyed across 16 municipalities.
According to Vorobyov, two people were killed and nine injured. Forty-seven private homes were damaged in several towns, while an apartment building in Lobanovo, near Domodedovo, was also hit.
Major oil facility targeted
Among the reported targets was the Volodarskaya Linear Production and Dispatch Station, a major Transneft facility and one of the Moscow region’s key fuel-storage and distribution hubs.
Power Cuts Return After Russian Strikes Damage Grid
The facility handles up to 3 million metric tons of petroleum products annually, including gasoline, jet fuel and diesel supplied from the Moscow and Ryazan refineries. Some of the fuel is delivered to airports serving the Moscow aviation hub.
The extent of any damage to the facility was not immediately clear.
The scale of the attack also disrupted air travel across Moscow. More than 200 flights were reportedly delayed or canceled at the capital’s airports from midnight.
The Sheremetyevo airport saw the largest disruption, with around 47 departures and 106 arrivals affected. The Vnukovo airport reported disruptions to 28 departing and 23 arriving flights, while four flights were affected at the Domodedovo airport.

articles.title: Ursa Major lands $91M to power a mini missile for F-35s
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded Ursa Major $137 million for solid rocket motors for the Compact Air-to-Air Missile and the Naval Modular Missile.
- The $91 million CAAM contract covers a 7-inch motor, and the $46 million NMM contract covers a 10-inch quad-pack motor.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Ursa Major two contracts worth a combined $137 million to develop and qualify solid rocket motors for two new missiles: a small air-to-air missile for fighter jets and a ship-launched interceptor meant to eventually replace the Standard Missile family.
The Colorado company announced the awards on Oct. 5. The larger contract, worth $91 million, covers the motor for the Compact Air-to-Air Missile, or CAAM. The second, worth $46 million, covers the motor for the medium-range version of the Naval Modular Missile, or NMM. Funding comes through the Office of the Under Secretary of War.
CAAM is a short-range missile the U.S. Navy is developing for close-in air combat, sized to be carried inside the weapons bays of stealth fighters and future carrier-based drones. The Navy first showed the concept publicly in August, and service officials described it as an “inner boundary” weapon meant to increase how many missiles an aircraft can carry internally.
For CAAM, Ursa Major is designing a 7-inch (178 mm) motor. That is the same diameter as the AIM-120 AMRAAM and wider than the 5-inch AIM-9X Sidewinder, the Navy’s current short-range air-to-air missile. The company says the motor uses Highly Loaded Grain, a propellant design that packs more fuel into the motor case, giving a small missile more energy in the same volume. Ursa Major said it is building the development motor with the same methods it plans to use in full production, so it can move to high-rate manufacturing once the design is qualified.
The second contract covers a 10-inch (254 mm) motor for the medium-range NMM. The company described it as a quad-pack motor, meaning four missiles are sized to fit in a single shipboard launch cell, as the U.S. Navy already does with the Evolved Sea Sparrow Missile. Ursa Major said the motor is designed for high annual production volumes and compatibility with existing Navy shipboard launch systems. The U.S. Navy wants NMM to reach full capability by fiscal 2032 as a replacement for the Standard Missile family.
“By investing in CAAM and NMM, the Navy and OUSW are building solid rocket motor capacity now and getting new tactical air and naval capabilities into development sooner,” said Jason Meredith, president of Solid Missile Systems at Ursa Major. “Our Lynx manufacturing approach and growing energetics capacity enable us to design, build, test, qualify and field these motors faster to support the warfighter. Production is the bottleneck in missile programs right now, and that’s the part we’ve been building for.”
Lynx is Ursa Major’s name for its manufacturing process, which uses additive manufacturing, or industrial 3D printing, to produce most motor parts. Solid rocket motor production in the United States has for years been concentrated in two suppliers, Northrop Grumman and L3Harris, which owns Aerojet Rocketdyne. The Pentagon has been funding new entrants to expand capacity as demand for interceptors and long-range missiles has grown.
The new awards follow earlier work with the U.S. Navy. In July, the Navy gave Ursa Major $10 million to take its version of the MK 104 motor through critical design review and static fire testing. The MK 104 is the dual-thrust motor that powers Standard Missile-2 and Standard Missile-6 interceptors on Aegis destroyers and cruisers. In February, the company completed a $25 million cost-share program with the Navy and the Office of Strategic Capital, in which it designed, built and static-fired a 10-inch Highly Loaded Grain motor and developed a proprietary propellant for it. That work was carried out with the Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division at China Lake, California, and the Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division in Maryland.
Ursa Major is headquartered in Berthoud, Colorado, and runs additive manufacturing operations in Youngstown, Ohio. The company said its next steps on both programs are design, testing and qualification of the motors.

Meet Kyiv’s New Jet-Drone Killer—12+ Sky Sentinel Turrets Are Already on the Hunt
Russia’s attempt to outrun Ukraine’s air defenses with faster jet-powered attack drones is now facing a different kind of threat over Kyiv—an AI-guided gun system that does not need to chase its target to shoot it down.
More than 12 automated .50-caliber turrets deployed across Kyiv to counter Russia’s jet-powered attack drones are Ukrainian-made Sky Sentinel systems, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed in an exclusive comment to UNITED24 Media.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“These are Sky Sentinel systems. They are already on combat duty and are being used to counter Russian attack drones,” Ihnat told UNITED24 Media. “The systems have already demonstrated results in combat. There are confirmed cases of them successfully engaging and shooting down jet-powered UAVs,” he added.
Ihnat’s confirmation comes after he revealed earlier on October 5 that the automated turrets had already intercepted Russia’s Geran-5 jet-powered drone.
“There have already been shootdowns of even jet-powered UAVs, even the Geran-5, using those same turrets,” Ihnat said during Ukraine’s national telethon.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy first revealed the deployment a day earlier, saying that more than 12 automated “fifties” had already been installed in Kyiv, with another eight set to be deployed across the Kyiv region.
Sky Sentinel is a Ukrainian-developed automated anti-drone turret that uses machine vision and artificial intelligence to detect, track, and engage aerial targets.
The system combines a heavy machine gun with an automated fire-control module. Once a target is acquired, its optics track the drone while onboard software calculates its speed, trajectory, distance, and the lead required for an interception.
Unlike an interceptor drone, Sky Sentinel does not need to chase its target. It calculates where the UAV will be and fires toward that point, allowing it to engage fast-moving aircraft within its firing envelope.
Previously published specifications indicate that Sky Sentinel can engage aerial targets traveling at speeds of up to around 800 kilometers per hour, placing Russia’s jet-powered attack drones within its theoretical capability.
The Geran-5, now increasingly used by Russian forces, flies substantially faster than conventional propeller-driven Shahed-type drones. Its vulnerability to Sky Sentinel, however, depends on altitude and range.
At higher altitudes, a jet-powered drone may remain beyond the reach of heavy machine-gun fire. But as it descends toward a target or operates at lower altitude, it can enter the turret’s engagement zone.
At that point, the key factor is no longer whether a weapon can catch the drone, but whether it can track it and calculate a firing solution quickly enough. Sky Sentinel’s machine vision continuously follows the target while its software determines the interception point in real time.
The system had already seen combat before its deployment around Kyiv.
UNITED24 raised approximately $3.3 million for 22 Sky Sentinel systems. In August, five were delivered to Ukraine’s 636th Separate Anti-Aircraft Machine Gun Battalion operating in the Sumy region to strengthen defenses against Russian attack drones.
The system had already demonstrated combat effectiveness during earlier deployments, with a Sky Sentinel prototype reportedly destroying multiple Russian Shahed-type drones.
Sky Sentinel is designed as a relatively inexpensive final layer of air defense around critical infrastructure, bridges, military positions, and other high-value sites.

Ukraine Quietly Fields Turkish Korkut Air Defense Guns Against Russian Drones
Ukraine is already operating Turkish-made Korkut gun-based air defense systems against Russian drones following a previously undisclosed delivery from Türkiye.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 5, citing Middle East Eye, a small number of the systems have entered Ukrainian service and are already successfully intercepting Russian drones. The delivery had not previously been publicly announced by either Ukraine or Türkiye.
An unnamed Ukrainian official told Middle East Eye that operators initially encountered some difficulties with the systems, but the issues were resolved through relatively minor adjustments. The official also said the Korkut’s price was considered appropriate for its capabilities and that Ukraine was interested in acquiring additional systems.
The exact Korkut variant delivered to Ukraine has not been officially disclosed. However, Middle East Eye’s reporting cited the use of 25 mm programmable ammunition against FPV drones, including fiber-optic-controlled UAVs—a detail that Defense Express said could point to the Korkut 100/25 SB.
Developed by Turkish defense company Aselsan, the Korkut 100/25 SB is a short-range air defense system built around a 25 mm automatic cannon. It can fire ATOM programmable airburst ammunition, which detonates near an aerial target rather than requiring a direct hit.
According to Defense Express, the Korkut 100/25 SB has an effective range exceeding one kilometer and a rate of fire of up to 600 rounds per minute. Its targeting suite includes an active electronically scanned array radar, thermal imaging cameras, a laser rangefinder, and AI-based algorithms for target detection and engagement.
The combat module can be integrated onto different vehicle platforms, including 4×4 armored vehicles such as the Ejder Yalçın.
Defense Express, citing Middle East Eye, reported that a Korkut system supplied to Ukraine consists of three gun vehicles and a command-and-control vehicle. It remains unclear, however, whether that configuration corresponds specifically to the Korkut 100/25 SB or another member of the Korkut family.
Aselsan also produces Korkut variants armed with 35 mm cannons, which offer an engagement range of up to approximately four kilometers and are designed to counter drones and other low-flying aerial threats, including cruise missiles.
Ukraine has previously selected 35 mm Korkut systems for its Ada-class corvettes, including the Hetman Ivan Mazepa and Hetman Ivan Vyhovskyi.
Neither Ukraine nor Türkiye has publicly confirmed the number of land-based Korkut systems delivered or identified the exact variant currently operating in Ukraine.

articles.title: As Air Force Goes Big on Autonomy, Are Cargo Drones Next?
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force’s plans to field 1,000 semi-autonomous fighter and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drones within just a few years made headlines at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last month.
But beyond the service’s signature Collaborative Combat Aircraft and Massed Modular Aircraft programs, a half-dozen or so firms are pitching another kind of autonomous aircraft: cargo drones to solve some of the thorniest logistics problems.
Textron Aviation and Merlin Labs unveiled a cockpit-less Cessna equipped with Merlin’s autonomy software and a nose hatch opening to a cavernous cargo bay.
“By pairing a proven aircraft platform with autonomy technology, we’re exploring new approaches to contested logistics operations while also examining how autonomy may enable more efficient cargo aircraft designs that increase usable volume, improve cargo accessibility and support mission sustainment requirements,” Bob Gibbs, Textron’s vice president for defense and special mission sales, said of the company’s Cessna SkyuCourier UX concept.
Reliable Robotics is offering its own modified Cessna 208B Caravan. Its aircraft flew in multiple Agile Flag exercises in 2024, installing actuators, sensors, and other gear in the cockpit and using a human pilot to command high-level direction from a ground station. Reliable announced a $17.4 million deal with the Air Force in 2025 to provide an aircraft for a yearlong test.
In a May blog post, Reliable’s certification flight test lead Chris Baughman wrote that the firm is targeting the start of fiscal 2027 to begin the test, which will focus on the Indo-Pacific region. The company is also seeking FAA certification for its autonomy software to operate in U.S. airspace, targeting 2028 for that certification.
Joby Aviation, which previously acquired autonomy startup Xwing, is also flying a modified Cessna Caravan, racking up 40 hours and 7,000 miles during last summer’s Resolute Force Pacific. Joby did not exhibit at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber, but sought to capitalize on the timing by announcing soon after that it completed 3,199 miles of autonomous flight across the U.S. this summer, including stops at Shaw Air Force Base, S.C., and near Washington D.C. At a press event Sept. 24, Joby’s Head of Defense Policy John Barranco told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the aircraft carried a safety pilot for those flights in case human intervention was needed, but the autonomy software never required a pilot intervention.
Coming at the same time that other vendors are developing autonomous fighters and reconnaissance aircraft with clean-sheet designs, the modified Cessnas might seem like minimalist efforts. But aviation firms see a gap they can fill in the Air Force’s logistics enterprise, a small airlifter that can do jobs that USAF’s workhorse C-130 cannot do as efficiently. The Hercules can haul 40,000 pounds of cargo, and the Air Force has only about 270. A Cessna could be ideal for shorter hops and smaller loads at a fraction of the cost.
“It’s a really robust, reliable existing cargo airframe that’s in the world, and there are many of them, and so we can retrofit a lot of those for the customers,” Barranco said.
USAF officials have spent years talking about Agile Combat Employment—the concept of dispersing small teams of Airmen and aircraft from large bases to operate from remote or austere locations and move quickly to counter adversary long-range missile attacks. But the ACE logistics is complex, especially in the vast and watery Indo-Pacific region.
Having small, unmanned aircraft to island-hop and resupply those forces so they can generate airpower—without taxing manned airlifters—could be a solution.
“Historically it’s about a logistics train where you’re trying to move a really big airframe and move a lot of stuff, and that takes time, and it takes Airmen, and it takes support, and that’s a really important mission,” said Barranco. “Sometimes you need to move a lot less really, really quickly, without standing up a mission, without 24 hours’ notice, without pulling folks together.”
Other concepts are also emerging to chase this possible market. DZYNE Technologies put its autonomous cargo drone, called Grasshopper, on display.
DZYNE and the Air Force Research Laboratory unveiled Grasshopper last May, as a self-guided glider capable of carrying up to 500 pounds after being dropped out the back of a C-130; from there, it could glide tens of miles to resupply troops in “high-risk environments.”
DZYNE has since offered a “Long-Range” powered variant with a turbine engine that can fly “10 times” further than Grasshopper and launched from “standoff” distances.
U.S. Special Operations Command has tested the concept, using the Long-Range Grasshopper in Exercise Trojan Footprint 26 in Romania and North Macedonia, where the drones were launched from a Romanian Air Force C-27J.
But the firms pursuing this niche want more than a narrow special ops use case, focusing on any mission where moving cargo quickly without risking crews could be attractive.
Grid Aero won $6 million in seed funding from the Air Force’s innovation arm, AFWERX, last August. CEO Arthur Dubois compared his company’s drone to a “flying pickup” truck at the time, saying it would be able to carry somewhere between 1,000 and 8,000 pounds from “Guam to Japan,” for example, a trek of some 1,500 miles.
Grid Aero’s Lifter Lite hasn’t made its first flight yet, but the firm was among seven selected in September to compete for the Air Force’s Massed Modular Aircraft program. It’s unclear if Lifter Lite or some other design is what the company envisions as its entry.
Dubois said last year that the idea for Lifter Lite sprang from asking military and commercial air cargo stakeholders about their pain points. For the military, that’s executing logistics in areas where U.S. assets could be attacked.
Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering, and force protection, noted as much during the conference: “The era of uncontested logistics is over,” Bell declared. “We will have to continue to fight our way in from a logistics standpoint and be able to sustain and regenerate ourselves while we’re in contact. … That is a concept that we certainly need to think through.”
Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach endorsed the concept of autonomous cargo drones during a media roundtable at the conference, albeit without completely committing to it.
“We believe that there’s some value in that as well,” he said in response to a question. “It certainly could be valuable in the Pacific, with the ranges that we’re talking about. And so we’re looking at several different options and evaluating them, but I would say, no program of record just yet, but certainly taking a look at some demonstrators and the like to see what’s available to us.”
Congress and Pentagon officials are also tuning in. When Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael culled the department’s list of “critical technology areas” from 14 to just six last November, “contested logistics technology” survived the cut.
The House Armed Services Committee directed the the Air Force to present a briefing on the topic in their version of the 2027 defense policy bill. Lawmakers also expect a proposed timeline for developing an acquisition strategy that could include rapid prototyping. They also want a strategy for the use of “low-cost and attritable Group 4 and 5 unmanned aircraft systems in contested logistics operations.”
Staff Writers Matthew Cox and Stephen Losey contributed reporting.

articles.title: When the UN agreed with the UK Green Party on Zionism
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
When the UN agreed with the UK Green Party on Zionism
The Green Party’s decision to adopt a motion classifying Zionism as a form of racism has caused uproar in the UK. The motion calls Zionism an ideology which supports an “ethnonationalist Jewish state” and calls for a “single democratic state in all of historic Palestine”.
The Green Party’s leader, Zack Polanski, did not vote on the motion, but found himself banned from Israel as a result.
Rabbi Charley Baginsky of the Movement for Progressive Judaism described the motion as “incredibly sinister” and told LBC she was “really distressed” at the vote, saying that Zionism was a key part of many Jewish people’s identity.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that the move would stoke “anti-Jewish hatred”, citing attacks on Jews in the UK in the past year.
The resolution was even opposed by leading members of the Green Party itself.
Caroline Lucas, the party’s former leader and its first-ever MP, said, “I view the Israeli government as racist, I believe its actions in Gaza amount to genocide, and I support the BDS campaign. And yet I remain firmly opposed to this resolution.”
She justified this by claiming that Zionism was historically a response to the racist persecution of Jews in Europe.
Media coverage in the UK has been extremely critical, with The Economist calling the motion “shameful” and the Daily Mail suggesting that the Greens were now the UK’s “first openly anti-Semitic party”.
It is often forgotten, however, that the UN itself once classified Zionism as racism.
UN condemnation of Zionism
While the UN was instrumental in the creation of Israel, with the majority of its members voting in favour of the 1947 Partition of Palestine, by 1975, African and Asian states had gained independence from European colonial rule and formed a large proportion of the world body’s membership. Most of these voted for UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, which determined that Zionism was “a form of racism and racial discrimination”, alongside the Arab League countries which sponsored and proposed it.
The Soviet Union, which was one of the first countries in the world to recognise Israel, had by that time become an ally of Arab countries and, along with its East European allies, also voted in favour. The resolution passed with 72 votes for and 35 against, with the US and its Western European allies voting against.
The vote took place at a time when Israel’s 1967 occupation of the West Bank and Gaza was relatively new. Israel subjected the Palestinian population of those territories to military rule while denying them citizenship. It also began establishing settlements in the territories in violation of international law.
Memories of the 1948 Nakba, in which Zionist forces expelled the vast majority of the Palestinian population, were also much fresher than they are today.
South Africa and Israel
Israel at the time was also a close ally of apartheid South Africa, with the two countries cooperating in defence, intelligence, and the development of nuclear weapons, with both viewing themselves as outposts of “civilisation” in a hostile environment.
As a South African government publication put it at the time, “Israel and South Africa have one thing above all else in common: they are both situated in a predominantly hostile world inhabited by dark peoples."
It was very easy to draw parallels between the two countries and the statements of Israeli leaders themselves appeared to confirm them. As Yitzhak Navon, Israel’s president between 1978 and 1983, said, “The very point of [the Israeli] Labor [party’s] Zionist programme is to have as much land as possible and as few Arabs as possible!”
These parallels helped explain the overwhelming African and Asian support for the UNGA resolution.
Israel, however, bitterly rejected the resolution, with its ambassador, Chaim Herzog (father of Israel’s current president), claiming that some of Israel’s Palestinian citizens – within the 1948 boundaries – had gained high-ranking positions within its government and military.
US ambassador to the UN Daniel Patrick Moynihan told the UN that it was “about to make anti-Semitism international law."
Repealing the resolution for ‘peace’
By 1991, the global environment had changed. The collapse of the Soviet Union had deprived Arab countries of a key strategic ally and supplier of weapons and changed the balance of power across the world. The Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and the subsequent Gulf War had left the US in a much stronger position in the Middle East.
Israel demanded that the UN repeal Resolution 3379 as a precondition for its participation in the 1991 Madrid peace conference, which eventually led to the 1993 Oslo Accords between the PLO and Israel.
The UN General Assembly duly repealed the resolution under US pressure, with even some Arab countries – such as Egypt, Morocco, and Oman – staying away rather than voting against.
However, all of the original factors behind the 1975 resolution remained. The Oslo Peace Process ended up entrenching Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, its settlement policies, and its encirclement and siege of Palestinian communities – notably Gaza.
The number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank has gone up from just a few thousand in 1975 to around 700,000 today.
Human rights groups such as Amnesty International have concluded that Israel is committing “the crime of apartheid” both within its 1948 boundaries and in the West Bank and Gaza, long after apartheid as a ruling system ended in South Africa.
Israeli leaders are engaging in much more bloodthirsty rhetoric than Navon’s “as few Arabs as possible” remarks, with far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir recently calling for “30-40” Palestinians to be killed every day.
What may have changed, however, is the increasing censorship regarding discourse on Israel and the growing and deliberate conflation of criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism.
Singers who chant “Free Palestine” at music concerts are attacked on the grounds that they make Jews feel unsafe, while artwork by Palestinian children displayed at a UK hospital is removed for the same reason.
By passing a motion equating Zionism with racism, the Green Party only stated a position once held by a significant section of global opinion. However, it did so at a time when Israel is far more aggressive in pushing its narrative than it was 50 years ago.

articles.title: Expert says moving Estonia's units near border has limited strategic impact
articles.body:
Expert says moving Estonia's units near border has limited strategic impact
As Estonia strengthens its defenses, the country is shifting military units closer to the Russian border and expanding long‑range strike capability. Security expert Rainer Saks says moving units by less than 100 kilometers offers little strategic benefit, arguing that Estonia's real vulnerabilities lie in air defense and attack‑drone capacity.
Recently, the EDF's 1st Infantry Brigade moved its Jõhvi staff company and brigade headquarters from Tapa, and next year a company will relocate from Jõhvi to Narva. The shift toward the eastern border is part of preparations for active defense.
"I wouldn't call this a strategic advantage. It's more routine work. A decision was made years ago that we begin defending the country at the state border. It makes sense to move certain functions and units closer to the border," said Tarmo Kundla, commander of the 1st Infantry Brigade.
"So that in a crisis we don't have to start moving there — we're already there. If someone thinks this makes us a target, they're right. If we're sitting in our bases as targets when war breaks out, then we've done something very wrong," said Defense Minister Martin Herem.
According to Saks, relocating units may be justified in terms of military planning, but strategically the change is minor.
"No matter where we place our forces, they are vulnerable if we lack air defense. If the air‑defense issue is solved, that becomes a major achievement in defense planning. Until air defense is sufficient, placing units at specific points is less important," Saks said.
Herem says air defense is improving month by month. Additional ammunition for existing systems will arrive this year, and long‑range strike capability is being developed.
"We have HIMARS. We previously received loitering munitions — essentially winged drones similar to Russia's Lancet. We already have them in Estonia, and the unit is trained," Herem said.
Some HIMARS munitions have already arrived, though not the 300‑kilometer‑range missiles.
"Russia could previously plan operations against Estonia knowing it could mass forces right near the border, use aircraft from close range, and fire missiles from close range. If Estonia could bring that 300‑kilometer zone under fire control, it would be a major change," Saks said.
The Financial Times reported on Monday about changes in Estonia's defense planning. Saks says it is important to show foreign media that Estonia is preparing countermeasures — sending a message to both Russia and allies that Estonia's defense forces are capable.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Argo Ideon

articles.title: Former German spy chief arrested on espionage charges. He made at least seven trips to Russia after leaving office.
articles.body:
Former German spy chief arrested on espionage charges. He made at least seven trips to Russia after leaving office.
Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office said it detained August Hanning, the former head of the country’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND), on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason. His former bureau chief, Manfred D., was detained along with him.
Hanning led the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. Investigators said that in 2010, he arranged for Manfred D. to pass him classified intelligence agency information in exchange for money. By 2022, Hanning had obtained roughly 2,000 internal BND documents, including materials on Iran’s nuclear program and the Russian armed forces.
In one instance, he used the documents to prepare an analytical report for an officer of a foreign intelligence service, though it is not clear which country was involved. Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR reported that this episode was not connected to Russia.
Hanning also communicated for many years with another foreign intelligence officer, whose country is also unclear, and passed him political information, including material he obtained from Manfred D.
The Insider, an independent Russian investigative outlet, found that Hanning flew to Russia at least seven times between 2015 and 2019. The trips were short, with some lasting less than a day.
Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that rumors about Hanning’s ties to Russia have circulated since his diplomatic work in East Berlin during the era of East Germany, though no evidence ever supported them.
In 2013, Hanning testified in a London court case as a security expert, backing businessman Oleg Deripaska in a dispute over the sale of a stake in Rusal.
Hanning also worked as a consultant in the Russian division of the London consulting firm G3 and served on the supervisory board of the Latvian PNB Banka. While working at PNB, he acted as a mediator in a dispute between two businessmen of Russian origin. Security firms linked to Hanning also include people with ties to Russia.

articles.title: French submarine fires new nuclear weapon
articles.body:
France has fired its latest submarine-launched ballistic missile for the first time from the boat Le Vigilant, with President Emmanuel Macron watching from the deck of a frigate, the president stated in a post published after the launch.
Writing in French from aboard the multi-mission frigate Auvergne, Mr Macron said: “Aboard the multi-mission frigate Auvergne, I witnessed the first firing of the new M51.3 ballistic missile from the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Le Vigilant. Very few nations possess such expertise.”
He thanked the defence procurement agency DGA, the Atomic Energy Commission, ArianeGroup, Naval Group and the French Navy, and said: “This technical success is a new demonstration of the credibility of our deterrence, whose sustainability is assured. To be free, one must be feared. And to be feared, one must be powerful.”
The missile was launched off Finistère in western Brittany without a nuclear warhead fitted, and flew to a designated impact area in the North Atlantic several hundred kilometres from any coastline. France has described the trial as validating the operational capability of Le Vigilant’s strategic weapon system after a long refit, and the boat has recently emerged from the major overhaul the French call an IPER before returning to the deterrent patrol cycle.
The M51.3 is the third operational version of the missile, which was declared in service last October with improved range, accuracy and penetration performance over the preceding M51.2, and carrying the newer TNO warhead. ArianeGroup builds the family, which entered service in 2010, and the missiles arm the four boats of the Triomphant class. A further version, the M51.4, was contracted to the same company in August last year and is expected during the next decade, alongside the third-generation submarines that will replace the current fleet.
Published range figures for the M51 run to somewhere between 8,000 and 10,000 kilometres, though France does not confirm them and the real figure is classified.
Mr Macron set the firing against his own record on defence spending, saying he had launched the renewal of French capabilities in 2017 and that the armed forces budget will have doubled over ten years. He added that the programme for hypersonic and manoeuvring strategic missiles that will arm the airborne component of the deterrent was launched this year, a reference to the weapon intended to succeed the ASMP-A carried by Rafale squadrons.
France designs, builds and owns every element of its deterrent, from the warhead through the missile to the boat, whereas the Royal Navy draws its Trident II D5 missiles from a common pool held at King’s Bay in Georgia.
The two countries are also closer on nuclear matters than they have been at any point since the war. Under the Northwood Declaration signed last year, Britain and France agreed to coordinate their deterrents and stated that there is no extreme threat to Europe that would not prompt a response by both, which was the first time either had said so in those terms.
Mr Macron closed by saying that French nuclear deterrence “protects us and will continue to protect us”.

articles.title: Poland and Lithuania prepare to evacuate one million Baltic residents to Poland in event of war
articles.body:

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland and Lithuania are jointly preparing plans for the evacuation of one million or more residents of the Baltic states into Poland in the event of a war or other major crisis, amid growing concern in the region over potential Russian aggression.
On Monday, the two countries’ interior ministers met to discuss the issue following a recent large-scale Lithuanian mobilisation exercise that also involved Polish officials. The pair also addressed their joint response to the migration crisis on the borders orchestrated by Russia’s ally Belarus.
“In crisis situations, it is best to cooperate. It is best to prepare such plans through mutual understanding, thus attempting to address potential situations,” said Lithuanian interior minister Martynas Katelynas, speaking alongside his Polish counterpart, Marcin Kierwiński, at the Budzisko-Kalvarija border crossing.
“As for this crossing here, this place that connects us with Poland, this plan foresees approximately one million, and perhaps even more, refugees who will be able to be evacuated from our countries in the event of war,” he added.
The three Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – are seen as a primary potential target for Russian aggression. NATO states, including Poland, have in recent months warned of the growing possibility of Moscow conducting some form of “provocation” against the alliance’s eastern members.
Lithuania last week finished a major exercise testing its national mobilisation system in the event of war or other crises. For the first time, it included elements relating to cross-border evacuation of civilians from the Baltic states to Poland.
Alongside thousands of Lithuanian officials, a 20-person Polish team, led by representatives of the interior ministry, took part in the exercise.
This has allowed Poland to develop “an agenda and action plan for what must be adjusted very quickly: cross-border evacuation plans, infrastructure and alternative border crossings in an emergency, as well as reception points”, said Kierwiński, adding that “we will begin intensive work” on implementation.
Poland already has extensive recent experience in receiving civilians fleeing conflict. In 2022, it became the primary destination for the millions of refugees fleeing Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Poland’s government and civil society quickly implemented measures to support the refugees, almost one million of whom remain in the country.

Both countries have been the target of a crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus, which has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross into Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.
In response, Poland last year introduced checks on its borders with Lithuania and Germany. Those measures have been repeatedly extended, including last week, when Poland announced that they would remain in force until at least March 2027.
“Border controls with Germany and Lithuania allow us to catch people illegally crossing the border from the Baltic states,” said Kierwiński on Monday. “As soon as there are grounds to end these controls, we will discontinue them. articles.title: France test-fires new nuclear-capable missile without warhead carried
articles.body:
PARIS, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- France on Tuesday test-fired a strategic ballistic missile without a nuclear warhead from a submarine off the coast of Finistere in western France, French media reported.
The missile was launched from the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Le Vigilant and landed in the North Atlantic Ocean, several hundred kilometers from any coast, French news channel BFM TV reported, citing French Ministry of Armed Forces.
The ministry emphasized that the test was conducted without a nuclear warhead and in strict compliance with France's international commitments.
French President Emmanuel Macron observed the test firing from a French Navy frigate, it reported.
In service since October 2025, the M51.3 missile has been deployed on France's four nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines, with at least one submarine continuously at sea somewhere in the world to ensure France's ability to launch a nuclear strike at any time, BFM TV reported, citing French Ministry of Armed Forces. ■

articles.title: Jetten: Ukraine needs more F-16 spare parts and ammunition; Netherlands to provide assistance
articles.body:
Ukraine requires additional maintenance resources, spare parts, and ammunition for its F-16 fighter jets, and the Netherlands will assist with this, stated Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten.
"President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and I discussed the latest developments in the war. Further strengthening Ukraine's air defense is literally a matter of life and death. To achieve this, Ukraine needs more maintenance, spare parts, and ammunition for its F-16 fleet. I assured him that the Netherlands would help Ukraine with this," Jetten wrote on X following his conversation with Zelenskyy.
For his part, Zelenskyy noted that the F-16s supplied by the Netherlands to Ukraine are responsible for shooting down a significant percentage of jet-powered "Shahed" drones, and that there are opportunities to support their operations with the necessary resources.
“We also discussed other ideas for protecting critical infrastructure and bolstering air defense. I am grateful for the readiness to help,” Zelesnkyy said on X following the talk.
He also informed Jetten about contacts with the U.S. team and potential trilateral meetings at the technical level between Ukraine, the USA, and Russia. “Realistic proposals that can bring peace closer are important. But Russia must take the negotiations seriously and not try to find more and more pretexts to drag the war out further,” Zelenskyy said.
The President of Ukraine thanked the Prime Minister and the Netherlands for their consistent and resolute support.
In his post, Jetten noted that Russian aggression against Ukraine continues to escalate.
"We saw this again this past weekend, particularly with the air strikes on Kyiv. Russia is deliberately targeting civilian sites and energy infrastructure, seeking to make Ukrainian cities uninhabitable and destroy the economy this winter. We cannot allow this to happen," the Dutch Prime Minister wrote.

articles.title: Northrop’s Talon Blue Collaborative Combat Aircraft Makes First Flight
articles.body:
Northrop Grumman’s Talon Blue YFQ-48A Collaborative Combat Aircraft took its first flight Oct. 3, heightening the competition for the Air Force’s future combat fleet.
Talon Blue is Northrop’s so-called “loyal wingman” drone, an autonomous aircraft designed to pair with crewed fighters. The Oct. 3 flight was an important milestone for the firm as it looks to break into the Air Force’s CCA program—thus far, the service has awarded production contracts to General Atomics and Anduril Industries, but more “increments” are expected in the coming years.
Northrop said the drone completed a fully autonomous flight, including taxi, takeoff, “in-flight maneuvers,” and landing from its Mojave, Calif., facilities.
Air Force leadership say they plans to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. While the service has not selected Talon Blue for production yet, the company has been bullish that the service could be a customer in the future. The Air Force also gave Talon Blue an official Department of Defense Mission Design Series designation, YFQ-48A, last December, signaling that it sees the aircraft as a competitor for future CCAs.
“Our customers made it clear they need autonomous systems that can be fielded faster and more affordably without sacrificing mission effectiveness,” Craig Woolston, Northrop Grumman’s vice president and general manager for research and advanced design, said in a statement. “We listened. Talon Blue’s first flight is one step toward a new generation of autonomous capabilities. Every flight and lesson strengthens our broader autonomy work and sharpens what comes next.”
The company’s CCA is a unique offering. It was first unveiled last December to a small group of reporters, including Air & Space Forces Magazine, as a self-funded effort. The company’s Scaled Composites subsidiary, known for its history of innovative aircraft, built it, and the company has touted how quickly it developed the aircraft. The time between when the aircraft was conceived and when it had “weight on wheels” was roughly 15 months, company officials said. When Northrop announced the aircraft, it said it expected the aircraft to fly around fall 2026, a milestone the company has now met.
Talon Blue falls under the company’s broader Project Talon. The project also includes the Talon IQ, an autonomous testbed for using Scaled Composites Model 437 aircraft. Talon IQ uses Northrop’s Prism mission autonomy software. So far, the Air Force has pursued a “software sold separately” approach to CCAs, running separate competitions for the mission autonomy software and the aircraft themselves.
While General Atomics’ FQ-42 Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ Fury FQ-44 have been awarded production contracts from the Air Force and are undergoing ongoing testing with the service as part of the Increment 1 of the service’s first autonomous wingman, Northrop Grumman is hoping to market Talon Blue for future Air Force purchases and to U.S. allies.
Northrop’s original CCA offering lost out on the Increment 1 contracts due to its cost, president of the company’s aeronautics division Tom Jones said, leading to what became Talon Blue.
“The idea was to see if we could build an aircraft that had all the same capability of our original offering, and do it faster,” Jones said at the unveiling last year. “So the outcome was an aircraft, but the outcome we’re shooting for was the process: How do we design and build things that perform at a high level, but that we can build quickly now and can do affordably?”
The Air Force has yet to spell out the requirements for Increment 2 of the CCA program.
“It’s getting defined as every day goes by,” Gen. Dale White, the Pentagon’s director of critical major weapon systems, told reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference when asked by Air & Space Forces Magazine about the status of Increment 2.
“The challenges I may have in the Indo-Pacific theater could be very different [from those] in the [U.S. Central Command] theater and different again in the [European Command] theater,” White said. “So how do we take all of those different requirements and make sure we have a [CCA] capability that can address many different mission sets across many different requirement centers?”
Whether Northrop’s Talon Blue fits into that picture is still unknown. But the YFQ-48A could also be appealing to U.S. allies, some of which have started rolling out their own CCAs, such as the U.K. government-backed, British-designed Brontanax CCA from BAE Systems. U.S. Air Forces in Europe and NATO Allied Air Command boss Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds said other European nations were watching the U.S.’s work on CCAs.
“You’re going to see a lot more interest from other nations inside Europe,” Hinds said at Air, Space & Cyber when asked about CCAs.
When the Talon Blue aircraft was unveiled last December, Jones said multiple U.S. military services and international partners are interested in the drone, and some had visited Mojave to see it.
“We’re still extremely good at making something very complex,” Jones said at the time. “This was really about broadening that paradigm to what it means to be a high-performing engineering, aviation, development, and manufacturing organization to encompass all aspects of it.
Talon Blue is important for Northrop’s future tactical aircraft efforts, as the company recently lost out to Boeing to build the Navy’s future F/A-XX sixth-generation fighter jet. The company is still building major weapons systems for the Air Force: the B-21 Raider stealth bomber, set to enter service next year and a project that will likely be expanded beyond the original program of record of 100 aircraft, and the LGM-35A Sentinel, the next-generation intercontinental ballistic missile.
The CCA market Talon Blue is competing for is crowded, not just by the FQ-42 and F-44, but also by Lockheed Martin’s new Vectis offering. Other possible competitors, such as Boeing’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat and Kratos’s XQ-58 Valkyrie, have been used by the U.S. military in tests and exercises alongside crewed aircraft.
The Air Force sees CCAs as a critical part of the future force.
“I can imagine a day in the future, 10 years [from now], maybe more, where a CCA autonomy algorithm does a better job flying a fighter airplane than I did as a captain,” Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s Chief Modernization Officer, said last month. “That hurts my ego a little bit. But at the same time, I see that this trend is happening, and we’ve got to find a way to do that.”

articles.title: Lithuania takes further step towards lifting nuclear weapons ban
articles.body:
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions.
Lithuania has taken a step towards removing a constitutional ban on nuclear weapons from its territory, bringing the Baltic state closer to the legal position of its neighbours as European allies debate how to strengthen NATO’s deterrence in the face of Russia.
The Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, voted 106-18, with six abstentions, on Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment removing a provision that bars weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from Lithuanian territory.
The change still requires a second vote after a constitutionally mandated three-month waiting period. At least 94 of the Seimas’ 141 members must back it on both occasions. The final vote is expected on January 12.
“This constitutional amendment would enable Lithuania’s armed forces to participate fully in the planning and exercises of all of NATO’s deterrence measures,” said Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen, leader of the Liberal Movement parliamentary group.
Currently, Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution stipulates that weapons of mass destruction and military bases of foreign states may not be located in Lithuania, which borders Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave. This means that under current laws, allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons could not enter Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes.
Added urgency in Lithuania's case
Supporters of the amendment argue that the constitutional provision has become a legal obstacle to Lithuania’s full participation in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements and leaves the country at a disadvantage compared with other NATO allies.
“Our neighbouring countries, such as Latvia, Estonia and Poland, have no such restrictions either,” Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee, said during a parliamentary session in September. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries. We must send a signal that Lithuania is a full part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence.”
NATO describes nuclear deterrence as part of its collective defence, alongside conventional and missile-defence capabilities. The Alliance also says its nuclear policy remains consistent with its commitments to arms control, disarmament and non-proliferation.
For Lithuania, the issue has taken on added urgency. “NATO deterrence, including nuclear deterrence, is part of collective defence,” Motuzas said, adding that Russia has rapidly modernised its nuclear arsenal in recent years and deployed nuclear weapons close to Lithuania — in Kaliningrad and Belarus.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Lithuania’s move, alongside broader plans to expand US and NATO military infrastructure in the region, risked further escalating tensions, Reuters reported.
The warnings come as Russia has stepped up its nuclear rhetoric towards NATO. Moscow recently threatened nuclear retaliation in the event of what it described as attempts to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave, which borders Lithuania and Poland.
Finland has already made the move
Lithuania is not acting in isolation.
Finland, which joined NATO in 2023 after decades of military non-alignment, removed its own statutory prohibition on nuclear weapons earlier this year, citing the need to ensure that Finnish law did not restrict the country’s ability to fulfil its obligations as a NATO ally.
In June, the Finnish parliament approved amendments to the Nuclear Energy Act repealing the country’s ban on nuclear explosives. The legislation entered into force on July 1.
“This historic reform strengthens the security of Finland and of NATO as a whole,” Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said on X.
Helsinki has stressed, however, that the change does not mean Finland intends to acquire or host nuclear weapons, and that NATO has no plans to station them there.
Finland has since joined a French-led initiative aimed at strengthening European security through closer cooperation on nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has proposed what Paris calls “forward deterrence” — closer cooperation with European allies around France’s independent nuclear capabilities.
The United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark, and Norway have already signed up to France's initiative.

articles.title: Houthis claim attacks on Saudi airports, state oil refinery, military sites
articles.body:
Mohammed Al Ragawi and Rania Abushamala
05 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Yemen’s Houthi group claimed Monday evening that it had carried out three military operations targeting two airports, an oil facility and military sites across Saudi Arabia.
In a statement on the US social media platform X, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the operations involved a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones.
Saree said the first operation targeted King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh, claiming it hit its target and disrupted air traffic.
The second targeted a refinery of state oil company Aramco in Rabigh, in the Mecca region, he said, claiming the attack caused a fire at the facility.
According to the statement, the third operation targeted Abha Airport, the Khamis Mushait base, and Akfa camp in the southern Asir region, along with what Saree described as other “sensitive sites” in Najran and Jazan in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
Saree claimed the operations were in response to 60 Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks over the preceding 24 hours targeting Sanaa and the Yemeni provinces of Al-Jawf, Taiz, Hajjah, Saada, and Marib.
He put the total number of airstrikes and missile attacks since the escalation began at 1,576.
Saree also warned international airlines using Saudi airspace against continuing their flights, saying it was now within the group’s area of operations, except for the airspace over Mecca and Medina.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the Houthi claims

articles.title: Why the U.S. Bomber Withdrawal From a U.K. Air Base Is Significant
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said Monday afternoon that "threats" had prompted the U.S. to remove all of its B-1 Air Force bombers from the RAF Fairford base in southern England over the weekend. The move came a week after several men were arrested nearby in relation to a suspected terror plot, which the U.K. government believes may be linked to Iran.
When asked if there was a specific threat that led to the bombers being moved, Trump told reporters: “Yeah, I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by accident. There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy… why should we leave them there? We moved them around a little bit, not very far.”
He added that Washington “actually knows the people that made the threat.” When asked if they are linked to Iran, Trump responded: “They would be linked to Iran.”
A U.S. Defense Department official had earlier told TIME that all the U.S. bombers had been ”re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” but did not offer a specific reason behind the move, instead saying that U.S. bombers “routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.” The official added that America’s bomber force remains “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities… anywhere, anytime.” Hours before Trump's remarks, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed the idea that the removal of U.S. bombers was directly connected to the foiled Fairford plot, insisting he has “confidence” in the security of U.S. bases.
A spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the RAF Fairford base remains safe, but refused to offer any specific comment on the military operations of “foreign nations.” The British Ministry of Defense directed TIME to the U.S. Air Force when approached for comment.
The move comes after five men, all U.K. nationals, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses on Sept. 27, following a suspected terror plot nearby RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base. Amid ongoing investigations, British counterterrorism police arrested a dual British-Iranian national in central London on Oct. 1 on suspicion of terrorist acts in connection with the incident. All arrestees have been released on bail.
David Dunn, a professor of international politics at the University of Birmingham, says the U.S. withdrawal from Fairford is “historic, unprecedented, and an indication of the sense of vulnerability” surrounding U.S. military assets abroad.
“Fairford is normally the place during a crisis where America sends bombers to beef up America's military capability and its formal operating bases, whether that's for operations in Europe, like the Kosovo campaign, or for operations in the Gulf through 2003 onwards, or indeed for operations in Iran,” Dunn tells TIME. “This [removal] is an indication of concerns about the safety of those assets in their forward operating bases.”
Dunn adds “the haste” with which the operation took place over the weekend is also noteworthy, referencing reports that some of the aircraft had only been there for a relatively short period of time, having arrived recently as part of a rotation.
U.K. and U.S. officials suspect Iranian involvement in RAF Fairford plot
Both U.K. and U.S. officials have voiced suspicion of Iranian involvement in the suspected terror plot that has led to several arrests.
Burnham on Sept. 30 said the U.K. believes Iran was likely involved in the incident. “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” he said, adding that British forces were “working closely” with U.S. counterparts.
Iran has vehemently denied any involvement. In the immediate aftermath of the initial arrests, the Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. After Burnham’s comments, Iran doubled down on its denial, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accusing the U.K. of “barking up the wrong tree.”
Trump previously said the five men arrested at the scene had been under “investigation” prior to the arrests and were looking to cause “big damage.” Asked whether Iran was involved in the suspect terror plot, he said, “it might be,” but did not offer further details.
Dunn says that although Iran “hasn't got the range to [directly] attack bases in the U.K.,” it does not necessarily remove the potential threat to U.S. assets stationed there. “Iran—by doing things via proxies, organized criminal gangs, or hiring people gangs through payments through the dark web—can still have a military effect and a deterrent effect on the operation of a base like Fairford,” he says.
Counter Terrorism Policing has said it is looking at all angles, citing possible foreign-state involvement as one line of inquiry. It has urged against conclusions being drawn in what is a high-profile and active investigation.
How RAF Fairford has supported U.S. military operations for decades
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. The base, which opened in 1944, has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
The U.S. Air Force describes RAF Fairford as its “preferred” European “bomber forward operating location” and previously said it has used Fairford “nearly continuously” since the base was constructed.
Former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer initially refused to allow U.S. access to U.K. military bases in its offensive strikes against Iran—a move that earned him the wrath of Trump. Starmer changed his position in March, authorizing the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned the base could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military, insisting it makes the U.K. a “participant in aggression” in the war.
Starmer had previously warned the British public of the general threat posed by Iran. On Feb. 28, in an address to the nation hours after the U.S. and Israel launched its initial strikes against Iran, he said: “Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community. Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil.”

articles.title: Report: Iranian drone plot to kill US pilots forced B-1 bombers out of UK base
articles.body:
The United States urgently withdrew all 12 of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain after intelligence warned of a potentially complex Iranian drone attack targeting the aircraft and U.S. personnel at the base, according to American media reports. 
The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. and European officials believed Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind plans to damage the bombers and kill personnel, including American pilots.
U.S. officials said the suspected plan may have resembled Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb, in which drones were smuggled deep into Russia and launched near military airfields, damaging several strategic aircraft. The possibility raised concerns that small drones launched close to a base could threaten even heavily protected military installations.
President Donald Trump acknowledged Monday that intelligence about a threat had influenced the decision to move the bombers. "We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there?" he said. Asked whether those behind the threat were linked to Iran, Trump said: "They would be linked to Iran."
Vice President JD Vance said Washington believed Iran was continuing a decades-long pattern of terrorism against the United States and others. "So we are being extremely cautious," he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was more cautious, saying he could not confirm a direct connection between the suspected plot and the redeployment.
British officials said RAF Fairford remained safe and declined to comment on U.S. military decisions. The U.S. Air Force said the bombers had returned to their home stations in the United States.
Trump later addressed the war with Iran during a campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, where he played down rising fuel prices. "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe," he said, adding: "They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay."
Trump also said the war would end "very soon" and was "essentially almost over with." Referring to Iran, he added: "They always say they have a big threshold for pain. They need it."

articles.title: South Korea has become one of Russia’s biggest fuel suppliers. Some shipments are arriving on sanctioned tankers.
articles.body:
South Korea has become one of Russia’s biggest fuel suppliers. Some shipments are arriving on sanctioned tankers.
By the end of summer, South Korea had become Russia’s second-largest supplier of petroleum products, and sanctioned tankers were among those used to ship the fuel, The Guardian reported.
Tankers made 14 voyages from several South Korean ports to Russia’s Far East in July and August, carrying 176,000 tons of fuel, mostly diesel, according to The Guardian.
Seven tankers plied the routes, three of them under British and EU sanctions. One, the tanker Chongchon, did not even enter South Korean ports: its fuel was transferred from another vessel at sea, a method that conceals the cargo’s origin.
In at least two more cases, sanctioned tankers loading at South Korean ports officially listed Japan as their destination but instead headed for Vladivostok. Exactly who owned and sold the fuel remains unclear.
Russia imported 368,000 tons of petroleum products by sea in August, with 112,000 tons supplied by South Korea. Only India supplied more fuel to Russia that month.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry declined to comment on the shipments or the use of sanctioned tankers. It said only that Seoul “supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”
South Korea has supplied Ukraine with humanitarian aid since the full-scale war with Russia began, along with non-lethal military equipment such as body armor and demining vehicles, The Guardian reported. But Seoul is trying to balance its support for Kyiv against its desire to maintain good relations with Moscow, and has only partially joined Western sanctions, mainly through export controls on industrial equipment and high-tech goods.
The fuel shipments, amid a crisis in Russia caused by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, could expose Seoul as a “weak link” in Western efforts to pressure the Kremlin, The Guardian concluded.
The Guardian’s report on fuel shipments from South Korea to Russia came amid a diplomatic row between Seoul and Kyiv. At the U.N. General Assembly in late September, Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had transferred to South Korea two North Korean soldiers captured in early 2025.
Seoul accused Zelensky of violating an agreement to keep the transfer secret, noting that Ukraine itself had originally insisted on the secrecy. South Korea demanded that Kyiv issue an official apology.
Today, South Korea’s foreign minister, Cho Hyun, said he had received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, but that its level was different “from the level we expect.” He said Seoul now intends to “take firm measures.”
