articles.title: From making interceptors to guarding sky: Ukrainian drone maker gets its own private air defense unit and will pay for it from weapon sales
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone maker just got its own air defense unit, and says it has already downed Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has issued an order granting the Night Hornets, the anti-Shahed unit of interceptor maker Wild Hornets, the status of a private air defense, and the company announced it is starting to build its own network of remotely launched interceptor drones.
Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-powered Shahed drones, which cuts the reaction time of Ukraine's mobile fire groups from about a minute to as little as six seconds. Now, a private company joins the air defense line, while Ukrainian military intelligence says Russia is producing up to 500 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones a month.
The planned network will combine remote-control centers, a grid of remote interceptor launches built on the company's Hornet Vision Ctrl technology, and field positions. Wild Hornets will not sell protection for individual sites and will pay for the unit from drone sales profit.
"The unit has more than 50 downed Shaheds to its name, including jet-powered ones. We create technologies that work. We use them ourselves to protect our country," the company says.
Air Force commanders will direct the crews
The crews already go on daily combat duty alongside the military and will take orders from the Air Force command. The unit draws on Wild Hornets instructors and test pilots, including veterans of the war and pilots who rose from beginners to instructors. The company wants to fold private air defense into the country's overall system, including over Kyiv.
Air alerts now swallow nearly a third of mall hours
Due to Russia's jet-powered drones, air-raid alerts covered 30.8 percent of shopping-center operating hours across Ukraine in September, a record, up from 22 percent in August and 14.1 percent a year earlier, the Ukrainian Council of Shopping Centers reports. The average mall has now lost 176.5 working days since the full-scale invasion, including 9.6 in September alone.
Kyiv shows the sharpest jump. The share of alert time during mall hours in the capital rose from 11.6 percent in August to 32.7 percent in September, the council said.
The damage reaches well beyond the malls. Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said on 12 September.

articles.title: NATO Uses Lessons-Learned in Ukraine to Plan Russian Defeat in 3D+ Battlespace
articles.body:
NATO is drafting a strategy designed to defeat a potential Russian attack on its eastern flank quickly and decisively by combining conventional military power with drones and artificial intelligence.
The document, titled “Theory of Victory,” is being developed under NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) Gen. Alexus Grynkewich and is expected to be presented in Poland on Monday, Oct. 12, Bloomberg reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bloomberg reviewed an unclassified version of the document, which is intended to clarify how NATO would respond if Russian forces entered the territory of an alliance member.
The strategy remains a planning document rather than an indication that NATO believes a Russian conventional attack is imminent.
“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage,” Grynkewich’s spokesperson, Col. Martin O’Donnell, told Bloomberg.
O’Donnell declined to discuss operational details but said the alliance needed to prepare now to deter aggression and prevail if attacked. He also stressed that NATO remained a “purely defensive” alliance.
Drones and AI would support conventional forces
Under the proposed strategy, NATO would initially seek to stop an incursion using land forces and capabilities developed through its Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.
These would include low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-assisted targeting integrated with conventional weapons and military units.
Russian Authorities Won’t Confirm Pneumonic Plague Outbreak in Central Siberia
After securing freedom of movement, allied forces would attempt to disrupt and destroy the enemy’s command-and-control structure, with the aim of defeating the attacking forces before they could establish a lasting foothold on NATO territory.
The plan emphasizes avoiding unintended provocations while demonstrating enough military readiness to convince an adversary that an attack could not succeed.
It also covers hybrid threats – hostile actions such as sabotage, cyberattacks, interference with infrastructure and covert operations that remain below the threshold of open warfare.
Russia has reportedly ordered its intelligence services to intensify hybrid operations across NATO and EU countries, including possible sabotage against military facilities, critical infrastructure and communications systems.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said there are currently no indications that Russia is preparing a conventional assault on the alliance. However, European governments expect Moscow’s hybrid campaign to continue and potentially intensify.
NATO applies lessons from Ukraine
The strategy reflects lessons from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, where inexpensive drones, electronic warfare and rapidly updated software have transformed even frontline 2D battlefield operations into 3D-plus battlespace operations.
NATO has already been testing drones, unmanned ground vehicles, counter-drone equipment and new communications systems under the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.
The alliance has also explored an AI-assisted automated defensive zone along its borders with Russia and Belarus. The proposed system would use interconnected sensors, drones and weapons to detect hostile movements while reducing the number of soldiers required to monitor exposed areas.
In July, NATO members agreed to invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over five years. The alliance is also developing a counter-drone marketplace and plans to train five times as many military drone operators by the end of 2027.
Allies face spending and force decisions
The proposal comes as European NATO members sharply increase defense expenditure but debate how to divide funding between tanks, artillery and other conventional weapons and newer technologies demonstrated in Ukraine.
The US reportedly sent allies a questionnaire during the summer asking about their defense spending and support for President Donald Trump’s policies as Washington considered reducing some American military assets assigned to Europe.
The questionnaire also asked whether NATO members could contribute additional forces to Grynkewich’s defense plans.
“Theory of Victory” is therefore intended not only to describe a possible military response but also to show governments what forces and technologies they would need to finance before a crisis begins.
The initiative comes amid growing concern about Russian drone incursions, sabotage and airspace violations along NATO’s eastern flank. Rutte has said the alliance deliberately keeps the precise threshold for activating Article 5 ambiguous, preventing adversaries from calculating how far they can escalate without triggering a collective response.

articles.title: Russia says potential deployment of NATO base, nuclear arms in Lithuania to raise tensions
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
The Kremlin said on Tuesday that the potential deployment of a NATO military base or nuclear weapons in Lithuania would inevitably be seen by Russia as a step toward raising tensions.
Commenting on a vote by Lithuania’s parliament to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on deploying nuclear weapons on the country’s territory, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a press briefing that the move cannot be viewed as “anything other than a step toward escalating tensions.”
“Neither of these moves will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary – and to our regret – they will mark yet another significant escalation of tensions,” Peskov said.
He added that Russia will, consequently, be compelled to take “all necessary measures to guarantee its own security.”
The remarks come as the Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, voted earlier Tuesday to advance a constitutional amendment that would remove a ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory.
According to public broadcaster LRT, the amendment passed its first reading with 106 lawmakers voting in favor, while the final vote for the amendment is scheduled for Jan. 12.
The parliament conducted a vote late last month on amendment, receiving 99-13, with five abstentions, in favor of the proposal.
Peskov also commented on remarks by US President Donald Trump concerning reports of cases of pneumonic plague in Russia, saying it is always good when mutual assistance is offered.
He said Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor is providing "comprehensive information" on the situation in the country's Siberian region of Irkutsk.
Last week, Russian media outlets said Rospotrebnadzor defined the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region as stable amid reports of a person being diagnosed of a “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
The reports said measures had been taken in connection with the case, which involved an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The employee has died.

articles.title: America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
articles.body:
America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
The Pentagon’s decision to relocate B-1 bombers from the British air base comes after months of frustration in the Trump administration over Britain’s defense spending.
LONDON — Britain and the U.S. sought to ease friction Monday after American bombers were suddenly moved amid major security concerns at the base that hosted U.S. aircraft used to strike Iran.
The U.S. move is the latest stumbling block in the special relationship between the allies and underscores reservations in Donald Trump’s administration about how the U.K. is handling its defense and security commitments.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday that it had removed all B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford air base — where they were deployed to conduct what have been termed as "defensive" strikes against Iran — and sent them back to their home stations in America.
Advertisement
Trump went further, telling journalists Monday evening: "We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there? ... If we're going to be threatened we're just going to move them, and that sort of alleviates that."
It comes as Britain's counter-terrorism agencies investigate a suspected terror plot against the air base, which the U.K. government believes involves Tehran.
Trump on Monday added: "We actually know the people that made the threat, and they've got themselves a big problem," adding in response to a follow-up question: "They would be linked to Iran."
He later said that he believes the U.K. is still a safe place for U.S. forces.
Downing Street had earlier insisted that the base was safe, but refused to comment directly on America’s decision to remove the bombers from the area.
The move comes as the Trump administration has grown increasingly frustrated with the U.K.’s defense spending and the White House's continuing anger that the U.K. didn’t send warships to the Middle East to help with the American blockade of Iranian shipping.
Advertisement
Something deeper is wrong
London has yet to outline a path to meet the NATO standard of spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035 — up from its current level of around 2.7%. It has also been shut out of a subgroup within the alliance convened by Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby. The group is slated to meet again in Poland some time later this month.
Late last month, Colby hinted at that frustration with London, saying the countries' long history will continue to bind them, but the British government needs to make the case to its people for spending more on defense.
“There's this incredible legacy, and that's what we want to rekindle,” Colby said. “Exactly how you convince the British people [to spend more on defense] I would not presume to say, but … there's probably sort of a degree of reconciliation between what the U.K. wants to be doing, what it spends, and what it spends on, because you know a modern military is not cheap.”
The U.S. is also conducting a sweeping review of its posture in European NATO countries — including the U.K. — which will determine the number of American troops and military assets on the continent.
Sophia Gaston, a senior national security researcher at King’s College London, said: “The Trump administration is undeniably sensitive to the costs of the Iran conflict as they head into the midterms next month, so their caution is understandable.
An armored vehicle is seen at RAF Fairford on Sept. 28, 2026. | Ben Stansall/AFP via Getty Images
“It’s also hard not to, at some level, perceive a degree of uncertainty about the capacity of the British services to currently prevent such an attack. That partly reflects the innate challenge drones and other aspects of modern warfare pose to the sitting ducks of expensive kit.
Advertisement
“But it also speaks to the American wariness towards the pressured state of Britain’s military capabilities. Not only does Washington no longer wish to be solely responsible for allies’ protection, its expectations for the security allies offer its bases has also increased.”
Trump on Monday praised his relationship with new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham. He said: "He's liberal, very liberal, but I hear he's going to open up North Sea oil if he does that in Aberdeen. If he does that, you're going to have a rich country. If he doesn't, you're going to have a bankrupt country."
Britain’s security concerns
In May, the U.K. raised its terrorism threat level to “severe” — meaning a terrorist attack is highly likely — after its MI5 security service said the U.K. had been “experiencing a gradual increase in terrorist threats for some time” including from hostile states like Iran.
In Britain, police and the security services are dealing with a three-fold threat from Iran-backed groups: attacks against Iranian dissidents, attacks against the country’s Jewish population, and the targeting of U.S. assets such as those used for strikes against Tehran.
Counter Terrorism Policing is currently investigating potential Iranian state involvement in a major incident at RAF Fairford on Sept. 27, when police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base.
Six men — including a British-Iranian national — have so far been arrested on suspicion of terror offenses. All have subsequently been released on bail while police continue their investigation.
Advertisement
US strike capability
Though the Pentagon stressed that bombers remain “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities” — including from the U.S. mainland — removing them would make any further American strikes on Iran more complex, since the bombers would have to double their flight path from the continental U.S. to the Middle East.
There is a fresh U.S. buildup in the region, with a third aircraft carrier currently steaming across the Pacific along with several large amphibious ships carrying 2,500 Marines, joining the 2,500 already at sea in the Middle East, giving President Donald Trump more options should he restart the bombing campaign after the U.S. midterm elections in early November.
Christoph Bergs, a research analyst at the RUSI defense think tank, said: “The basing of US B-1 bombers at RAF Fairford for operational employment against Iran was based on the UK stipulation that these were only used for defensive strikes. This likely included a more modest targeting list. Their withdrawal reduces the capacity to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat.”
The Pentagon declined to comment on whether it will, or is considering, the removal of other aircraft from British bases used to support operations against Iran.
This article has been updated with comments from Donald Trump.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis claim striking Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis claim striking Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
Iran-backed Houthis on Monday said they had struck Riyadh's international airport, an Aramco refinery and several other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.
Pakistan and Turkey meanwhile pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.
The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.
Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on X that its naval forces had hit "military targets" belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.
They "destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines" and had "thwarted a planned attack" targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.
Loud explosions rattled Riyadh on Monday evening as the fighting escalated, and a Houthi spokesman said the group had hit the Saudi capital's King Khalid International Airport as well as an Aramco refinery and other targets in the kingdom's south.
The government announced on Sunday the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory, home to most of Yemen's population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
Last month the Iran-backed group seized swathes of coastline along the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a chokepoint for oil and cargo shipping, in Yemen's deadliest fighting in years.
The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen's civil war flared back to life, and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.
On Monday, representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other's aid in the event of any attack.
They also agreed "to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom".
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", and condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia.
Global oil system 'straining'
Houthi attacks have also targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.
A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack on Sunday had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom's exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.
Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war, before the Houthis began targeting the world's largest oil exporter.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles were "scarily thin" owing to the war.
"The system is already straining," Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.
Mocha fighting
Yemeni military sources said Monday that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the Houthi-held city of Mocha, but stopped short of confirming an official announcement of the port's recapture.
While the war in Yemen predates the broader Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, it has become its most active front in recent weeks. According to UN figures, the fighting has displaced more than 184,000 people.
Yemen's civil war broke out in 2014, with the Saudis intervening the following March, but fighting was paused by a 2022 ceasefire that held until July of this year.

articles.title: Can Yemen's divided coalition turn the tide against the Houthis?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Can Yemen's divided coalition turn the tide against the Houthis?
When the Houthis launched attacks along Yemen's western coast on 3 September, internationally recognised government-aligned forces were unprepared for what was the largest offensive since the ceasefire signed in 2022.
Their response revealed a series of operational failures that allowed the Houthis to advance across 5,000 square kilometres, seizing the port city of Mocha, several coastal positions, and the islands of Mayyun and Hanish to gain control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Reported accounts of the initial Houthi offensive show that the fragmented government-aligned forces lacked military coordination and timely support from Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The Houthis penetrated opposition communications, tracked troop movements, and cut off frontline units from command. They reportedly relied on Iranian advisers, who provided direct support for their blitzkrieg.
Over the following days, Saudi airstrikes and Yemeni government-aligned counterattacks sought to reclaim lost ground, including areas along the Taiz–Aden route.
Combat is currently concentrated in Taiz province, where the Houthis are attempting to consolidate control over captured territory.
"Their objective is to consolidate gains by securing the mountainous areas overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and blocking the road between Taiz and Lahej and Aden to cut off military support," Yemeni political analyst and journalist Mohammed Al-Qadhi told The New Arab.
"By recapturing these zones lost in 2017, the Houthis shield themselves from government and Saudi counter-offensives, avoiding exposure in the flat coastal areas."
Reports also suggest Houthi troop movements towards Saada province on the Saudi border.
The fault lines in Yemen's anti-Houthi camp
Regional and Western officials told Reuters last week that Saudi Arabia was planning a large-scale offensive against the Houthis, including a possible coastal push to secure Red Sea shipping, or an assault on multiple fronts.
On Sunday, Yemen’s government then announced the ambitious goal of retaking all Houthi territory, with operations beginning at dawn.
So far, according to the Saudi-led coalition, the military has carried out over 1,000 airstrikes using 100 warplanes as part of Operation 'Dawn of Yemen'.
The Houthis effectively encircled the city of Taiz the same day, cutting off the main supply route linking the city to Aden, the capital of the government.
As the war unfolds, the Houthi offensive could expose the limits of Yemen’s anti-Houthi coalition, with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government struggling to overcome fractured command structures and competing political agendas threatening to undermine their campaign.
Yemen's anti-Houthi camp has never been a single bloc, with the Saudi-backed government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), an uneasy coalition of rival factions.
Among them is the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a UAE-backed separatist movement that had been represented on the council until January and seeks an independent southern Yemen.
Its offensive to expand control, launched in December 2025, was rapidly reversed by Saudi-backed forces in January, prompting the UAE to withdraw its remaining forces from Yemen.
Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late president Ali Abdullah Saleh, meanwhile, commands the National Resistance Forces (NRF), which favour a unified Yemen but were long backed by Abu Dhabi.
Islah, the Sunni Islamist party with historical ties to the Muslim Brotherhood - an association it denies - has long opposed the southern separatist project and supports a unified Yemen.
The UAE-backed Giants Brigades and National Resistance Forces (NRF) retain distinct command structures, even as Riyadh seeks to bring Yemen's fragmented armed groups under a more unified state command through the Nation's Shield and other security and military structures.
Operationally, the NRF, Giants Brigades, and National Shield Forces (operating under the PLC) maintain separate command structures and logistics rather than a unified field command, while the PLC itself has yet to establish an integrated military leadership.
Coordination is made even harder by lingering anger in the south after the STC's contested dissolution in January, the rise of the southern region of Hadhramawt as an independent political force, and Islah’s mistrust of UAE-backed groups.
"On this basis, a unified front under a single command with a shared offensive objective appears unlikely in the coming months," Ahmed Alshargabi, a research analyst at the Yemen Policy Centre, told The New Arab.
“The more probable outcome is defensive coordination aimed at blocking further Houthi advances toward Lahj, Aden, Bab al-Mandeb and Marib, without any real integration of forces.”
He added that a real alliance depends on an understanding between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, unified funding, southern political guarantees, and an empowered field command.
Rival regional visions for Yemen
The Saudi-UAE rivalry plays a critical role in the anti-Houthi coalition’s internal fragmentation.
As Andreas Krieg, associate professor in Security Studies at King’s College London, explained to The New Arab, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have different interests and cultural approaches to Yemen.
Abu Dhabi does not see a unified Yemen as a necessity, while Riyadh favours a unified sovereign state. The result is a fragmented landscape in which few Yemeni forces have a stake in fighting beyond their own regions.
“It’s unrealistic to think that the southerners will fight in the north against the Houthis, which most southerners see as a problem for northerners,” he told The New Arab.
“Even if there is a reconciliation between the UAE and Saudi Arabia, it’s very unlikely the southerners will volunteer to take the war into northern Yemen. They have no stakes there. So ultimately what we end up with is a shifting stalemate.”
Last week, UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed visited Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh. It was the first visit by a senior Emirati official since a diplomatic rift erupted between the two Gulf states in January.
Alshargabi said the meeting reflects a tactical rapprochement driven by Houthi advances and Riyadh’s reliance on UAE-backed forces, but Abu Dhabi’s potential demands could fuel new instability and leave their rivalry unresolved.
Krieg added that potential UAE support is unlikely to alter the war’s trajectory, given the fragmented command structures and the limited reach of southern forces.
In early 2026, Yemen's government attempted to consolidate southern forces by integrating former STC units into the Interior Ministry, reshuffling commanders, and tolerating hybrid arrangements. Some experts argue that a state monopoly on force is unlikely given Yemen’s tribal loyalties, whereas reducing the number of non-state armed actors is more realistic.
Forging military cooperation among anti-Houthi forces is far easier than achieving political unity, according to Anas Alqaed, director of programmes at the Gulf International Forum, because battlefield coordination requires no formal political agreement.
“The coalition lost ground mainly due to a breakdown in command and control, and fixing that could take anywhere from a few months to two years,” he told The New Arab.
“However, I do not believe the anti-Houthi coalition is ready to reverse the Houthi advance, and we will not see a joint Saudi-Emirati or global coalition form against them until they actively move to close the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.”
After the US declined Saudi Arabia’s request for military support, Riyadh turned to Pakistan and Turkey, signatories of the recent Mecca defence pact. Both have limited their commitments to technical support, while their defence and foreign ministers and military chiefs are due to meet in Riyadh this week.
Riccardo Gasco, foreign policy coordinator at InstanPol Institute, said expectations around the Mecca Pact are inflated, particularly over the prospect of automatic military support.
“Turkey has a clear interest in stopping the Houthis in relation to Bab al-Mandeb Strait as a trade corridor, but strictly automatic military support remains highly improbable,” he told The New Arab.
Among Saudi Arabia's other allies, Britain offered air refuelling, while France announced the deployment of military personnel to the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.
Unconfirmed reports say Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has offered to help Gulf states in a wider campaign against the Houthis. But Krieg argued that "the Israeli intelligence networks in Yemen are very poor", with Riyadh and Abu Dhabi far better placed.
"That is not something the Israelis can deliver," he said, adding that Israeli involvement could further fracture the anti-Houthi camp and fuel Houthi propaganda, while Tel Aviv may use its assistance as a card to play in its push for normalisation.
A new stalemate?
While the fragmentation of the anti-Houthi camp benefits the Houthis and Iran - exerting pressure on a second strategic chokepoint after Hormuz and handing Tehran greater leverage in US negotiations - it also strengthens the Houthis' position against Riyadh.
As the trajectory of the Yemen war remains uncertain, experts lay out several scenarios. One is containment, with the Houthis consolidating gains as far as Bab al-Mandeb and front lines settling around Lahj, Taiz, and Marib.
This would leave Yemen de facto partitioned and Riyadh entering negotiations from a position of weakness.
Alternatively, a limited counter-offensive could see coalition forces retake ground around Dhubab and Mokha, though this would require unified command and Saudi–Emirati coordination.
Other possibilities include regional escalation via attacks on Saudi infrastructure or shipping, or a return to UN-led diplomacy.
Dario Sabaghi is a freelance journalist interested in human rights
Follow him on X: @DarioSabaghi
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: US nuke test detection experiment bid to assert its hegemony: Ex-nuclear chief
articles.body:
MUMBAI: Former chief of Atomic Energy Commission of India, Anil Kakodkar, who played a key role in the Pokhran nuclear weapons tests, said the main aim of the US conducting what is called a non-proliferation experiment last week was to assert its global nuclear hegemony and prevent other nations from conducting atomic tests.On Sept 30, the US conducted an experiment which will enable it to detect whether countries are carrying out low-yield nuclear explosions.Kakodkar told TOI, “The US is attempting to get more sensitivity in terms of nuclear tests detection. There is a generic understanding that nuclear tests will not be carried out. But what if a country executes a test camouflaged?”Asked whether the motive of the test jeopardised nuclear sovereignty of countries, he said the main aim was to assert global US nuclear leadership and stop other countries from carrying out atomic weapons tests.A recent study by Federation of American Scientists says that currently India has 190 nuclear warheads and has enough military plutonium for 140 to 225 nuclear warheads.Anil Anand, considered the father of India’s nuclear submarine programme, quoted US National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) and told TOI that in the experiment researchers gathered measurements using a broad suite of advanced sensors, including accelerometers, seismometers, chemical and radiotracer samplers.
He said, “Together these measurements will improve scientists’ understanding of the signatures produced by underground explosions and strengthen US’ ability to detect and characterise nuclear explosive events.”According to NNSA, it “conducted a subsurface, non-nuclear chemical high-explosive experiment” at the Nevada National Security Site. An FB post by NNSA states, “If foreign countries test in secret, we will know.
The goal? Keeping the US one step ahead.” It further said the experiment assumes significance in the context of China supposedly having conducted a nuclear test in June 2020 secretly.
“It takes nuclear expertise to detect nuclear activities, and experiments like these ensure America remains unmatched in detection,” said Brandon Williams, NNSA administrator. “Trump Administration has made it clear that the US will lead from a position of strength. You cannot evade American innovation. With this experiment, we are sending a clear message that under this administration, America will never be outmatched.”

articles.title: Ukraine using AI-enabled robot guns to counter Russian drones
articles.body:
Ukraine commenced using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to bring down Russia's new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, according to its air force on Monday.
For months, Kyiv has been seeking a way to intercept the new Russian drones pounding the Ukrainian capital, even as it faces a dire lack of suitable ammunition to take them out.
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shahed drones.
As part of Ukraine's efforts to respond, "robotic turrets are now being installed on bridges," air force spokesperson Col. Yuri Ignat told national television.
"There have already been shoot downs," of the drones, including the bigger, faster and more powerful Geran-5 version, he told national television.
Speaking to Agence France-Presse (AFP), Ignat explained that the new turrets, which have been seen by AFP journalists in the Ukrainian capital, use "optical vision and artificial intelligence to eliminate the human factor and deliver strikes."
Sergiy Beskrestnov, a technology adviser to the Ukrainian defense ministry, explained on Telegram over the weekend that the new automated turrets were "an innovative Ukrainian solution that shoots down (drones) using machine guns controlled by artificial intelligence."
He said that 12 of the turrets had been installed in Kyiv, adding that "more turrets will be installed in the future."
Ignat acknowledged that the new system had a small operating radius.
"It can operate at about one kilometer plus (0.6 miles). And it works when conditions are favorable, when the attack approach angle is suitable," he told AFP.
"This is not some kind of panacea," he said, stressing that the turrets were part of "an integrated air defense system that provides engagement of these targets at different tiers."
"Of course, we rely on all available assets."
Ukraine has been accelerating the integration of artificial intelligence into its defense capabilities and is already using the technology on the frontlines to guide drones, detect targets for strikes and coordinate large-scale operations.

articles.title: Kremlin Warns Lithuania Lifting Nuclear Arms Ban Risks Escalation
articles.body:
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned that a preliminary decision by NATO member Lithuania to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear arms on its territory could lead to a new round of escalation in the region.
Lithuania's parliament on Tuesday voted in favor of removing the ban, in the first of two ballots required for the change.
Asked by reporters how Russia viewed that development, as well as a proposal floated this month by U.S. President Donald Trump to build an American military base in the Baltic country, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said:
“If the military infrastructure of what is, in effect, NATO's leading country (the U.S.) is moving closer to our borders, then, of course, this cannot be perceived as anything other than a step towards escalating tensions.”
He added: “The same applies to the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighboring state. Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent; on the contrary, they will, much to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions.”
Lithuania, a member of the EU and NATO, borders Russia and close Moscow ally Belarus. The U.S. has kept an armored battalion of almost 1,000 troops there since 2019, in overlapping rotations, meaning the troops arrive and leave every few months.
The legal overhaul of the nuclear arms ban, which requires a two-thirds majority in two parliamentary votes to go into effect, is set to remove prohibitions put in place more than three decades ago after Lithuania broke away from the Soviet Union.

articles.title: Cambrian Patrol expands for largest exercise yet
articles.body:
Exercise Cambrian Patrol has expanded to its largest edition since the event began in 1959, with 140 patrols taking part in a demanding two-day assessment across the Welsh mountains, according to the British Army.
Running from 2 to 13 October, the 2026 exercise has been increased to meet demand from British units and international partners, with additional phases and patrols added to the programme.
The field includes 75 Regular Army patrols, 15 Reserve teams and 13 from University Officer Training Corps units, alongside 35 international patrols and two combined British Army and international teams. More than 350 personnel are supporting the exercise.
Each eight-person patrol begins near Builth Wells after an initial equipment inspection at Beulah, before receiving orders and completing its battle preparation. Teams then cover up to 40 miles across the Welsh mountains over roughly 48 hours before finishing at Sennybridge. Performance is assessed throughout the route, with teams competing for gold, silver and bronze medals or a completion coin.
According to a news update from the British Army, Major Darren Pridmore, Officer Commanding Exercise Cambrian Patrol 2026, said: “This is all designed to test the skills that soldiers need to survive and fight on the modern battlefield. It is a demanding assessment of leadership, resilience, tactical judgement and teamwork under pressure.”
The exercise is delivered by 160th (Welsh) Brigade on behalf of Commander Land Forces, with training direction provided by the Director Land Warfare Centre. Tasks this year include casualty evacuation, intelligence gathering, artillery fire planning, vehicle recognition, simulated chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear incidents, reconnaissance, minefield crossings and attacks on enemy positions.
Organisers have also increased the emphasis on small-unit leadership, placing junior officers and non-commissioned officers in situations where they must make tactical decisions while managing fatigue and maintaining the momentum of their patrol. The 2026 exercise has been adjusted to incorporate lessons associated with contemp rary conflicts, particularly the increased prevalence of persistent surveillance and unmanned aircraft.
Patrols will be tracked by both ground forces and unmanned aerial systems, requiring teams to consider concealment, routes and movement patterns while completing their assigned tasks. Mobility and survivability assessments include crossing the Forward Line of Own Troops, river crossings and navigating minefields during reconnaissance missions.
The exercise also includes a greater emphasis on the collection and integration of battlefield information. Patrols will use safe houses, static sensors and unmanned aerial systems to build an intelligence picture, combining information gathered from several sources before identifying and reporting targets.
Major Pridmore said: “We’ve preserved the spirit of Cambrian Patrol while adapting it to reflect the realities of contemporary conflict.
“From drones and persistent surveillance, to intelligence integration and CBRN readiness, this year’s exercise better reflects the challenges soldiers can expect to face on operations.”
Chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear readiness will also receive greater scrutiny during the exercise, with teams assessed on whether they arrive with the necessary equipment and can continue operating in a simulated contaminated environment.
The changes reflect the Army’s wider effort to adapt training to battlefield conditions in which small units can face persistent observation, widespread use of drones and a greater requirement to combine information from distributed sensors.
Pridmore added: “The battlefield is evolving rapidly and success increasingly depends on close collaboration between operators, innovators and industry.
“Cambrian Patrol provides a unique opportunity to bring those communities together, helping us adapt faster, exploit emerging technologies and maintain operational advantage.”
International participation remains a major part of the event, with 35 overseas patrols taking part alongside British teams this year.
Cambrian Patrol has long been used by foreign armed forces as an opportunity to test their troops against British units in difficult terrain, while exposing participants to different tactical methods and operating procedures.
Major Pridmore said: “The United Kingdom does not fight alone. Future operations will be conducted alongside allies and partners, making interoperability and mutual understanding essential.”
The exercise takes place over terrain around the Brecon area of Wales, where weather, elevation and distance add to the tactical assessments faced by teams. Patrols must continue completing military tasks while carrying their equipment across the route and operating with limited rest.
Once the field phase is complete, teams undergo a detailed debrief and reporting process before their overall performance is assessed and the final medal standard determined.

articles.body:
PARIS, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- France on Tuesday test-fired a ballistic missile from the nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine Le Vigilant off the coast of Finistere in western France, French television channel BFM TV reported, citing the French Defense Ministry.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine prepares new contracts for air defense systems and missiles as infrastructure protection remains key challenge
articles.body:
Zelensky: Ukraine prepares new contracts for air defense systems and missiles as infrastructure protection remains key challenge
According to Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky made this statement during an evening video address, as reported by Ukrinform.
“Today, I spoke with Ukrainian Prime Minister SerhiyiKoretskyi about additional security measures. The Minister of Defense, the Minister of Infrastructure, and the Armed Forces of Ukraine all provided important briefings today. And we are increasing our level of protection every day. This applies to both turrets and special units tasked with shooting down ‘Shaheds.’ “We expect manufacturers to move quickly with the interceptors. The tasks have been defined, and funding is in place,” Zelensky noted.
According to him, Ukraine is preparing new contracts for air defense systems and missiles. The President emphasized that there are currently no public details regarding these agreements, but there may be “positive developments,” and he stressed that having the right solutions in place is crucial.
“It is important for us that these decisions exist. And I also ask our partners: we need more anti-ballistic systems to protect our infrastructure—that is the main challenge right now,” the President noted.
At the same time, he emphasized that world leaders understand the situation and recognize that Russia has no intention of shifting from escalation to negotiations.
Zelensky called on Ukraine’s leaders and partners in Europe and the United States to maximize protection against Russian strikes and diplomatic efforts in October following Russia’s attack on Kharkiv.
“Rescue operations continued all day today in Kharkiv following the Russian bombing. More than 50 people were injured. Searches were conducted for people trapped under the rubble, and, unfortunately, there have been fatalities. My condolences go out to all the families and loved ones,” Zelensky said.
The president emphasized that all of Ukraine’s leaders and partners in Europe and the United States need to focus their efforts specifically in October to maximize protection against Russian strikes and utilize all diplomatic avenues.
“Thank you to everyone who is truly helping out! And please, take care of yourselves,” he concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky held a meeting with the team from the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine and the diplomatic team from the Office of the President regarding the schedule for arms deliveries from partners, and also set new tasks for long-range operations.

articles.title: US conducts first flight test of HACM hypersonic missile — web portal
articles.body:
NEW YORK, October 6. /TASS/. The United States has carried out the first flight test of the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) at a test range in Australia, The War Zone (TWZ) portal reported.
The US Air Force’s hypersonic missile, developed by Raytheon in collaboration with Australian specialists, has finally entered, according to the website, "the flight test phase." At least one test has been conducted so far at the Woomera Test Range in Australia.
The HACM program has faced significant delays, the website reports, and the US Air Force took a risky step by scaling back the overall scope of testing in an effort to stay on schedule. The stated goal is "to initiate a rapid fielding effort and procure HACM in fiscal year 2027," according to TWZ.
According to a US Air Force spokesperson, the HACM tests were conducted as part of joint "continuous work to advance long-range strike capabilities." He did not specify when the testing occurred.
The technical specifications of the HACM missile are classified. According to media reports, the missile consists of two stages, a rocket booster and a scramjet cruiser, which separates from the booster and eventually dives toward its target. The missile is capable of reaching speeds of up to Mach 7. Its range is approximately 500 km.

articles.title: Taiwan Air Force plans US F-16V support talks next year
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force plans to send personnel to the US next year to attend a meeting on procuring operational-support equipment, weapons, and ammunition for its F-16V Block 70 fleet.
According to Ministry of National Defense budget documents, two officials will travel to the US for six days to review the procurement project’s progress and confirm that its milestones are completed on schedule and to the required standards, Liberty Times reported. They will also coordinate and manage action items. The trip is budgeted at NT$313,000 (US$9,860).
The F-16V Block 70 program involves more than delivering the aircraft themselves. Establishing operational capabilities also requires integrating avionics, electronic warfare systems, logistical support, and various weapons, Liberty Times reported.
The new fighter variants are equipped with the L3Harris Viper Shield all-digital electronic warfare system, which can detect, identify, and counter electronic threats. The system is integrated with the AN/APG-83 Active Electronically Scanned Array radar.
Taiwan’s F-16Vs can carry AIM-120 beyond-visual-range air-to-air missiles, AIM-9-series short-range missiles, AGM-88 anti-radiation missiles, AGM-84 Harpoon anti-ship missiles, and Joint Direct Attack Munitions.
The first two F-16V Block 70 jets landed at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung on Friday.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukrainian pilots to start training on French Rafale jets soon
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian pilots will soon start training in France on French Rafale fighter jets, and also announced the preparation of a new package of defense supplies from France.
"A good conversation with President Emmanuel Macron. Thank you for France's full support. We discussed Russia's terrorist escalation and our defense needs. New defense supplies are currently being prepared, and we expect the new package to arrive in Ukraine soon. We discussed its contents," Zelenskyy said in a post shared on Facebook on Monday.
According to him, Ukrainian pilots "will start training on French Rafale aircraft in France in the very near future."
"This is a significant step for Ukrainian combat aviation," the president said.
Zelenskyy also said Ukrainian and French teams are continuing to work on localizing the production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine.
"We are actively preparing the FREYJA system. We discussed where we can speed things up. We agreed to discuss everything in more detail during the meeting," he said.
Ukraine and France have agreed on the purchase of 16 Rafale fighter jets for the Ukrainian Armed Forces as the first batch of 100 aircraft, the acquisition of which was provided for in an agreement between the two countries in November 2025. The presidents of Ukraine and France, Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Emmanuel Macron, signed a joint declaration to that effect on July 14, 2026.
According to the agreement, the first four Rafale jets are to be handed over to the Ukrainian military upon completion of the training cycle for Ukrainian pilots and mechanics. Training was scheduled to begin in France in 2026.
The French side said the first Rafale jets could appear in Ukrainian skies in 2028-2029. At the same time, the agreement provides for the supply of weapons for the aircraft, including AASM bombs, MICA and Meteor missiles, as well as laser-guided missiles to counter drones.
The President of Ukraine also said that training for Ukrainian pilots and mechanics in France will begin as early as this year, after which the Ukrainian Armed Forces are set to receive the first four Rafale jets.

articles.title: Commandos land from German submarine on Scottish coast
articles.body:
British commandos have come ashore at Cape Wrath from a German attack submarine and directed the guns of a Portuguese frigate onto targets inland, during the largest test of every part of the UK Commando Force in fifteen years, according to the Royal Navy.
The landing took place during Exercise Strike Warrior, which the service describes as the first occasion since the war in Afghanistan on which all the specialist elements of the formation have worked together. More than 2,000 personnel from six nations are taking part, drawn from the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Canada, Germany, Norway and the United States, and deployed across the Western Isles, the North-West Approaches, Galloway, the Borders and the North Sea.
Navy and Army commandos from 148 Battery Commando Forward Observation Battery, the unit trained to carry out reconnaissance and call down naval gunfire from behind enemy lines, left the submarine in inflatable raiding boats and established an observation post on the cliffs at the most north-westerly point of mainland Britain. From there they directed the guns of the Portuguese warship NRP Dom Francisco de Almeida onto positions ashore.
The battery’s operations officer, who cannot be named for operational reasons, said: “This level of complexity and coordination of live assets has not been achieved by 148 Battery for nearly 30 years.
“We wanted to demonstrate to our partners across the United Kingdom Commando Force, wider UK Defence and NATO Special Operations Force community the type of missions we are prepared to execute against future threats.
“Warfighting is our focus, and we are prepared to employ specialist assets to deliver Multi-Domain Fires and Targeting.”
Three navies were involved in the single sequence at Cape Wrath. The German submarine found the targets, the commandos put themselves ashore without being seen, and the Portuguese ship supplied the firepower. The Royal Navy has not identified the submarine.
Earlier in the exercise the same battery controlled the naval gunfire of ships from Standing NATO Maritime Group One, the alliance’s standing task group in northern European waters. The Dutch frigate HNLMS Van Amstel and the Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS St John’s both worked with commandos in observation posts to bring their guns onto targets.
Eight warships and 19 aircraft are taking part in Strike Warrior, which began on 28 September and finishes on Friday. Alongside the gunnery serials, the exercise has covered amphibious landings, boarding operations, intelligence and surveillance missions, logistics and sustainment, maritime security and anti-submarine warfare. Commandos have flown drone missions including strikes and resupply to troops in contact, and have built underground medical facilities.
Cape Wrath matters to this kind of training because it is the only place in Britain, and one of very few in Europe, where warships can fire live rounds at a land target. The range takes in Garvie Island off the headland, and the combination of the cliffs behind and the open Atlantic in front is what allows observation parties to work close to live naval gunfire.
The participation of a German boat and a Portuguese frigate alongside Dutch and Canadian ships reflects how the Commando Force now expects to operate, which is as the land element of a NATO maritime group rather than as a national force working alone. Norway and the United States also have personnel committed, and the stated purpose of the exercise is rehearsing allied crisis response in the High North and the North Atlantic.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones kill two in Moscow Region – officials
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones kill two in Moscow Region – officials
Two civilians have been killed and nine injured after Ukraine launched 650 drones toward Moscow and the surrounding region overnight, local officials have said.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in the early hours of Tuesday that most of the UAVs were destroyed at “distant lines,” while 134 were intercepted on the approaches to Moscow itself.
In Moscow Region, air defenses neutralized 185 drones, Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported. A 20-year-old man was killed in the settlement of Radumlya, northwest of Moscow, while rescuers found a 71-year-old man dead beneath the rubble of a destroyed private home in Barybino, south of the capital, with a woman in the same building receiving injuries.
A man in Pokrovskoye, west of Moscow, was hospitalized with shrapnel wounds, while two residents of the Istra area, also west of the capital, were taken to hospital. Three people in Lyakhovo, south of Moscow, received medical care but declined hospitalization, Vorobyov added.
Vorobyov said a total of 47 private homes were damaged across the region. In Lobanovo, south of the capital, windows and balcony glazing were blown out in four apartments, while a nearby boiler house was also damaged. Three cars were hit, and a small fire at a warehouse in Litvinovo, northwest of Moscow, was extinguished, according to the governor.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, a total of 868 Ukrainian drones were intercepted across the country overnight.
On Tuesday, Rodion Miroshnik, the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry mission tracking alleged Ukrainian war crimes, told TASS that 29 civilians, including two children, were killed and 206 injured in Ukrainian attacks on Russian regions over the past week alone. He added that 98% were victims of drone strikes.
Ukraine has ramped up attacks deep into Russia in recent weeks, targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure. After Vladimir Zelensky pledged to escalate the strikes even further, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Sunday that it had “taken note” of the statement, vowing to intensify attacks on Ukrainian military and defense industrial facilities as well as related infrastructure. Moscow maintains it never targets civilians.

articles.title: Russia Says Ukraine Just Launched Its Biggest Strike of the War—1,750 Drones and 17 Flamingo Missiles

Russia Says Ukraine Just Launched Its Biggest Strike of the War—1,750 Drones and 17 Flamingo Missiles
Ukraine launched what Russia described as the largest combined drone and missile strike of the war, with 1,750 fixed-wing UAVs and 17 Flamingo cruise missiles allegedly used against targets across Russia over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed on October 6.
Moscow also said its air defenses intercepted two guided aerial bombs and one HIMARS rocket during the same period. The figures have not been independently verified.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
If accurate, the drone count would exceed Ukraine’s previous reported record from August 18, when Russian authorities said 1,671 UAVs were detected over 15 regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
The reported use of 17 Flamingo cruise missiles would also represent a major jump from earlier strikes, when launches were generally reported in groups of three to six.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said 11 regions, occupied Crimea, and targets over the Azov Sea came under attack overnight.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones were flying toward the Russian capital during the attack. He initially reported 105 intercepted on approach to Moscow and later said another 68 had been destroyed.
Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 UAVs were intercepted across 16 municipalities.
Russian authorities also reported damage to 47 private homes in Volokolamsk, Stupino, Dmitrov, Naro-Fominsk, Serpukhov, Domodedovo and Istra, as well as damage to an apartment building in the village of Lobanovo.
The scale of the overnight attack also caused major disruption at Moscow’s airports, where more than 200 flights were delayed or canceled after midnight.
Sheremetyevo saw the largest impact, with about 47 departing flights and 106 arrivals affected. Another 28 departures and 23 arrivals were disrupted at Vnukovo, while Domodedovo reported changes to four flights.
Previous reports indicated that Ukrainian forces recorded more than 11,000 confirmed strikes against Russian targets located over 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the front line in September, while also hitting a record number of Russian air defense systems.
September marked the first time the number of confirmed strikes beyond 20 kilometers exceeded 11,000 in a single month. Ukrainian forces also recorded their highest number of strikes against targets located more than 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the front.

articles.title: Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
What began as a Kremlin-backed “patriotic” family initiative has grown into nationwide military-style competitions where children as young as 11 train alongside their parents, handle weapons, practice battlefield skills, and are coached by veterans of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Russia has expanded its military-style youth training into entire households, bringing parents and children together for nationwide war games that include shooting, grenade throwing, drone operations, and tactical exercises.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Barents Observer on October 6, families from nearly every Russian region are taking part in the “Family Zarnitsa” competition, a Kremlin-backed initiative promoted as a way to strengthen “traditional values” and ties between generations.
Teams consist of two adults and two children aged 11 or older. Participants wear military-style uniforms and compete in exercises including grenade throwing, dismantling and reassembling Kalashnikov assault rifles, marksmanship, tactical field operations, first aid, and evacuating simulated casualties.
The training grounds are designed to resemble combat environments, while each family is assigned a coach who is a veteran of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The project was formally presented in early 2025 by Russian Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilova and was later backed by Vladimir Putin.
“Today, the ‘Family Zarnitsa’ project brings families together, strengthens the bond between generations, and integrates veterans of the Special Military Operation into a system of mentoring and patriotic education for young people,” Tsivilova said, using Russia’s official term for its war against Ukraine.
The competition is organized by several Kremlin-linked groups involved in the militarization of Russian youth, including Yunarmiya, VOIN, and Movement of the First, alongside the state-run Defenders of the Fatherland fund.
Russia has spent years expanding military and patriotic education among children and teenagers through organizations such as Yunarmiya and VOIN, whose combined membership now reaches hundreds of thousands of young Russians.
After regional qualification rounds, successful families advance to a national final. One of this year’s participants was the Maksimenko family from Zaozersk, a closed naval town on Russia’s Kola Peninsula.
The family defeated teams from Pechenga, Lovozero, and Murmansk before reaching the national final in Volgograd, where it finished 10th among 89 teams.
Yevgeniya Maksimenko, the family’s mother, said the competition included drones, mines, shooting, grenades, radio communications, and first aid, but described teamwork as its main lesson.
“We’ve become a REAL team. There are no ‘mums,’ ‘dads,’ or ‘kids’ here,” she wrote on social media.
Maksimenko has also been active in Russia’s ruling United Russia party. In 2025, she received an award from former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev for her work with the party’s women’s movement. Her eldest daughter, Liza, is a member of the VOIN military youth organization in Murmansk.
Earlier, in March 2025, Putin ordered the nationwide launch of “Family Zarnitsa,” a military-patriotic competition for parents and children proposed by Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilyova. The initiative was designed to combine physical challenges with patriotic education and activities focused on Russian history and culture.

articles.title: Ukraine Records 11,000+ Deep Strikes in September, Hits More Russian Air Defenses Than Ever
articles.body:
- Category

Ukraine Records 11,000+ Deep Strikes in September, Hits More Russian Air Defenses Than Ever
Ukrainian forces recorded more than 11,000 confirmed strikes against Russian targets located over 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the front line in September, while also hitting a record number of Russian air defense systems, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the ministry, September marked the first time the number of confirmed strikes beyond 20 kilometers exceeded 11,000 in a single month. Ukrainian forces also recorded their highest number of strikes against targets located more than 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the front.
The largest concentration of these longer-range strikes occurred along the Russian military logistics route linking temporarily occupied Mariupol with Crimea, the ministry said.
September also saw the highest number of Russian air defense assets hit since the launch of Ukraine’s ePoints battlefield performance program. The targets included radar systems, with one Russian air defense asset struck at a distance of 552 kilometers (343 miles).
In total, Ukrainian units recorded 33,087 confirmed strikes against Russian personnel during September. Only March and April saw higher monthly figures in 2026 under the ePoints program.
The Defense Ministry said all results counted by the program are supported by video recorded in Ukraine’s DELTA battlefield management system and subsequently verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
Ukraine also reported increased effectiveness against Russian Shahed-type attack drones. Ukrainian forces downed 28% more Shahed-type UAVs in September than in August, despite Russia changing its aerial attack tactics and deploying a growing number of jet-powered drones.
The ePoints program tracks battlefield results across Ukrainian military units, allowing defense officials to compare the effectiveness of different weapons and tactics and expand successful approaches across the Defense Forces.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces reported hitting or destroying 300 Russian air defense assets in the first 261 days of 2026, including 162 air defense systems, 124 radar complexes, and 14 electronic warfare systems.

articles.title: India expands Navy’s BrahMos strike capability
articles.body:
India expands Navy’s BrahMos strike capability
India has contracted for more BrahMos missile launchers and fire-control systems for its Navy warships, expanding deployment of its primary maritime-strike weapon across the fleet.
The Defense Ministry signed the roughly $69 million contract with BrahMos Aerospace Private Limited in New Delhi on Tuesday. The order covers fire-control systems and launchers for Indian Navy ships and was made under a scheme to buy items that are indigenously designed and manufactured.
Several frontline Indian warships including destroyers and frigates already are armed with BrahMos missiles. New ships commissioned in recent years have received the system as standard equipment, while older vessels are being retrofitted in phases as part of a wider push to expand BrahMos deployment across the fleet by 2030, reports said.
BrahMos can be launched vertically or at an incline from naval platforms and is capable of striking both ships and land targets at extended ranges at supersonic speed.
The Indian Navy has operated BrahMos since 2005, when its anti-ship variant was integrated onto Rajput-class destroyers. The system has since become the service’s principal surface-to-surface weapon.
The latest purchase follows much larger contracts signed in 2024 when the missiles were ordered for the Navy’s combat and training requirements, along with additional shipborne BrahMos systems.
BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India’s Defense Research and Development Organization and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyenia. The program has produced ship-, land-, and air-launched versions of the supersonic cruise missile.
The new project will have at least 68% indigenous content and involve Indian companies, including micro, small, and medium enterprises. The ministry said the program is expected to generate employment over three years while increasing domestic participation in advanced military technology.

articles.title: Russia says it’s fighting scammers. Its latest proposals would push VPN services off Russian servers, tie eSIMs to devices, and expand telecom data retention.
articles.body:
Russia says it’s fighting scammers. Its latest proposals would push VPN services off Russian servers, tie eSIMs to devices, and expand telecom data retention.
Fighting fraud has been a major focus of Russian lawmaking in recent years. The country has already adopted two sweeping packages of anti-fraud measures, and the authorities often use the fight against fraud as a pretext to push through repressive measures. This was their justification, for example, for banning voice and video calls on Telegram and WhatsApp. This week, Russia’s Digital Development Ministry published provisions from a third package aimed at telephone and online fraud. It includes another set of major proposals that could impose much tighter restrictions on internet use in Russia. Meduza reviewed the document and breaks down its key proposals.
VPN services would find it harder to use Russian hosting providers
Roskomnadzor, Russia’s communications regulator, would create a separate registry of Russian hosting providers’ customers who use rented computing resources to run proxy or VPN services that help circumvent internet censorship. Individuals or companies found to be circumventing blocks would be barred from signing new contracts with any hosting provider in the country for a full year.
The government would have to establish a procedure for Roskomnadzor and hosting providers to exchange this information.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 10²⁻¹. Special rules governing hosting providers
5³. The federal executive authority responsible for regulating and overseeing the media, mass communications, information technology, and telecommunications shall maintain, under a procedure established by the Government of the Russian Federation, a registry of persons who use hosting providers’ computing resources to host information and telecommunications networks or information resources (a website and/or webpage on the Internet, an information system, or a computer program) that provide access to information resources or information and telecommunications networks blocked within the Russian Federation under this Federal Law, and whose owners have failed to comply with the requirements of paragraph 1 of part 7 of Article 15⁸ of this Federal Law. The Government of the Russian Federation shall determine what information must be included in this registry.
5⁴. A hosting provider may not supply computing resources for hosting information in an information system permanently connected to the Internet to persons listed in the registry provided for in part 5³ of this Article who apply to the hosting provider within one year of being added to the registry.
Russian hosting providers would have to disconnect customers at the FSB’s request
It is unclear whether, in practice, the security service, which oversees internet blocking, would use this power solely to combat cyberattacks or also against VPNs. The amendment reads:
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 10²⁻¹. Special rules governing hosting providers
12. A hosting provider must cease supplying computing resources upon receiving a request to that effect from an agency conducting criminal intelligence operations or from the organization specified in paragraph 2 of part 2 of Article 5 of Federal Law No. 187-FZ of July 26, 2017, “On the Security of the Russian Federation’s Critical Information Infrastructure,” where necessary to counter cyberattacks.
Related reading
Companies would have to report their VPN use to Roskomnadzor
The authorities currently allow companies to use VPNs capable of circumventing Russian blocks, provided they meet two conditions:
The company needs the VPN “for technical purposes necessary to its operations”
The company determines in advance which employees will use the VPN
Under the proposal, companies would have to notify Roskomnadzor that they are using VPNs to circumvent blocks, though the notification process remains unspecified. There would also be unspecified requirements for employees with VPN access, along with rules governing its use. The government would draw up these requirements and rules subject to the FSB’s approval.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 15.8. Measures to counter the use within the Russian Federation of information and telecommunications networks and information resources that provide access to information resources and information and telecommunications networks blocked within the Russian Federation
17. The provisions of this Article shall not apply to operators of state information systems, government bodies, or local government bodies, or to the use of software and hardware that provide access to blocked information resources and information and telecommunications networks, provided that the owners of that software and hardware determine its users in advance and that it is used for technical purposes necessary to the operations of the person using it.
18. The Government of the Russian Federation, with the agreement of the federal executive authority responsible for security, shall establish requirements and rules governing the use of software and hardware that provide access to blocked information resources and information and telecommunications networks in the circumstances specified in part 17 of this Article and by the persons specified in that part. These shall include the procedure for notifying the federal executive authority responsible for regulating and overseeing the media, mass communications, information technology, and telecommunications of the use of such software and hardware, and the content and format of the information to be submitted.
All websites and apps would have to give the FSB users’ registration and login data
The proposed requirement would apply to both Russian and foreign services. They would have to keep records of users’ registrations and every account login for three years. They would also have to give this information to the FSB, with “the information to be supplied and the procedure” still to be determined by the government:
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 8. The right of access to information
10. The owner of a website and/or webpage on the Internet, and/or an information system, and/or a computer program, operating on the Internet within the Russian Federation, where access to information on that website and/or webpage, and/or in that information system, and/or computer program is provided to users who have logged in, must:
2) retain information on users’ account registrations, logins, and account closures for three years after those actions have been completed, and provide that information to authorized government agencies conducting criminal intelligence operations or ensuring the security of the Russian Federation, with the information to be supplied and the procedure determined by the Government of the Russian Federation.
Related reading
Foreign websites and apps would have to authenticate Russian users exclusively by phone number
Currently, authentication requirements apply only to websites, information systems, and programs owned by Russian citizens or legal entities. They can choose how to authenticate users: by phone number, through the Gosuslugi government services portal, through the Unified Biometric System, or through another Russian system.
Article 13.55 of the Code of Administrative Offenses already allows fines of 500,000 to 700,000 rubles for companies that violate this requirement.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 8. The right of access to information
10¹⁻¹. A person specified in part 10 of this Article who is neither a Russian legal entity nor a citizen of the Russian Federation must authenticate users located within the Russian Federation using a mobile phone number.
Sole proprietors and private individuals would no longer be able to sell SIM cards on telecom operators’ behalf
Currently, private individuals, sole proprietors, and legal entities can all sell SIM cards if they have an agency agreement with a telecom operator.
The bill proposes removing that right from the first two groups. Only employees of those legal entities, working under employment contracts, would be allowed to sell the cards. Telecom operators would have to verify the information provided about those employees.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 44. Provision of communications services
7. Legal entities that are not telecom operators may enter into mobile telephone service contracts and process subscribers’ payments for those services only if they have written agency agreements authorizing them to act on a telecom operator’s behalf. The powers granted under those agency agreements may not be delegated to third parties. Such agency agreements may not be concluded with sole proprietors or private individuals.
For legal entities that are not telecom operators, employees working under employment contracts with those entities shall enter into mobile telephone service contracts and process subscribers’ payments for those services.
A telecom operator must verify the accuracy of information about an employee of the telecom operator or a person acting on its behalf who arranged the signing of a mobile telephone service contract, using the procedure and methods established in paragraph 6 of this Article.
Telecom operators would have to store additional information alongside the traffic data and metadata required by the Yarovaya law
Operators would have to store information “on network addresses and ports” used by a customer when signing a contract for communications services. They would have to keep it for three years. The government has yet to determine “the procedure for storage and the amount of information to be stored.”
It is hard to say exactly why the authorities want this information. Most likely, it would allow them to determine after the fact whether a subscriber had masked their IP addresses with a VPN or proxy servers when signing a contract.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 64. Telecom operators’ obligations and restrictions on communications service users’ rights during criminal intelligence operations, measures to ensure the security of the Russian Federation, investigative actions, the detention of criminal suspects and defendants, and the enforcement of prison sentences
1. Telecom operators must store the following within the Russian Federation:
3) information on network addresses and ports used by the subscriber and the telecom operator when concluding a communications service contract over the Internet, including the time the contract was concluded — for three years after those actions have been completed. The Government of the Russian Federation shall establish the procedure for storage and the amount of information specified in this subparagraph to be stored.
Embedded SIM cards would be tied to specific devices
When someone buys an eSIM, their contract with the telecom operator would include the identifier (IMEI) of the specific phone, tablet, or smartwatch they use. When an eSIM is reissued for another device, the contract would apparently be amended at the same time. Most likely, this is intended to deter fraudsters from even attempting to clone their victims’ eSIMs (which is no easy task).
Roskomnadzor would monitor telecom operators’ compliance with this requirement.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 44. Provision of communications services
1.1. To conclude mobile telephone service contracts, a telecom operator or a person acting on its behalf must use the following, which must meet requirements established by the Government of the Russian Federation:
