articles.title: Ukraine’s drone pilots hit 76.5% more Russian infantry than two months ago: 2,699 in first five days of October
articles.body:
Ukraine's drone pilots are killing and wounding far more Russian infantry than they did a month ago. Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces confirmed that their pilots took out 2,699 Russian infantry from 1 to 5 October, 39.7% more than in the first five days of September, Commander Robert "Madiar" Brovdi wrote on Telegram on 6 October.
The Unmanned Systems Forces, the branch of Ukraine's military that fights with drones, count only losses verified by their own pilots in the military's Delta system, so the full picture of Russian losses is larger, Brovdi stressed. Compared with the first five days of August, the rise is 76.5%, from 1,529 losses, which he ties to denser and more frequent Russian assaults.
The sharpest growth occurred in the area of the 1st Azov Corps of Ukraine's National Guard on the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk axis in Donetsk Oblast, as fighting for fortress-belt cities continues. Drone pilots recorded 1,268 Russian losses there, 43% more than the 884 of early September and 91% more than the 664 of early August.
"Russia's hidden mobilization is in action. This is the beginning," Brovdi said ironically.
Russia doubles its monthly recruitment pace
Russian recruitment, mobilization, and contracts run at about 70,000 people a month, twice the 35,000 monthly average from January to August 2026, Brovdi noted on 16 September, when he forecast 12,500 losses for his pilots in September.
He expected the toll to keep climbing. Bigger records still lie ahead because of Russia's unannounced mobilization, Brovdi added on 24 September.
Drone pilots outpaced August by a quarter
September was completed above that forecast. The pilots logged 13,358 Russians killed or wounded, 25.35% more than the 11,010 of August, an average of 445 a day against 355, Brovdi reported. By his count, that equals the full assault infantry of one battalion every day, and his pilots hit a Russian target every 42 seconds.
Two sets of axes took the heaviest toll. In the first 24 days of September, the Dobropillia and Pokrovsk axes accounted for 4,018 losses, and the Oleksandrivka and Huliaipole axes for 3,021, according to Brovdi. The first of those groups covers the same Dobropillia-Pokrovsk axis where the Azov corps zone recorded the sharpest October rise.

articles.title: Russia Tests Balloons Equipped with Cables to Defend Against Drones
articles.body:
Russia has begun testing balloon barriers against Ukrainian drones.
The tests were shown by the Rossiya 1 TV channel in the VESTI program.
The system consists of balloons with a cable stretched between them, to which Kevlar threads are attached, hanging down.
The idea is that a drone that gets caught in this net will wrap the threads around its propeller and lose control.
According to the designers, the technology is already ready for mass production.
However, protecting a single large facility will require launching at least 10 such balloons into the sky.
Similar balloons were used during World War I and, especially extensively, during World War II to counter enemy aircraft. They forced bombers to fly at higher altitudes, which reduced the accuracy of their strikes.
Presumably, in the case of modern aerostats, the objective will be similar — by posing the threat of collision with cables, to force Ukrainian drones in certain areas to fly at higher altitudes, thereby making it easier for radar to detect them and for air defense systems to engage them.
Earlier, a Russian chemical company announced a tender to purchase airships to protect its facilities from attacks by Ukrainian drones.
In addition to deploying cables against drones, airships are also used for other purposes in modern warfare. In particular, the Russian state-owned holding company Rostec has developed an airship to ensure stable communications.
Unlike mobile base stations, lifting a radio module into the air minimizes the impact of terrain on signal quality. In Ukraine, balloons are viewed as platforms for launching drones and missiles against the enemy.
Missiles can be launched from stratospheric balloons at altitudes ranging from 12 to 18 kilometers.

articles.title: Turkey, Pakistan agree rapid troops deployment in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Turkey, Pakistan agree on rapid troops deployment in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
RIYADH – Turkey and Pakistan will undertake a “rapid deployment” of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defence alliance, the three countries said on Oct 5, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen’s Houthis.
The trio in August signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, committing them to come to each other’s aid if attacked.
The pact unites NATO’s second-largest army, that of Turkey, with the Islamic world’s only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, as well as the leading Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.
Their representatives held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct 5 where they noted recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular those targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Iran-backed Houthis by name.
The three countries “reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the kingdom’s security and territorial integrity”, they said in a joint statement.
They also agreed “to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom”.
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has faced repeated Houthi attacks targeting its cities, oil infrastructure and ships ever since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
In September, the group launched a new offensive that seized swathes of territory from Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which on Oct 5 launched a counteroffensive with Riyadh’s support seeking to retake all Houthi territory, some of it held for more than a decade. AFP

articles.title: France test-fires new nuclear-capable missile from submarine for first time
articles.body:
"To be free, one must be feared," Emmanuel Macron has posted, weeks after vowing that hybrid attacks blamed on Russia would "not go unanswered".
France has test-fired its new M51.3 nuclear-capable ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time, in a launch President Emmanuel Macron said proved the credibility of the country's nuclear deterrent.
The missile, which carried no warhead, was launched on Tuesday from the nuclear-powered submarine Le Vigilant off Brittany. It came down in the North Atlantic, hundreds of kilometres from any coastline, the defence ministry said.
Macron watched from the warship Auvergne and posted a video of the launch on X.
"To be free, one must be feared. And to be feared, one must be powerful," he wrote. "This technical success further demonstrates the credibility of our nuclear deterrent, whose long-term viability is assured."
The ministry said the test was carried out "in strict compliance with France's international commitments".
The launch comes after Macron warned of a shift in "Russian aggression and threats" against European countries following a series of hybrid attacks blamed on Moscow. In mid-September he vowed they would "not go unanswered".
France is the European Union's only nuclear-armed state, and Macron proposed this year that European partners join its "advanced" deterrence framework.

articles.title: Ukraine says its strikes have knocked out more than 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity
articles.body:
Ukraine's Security and Defense Forces have "put out of action" more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity through recent long-range strikes, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said in a statement published by the Defense Ministry on 4 October. These "carefully thought-out" actions were aimed at "bleeding the Russian war machine" and "destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said.
Ukraine treats Russia's refineries as a priority target because their revenue helps fund the war. Even Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed on 1 October that the strikes had cost Russia 1% of its GDP and had "partially" achieved their goal, Interfax reported.
The ministry did not publish how it calculated the figure.
"The consequences of Ukrainian operations are not always visible immediately. But the effect accumulates and produces a tangible result," the ministry said.
Ukrainian deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory
The ministry named eight recently struck facilities, among others. One of them is the Moscow Oil Refinery, which Ukraine targeted in a massive drone attack on the night of 20 September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The refinery, operated by Gazprom Neft in Moscow's Kapotnya district, supplies about 40% of Moscow's fuel market and 70% of the Moscow region's demand for gasoline and aviation fuel, according to Russian news Telegram channel Astra.
Another was KINEF, which Ukraine has attacked repeatedly. It is Russia's second-largest oil refinery by capacity, and the Ukrainian military struck it on the night of 30 August, setting off a fire at the facility.
The ministry also named the Yaroslavl, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran refineries and the Ust-Luga port complex.
Ukraine triples production and procurement of long-range drones—and this is not the end
This year, Ukraine has tripled the production and procurement of long-range attack drones, the ministry said.
"This is not the limit. We will continue to scale up deep-strike capabilities," the statement said.
International cooperation is part of that push. Berlin will fund the production of additional DeepStrike-class long-range drones in Ukraine, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said after a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group on 15 April. The sides also agreed to jointly develop and produce a medium- and long-range drone system.
Ukraine and Germany also signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars drones, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on 8 July. The Bars' modular design allows it to be used for deep strikes, among other missions.
Oil refinery output has fallen
Russian refineries cut crude oil processing by 14% in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period last year amid Ukrainian drone attacks, according to calculations by two industry sources.
Experts' estimates of the decline differ widely. In August, Serhii Vakulenko of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center put it at 25–28%, while Russian economic commentator Vyacheslav Shiryaev put it at 65–70%, according to Defense-Aerospace.
Fuel production data give a more concrete picture: in July, Russia's gasoline and diesel output was about a quarter to a third lower than in March 2026, the outlet reported.

articles.title: Trump blames Ukraine for US fuel price surge (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Trump blames Ukraine for US fuel price surge (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump has blamed Kiev for record-high fuel prices in the US, saying they are no longer driven by the Iran war but by Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries. He also pointed to policies pursued by Democrat-led states as a contributing factor.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump said: “What’s driving up gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz, because record numbers of barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘refineries,’” adding that Russian refineries “are being blown up by Ukraine.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries and other petroleum-linked facilities in recent months, disrupting production and contributing to fuel shortages and price hikes.
Moscow responded by restricting exports of gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products. The diesel ban is currently in effect until the end of October. Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged that the strikes cost around 1% of GDP, but said damaged facilities are being quickly restored and the country’s energy system has significant reserve capacity.
https://t.co/FuWlIHEEeZ
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 5, 2026
This is not the first time Trump has lashed out at Kiev over the strikes. During a visit to Ireland last month, he blamed Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky directly, saying: “Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia… Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”
Earlier, Trump said Ukrainian attacks caused Russia to lose “control of its diesel oil industry,” calling for and end to “this ridiculous and never-ending war,” as “the whole world suffers.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy assets and refined products are contributing to a wider “energy shock.”
Despite repeated warnings about the global fallout, Zelensky vowed over the weekend to intensify strikes on Russian oil facilities. The Ukrainian Defense Ministry also claimed that its long-range attacks have disabled 51% of Russia’s refining capacity, though Moscow has not corroborated the figure.
Russia, which has retaliated by expanding strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and severely disrupting Ukrainian logistics and Black Sea shipping, pledged on Sunday to step up its campaign.
Can Trump blame his way out of the fuel crisis?
With the midterm election just weeks away, Trump also blamed high fuel prices on the Democrats, lashing out at the “Dumocrats” for jeopardizing supplies “in Blue States, like California” through refinery closures.
California has lost around 17% of its refining capacity following the closure of two major facilities. The US Energy Information Administration warned that this could tighten supplies and increase price volatility. State officials reject claims that policy alone drove the closures, citing broader industry changes, although refiners have pointed to pressures linked to California’s regulatory environment.
Trump has also sought to play down the impact of the Iran war. The months-long disruption of the Strait of Hormuz – which once handled around 20% of global oil supplies – earlier pushed crude oil above $100 per barrel. Crude oil flows have since largely recovered through pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers, but refined oil supplies, particularly diesel, remain constrained. US diesel prices hit a record $6.52-$6.53 a gallon on September 22 and remain near historic highs, with prices in states such as California exceeding $8.21 a gallon, while regular gasoline stood at around $4.36 as of October 5.
The price surge has prompted emergency measures. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott declared a disaster over record diesel costs, temporarily allowing truckers to use cheaper red-dyed diesel, normally reserved for agricultural and off-road equipment, and raising truck weight limits to 95,000 pounds to reduce trips and fuel use. Nine other states have since temporarily allowed dyed diesel for some on-road use.
Trump signed an executive order on Monday expanding the measure nationwide and deferring the federal fuel tax through the end of the year. However, an AP-NORC poll found that 65% of Americans blame Trump’s policies for the high prices, and 69% said the economy is worse off now than when he returned to office.
With fuel costs squeezing truckers, farmers, and consumers, the issue has become a political liability for Republicans heading into the midterms. RT’s Caleb Maupin reports on the mounting pressure – and whether voters will make Trump pay at the ballot box.

articles.title: Ukrainian Vulcan Assault Rifles Spotted with Indonesian Special Forces
articles.body:
Soldiers from the Indonesian Rapid Response Force (Kopasgat) were spotted carrying Ukrainian Vulcan special assault rifles in a bullpup configuration.
Photos of the soldiers with Ukrainian assault rifles were published by the Indonesian defense website KERIS Reborn. The soldiers’ affiliation with Kopasgat is indicated by their corresponding sleeve insignia.
In the published photo, the Ukrainian Vulcan can be identified by its distinctive layout, receiver shape, and controls. Judging by the photo, the version is chambered in 7.62×39 mm.
It is currently unknown how many Ukrainian assault rifles the Indonesian unit received or what their status is, whether they are part of the standard issue or in a trial phase. There is also no publicly available information regarding Indonesia signing a production contract for the purchase of Vulcan rifles.
Kopasgat (Korps Pasukan Gerak Cepat) is a special corps of the Indonesian Air Force. Its units are tasked, in particular, with protecting air bases and other Air Force facilities, conducting special operations, and supporting aviation operations.
The Vulcan is a Ukrainian special-purpose assault rifle designed in a bullpup configuration. In this layout, the magazine and the main components of the firing mechanism are located behind the pistol grip.
This design allowed the weapon to be made compact without significantly shortening the barrel. With an overall length of approximately 712 mm, the rifle has a barrel length of 415 mm.
The weapon is based on the Kalashnikov family of assault rifles, featuring a gas-operated system and a rotating bolt that locks the barrel bore. At the same time, the design was significantly modified to accommodate the bullpup configuration.
The rifle features a new receiver, modified controls, and Picatinny rails for mounting optical, red-dot, and other sighting devices. The design also allows for the use of magazines from Kalashnikov assault rifles of the corresponding caliber.
The Vulcan is available in 5.45×39 mm, 7.62×39 mm, and 5.56×45 mm calibers.
The history of the assault rifle began with the Malyuk project, work on which started in 2005 following the signing of a contract with the Scientific and Technical Directorate of the SSU.
The developers were tasked with creating a bullpup-style assault rifle, making maximum use of existing Kalashnikov components. In late 2006, prototype models were handed over to members of the SSU’s Alpha special forces unit for testing.
Subsequently, the project attracted the interest of the Ministry of Defense, but further development of the design dragged on for several years.
A new phase began in 2014, when representatives of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine contacted the developers. They proposed refining the assault rifle in accordance with military requirements and experience in the combat use of small arms.
It was this refined design that was given the code name Vulcan. According to Serhiy Lugovskyi, chief designer at InterProInvest, the assault rifle underwent such significant changes during development that only about 20% of the design elements from the original Malyuk version remained.
Therefore, it is more accurate to view Malyuk and Vulcan not simply as two names for the same unchanging assault rifle, but as different stages in the development of a single design. Malyuk became the initial project, while the model refined for military needs received the official designation Vulcan Special Assault Rifle.
At the same time, the name Malyuk has not disappeared and continues to be used by the manufacturer and in open sources regarding this family of weapons.
The common designation Vulcan-M is not the official name of the assault rifle. According to Lugovskyi’s explanation, it appeared in the industrial design documentation as one of the proposed names for the product’s appearance, after which it spread among journalists and in open sources.
According to the documentation, the military model is named the Special ‘Vulcan’ Assault Rifle.
Separately, based on this design, the civilian self-loading hunting carbines Malyuk K-01 and K-02 were developed. Unlike the military Vulcan, they do not have an automatic fire mode: a single pull of the trigger fires a single shot.
The first prototype Malyuk rifles were handed over to the SSU’s Alpha special forces unit for testing as early as 2006.
After the start of the Russian-Ukrainian war, testing of the rifle continued, now incorporating lessons learned from combat operations. Representatives of military intelligence joined the effort to refine the design.
In the mid-2010s, Ukrainian special forces tested the weapon, particularly in combat conditions in the Donbas. The assault rifles also underwent trial use in units of the Special Operations Forces.
In 2017, the Armed Forces of Ukraine adopted the 5.45×39 mm and 7.62×39 mm versions under the official designation Vulcan Special Assault Rifle.
Subsequently, this weapon was spotted in the hands of service members of the Main Intelligence Directorate, Special Operations Forces, Airborne Assault Troops, and the Marine Corps. Vulcans were also supplied to certain special-purpose units of the Military Law Enforcement Service.
Thus, the assault rifle primarily spread among units for which the weapon’s compact size, while retaining a full-length barrel, could be advantageous when operating in vehicles, buildings, and other confined spaces.

articles.title: India is one of Russia’s biggest energy buyers. Can it also help broker peace with Ukraine?
articles.body:
India is one of Russia’s biggest energy buyers. Can it also help broker peace with Ukraine?
India is beginning to take a more active role in efforts to reach a settlement between Russia and Ukraine, Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said. Bloomberg reported that his explicit statement signals New Delhi’s shift toward a more active stance after years of caution over the war, driven partly by its close economic ties with Russia.
Speaking at a Munich Security Conference meeting held away from its usual venue, Jaishankar said India had become “a little bit more involved” in the peace process in recent months. He said New Delhi is now in talks with both Russia and Ukraine:
We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue, but going beyond that to cover some immediate concerns which both of them have on grain exports, on energy exports, on non-attack possibilities. So those are ongoing conversations right now.
Jaishankar gave no details about the progress of the talks. He also said India sees Russia, as the Soviet Union’s successor, as a partner that has traditionally helped it in its conflict with Pakistan.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has discussed the war twice in meetings with Vladimir Putin over the past few weeks — first at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, then at the BRICS summit in New Delhi. After the latest meeting, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Modi had “actively offered his good offices” to help secure a peaceful settlement.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on October 1 that four international mediators, including India, had put forward proposals for a peaceful settlement. “We have four proposals. India’s is the most comprehensive. For the first time, India has offered to play a role,” Sybiha said. He did not specify what India’s proposals involved.
India and China are currently the biggest buyers of Russian energy, and Russian energy’s share of India’s imports has risen sharply since the war began. The U.S. has repeatedly pressured India to stop buying Russian oil in exchange for lifting tariffs. In early 2026, Donald Trump said an agreement had been reached. But India later resumed purchases after war broke out in the Middle East and energy shortages emerged.
Negotiations over a trade deal between India and the U.S. are ongoing. In recent weeks, the talks have been complicated by the U.S. passage of the so-called “sanctions from hell” law. It allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying substantial amounts of Russian oil — above all, India.

A discussion is still underway over whether Poland should agree to Ukraine's request to shoot down Russian drones over Ukrainian territory.
Source: Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski speaking to journalists, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sikorski said Poland is changing its rules on the use of force in the border area with Ukraine. However, Poland cannot unilaterally decide to shoot down aerial assets directly over Ukrainian territory.
Quote: "Personally, I understand Ukraine's request to shoot down drones over its territory. I believe that drones or missiles that pose a direct threat to our border constitute a hostile act and therefore provide grounds for self-defence. However, as you know, NATO has established an integrated defence system for the entire eastern flank. This means that the decision does not depend on Poland alone. So the discussion is ongoing, but we have not yet reached the decisions that would satisfy you."
Background:
- Poland recently announced that from 1 October it is changing its air defence procedures in response to Russian airstrikes on Ukraine. The changes concern simplified rules for detecting and shooting down foreign aerial assets in Polish airspace.
- Poland is also preparing a law on a "pre-war state", which is intended to establish rules for action in a situation where the country is not formally at war but the level of threat is already significantly higher than in peacetime.

articles.title: France conducted a test of the new M51.3 nuclear missile - Macron observed it
articles.body:
France conducted a test of the new M51.3 nuclear missile - Macron observed it
Kyiv • UNN
Macron attended the first launch of the M51.3 missile from a nuclear-powered submarine off Finistère. The missile was tested without a nuclear warhead.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday, October 6, attended a test of a new French nuclear missile launched unarmed from a submarine. UNN reports this, citing Le Parisien.
Details
Emmanuel Macron witnessed the "first test launch" of an intercontinental ballistic missile launched from a nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine off the coast of Finistère on Tuesday morning, the Élysée Palace and the country’s Ministry of the Armed Forces announced.
Macron observed the launch from a French Navy frigate, the president’s office told AFP.
The missile, the third version of the M51 class "sea-to-surface" strategic ballistic missile (M51.3), which was commissioned a year ago, fell "into the North Atlantic several hundred kilometres from any coastline" without a nuclear payload, according to a statement from France’s Ministry of the Armed Forces.

articles.title: Ship Sunk Off Bulgaria’s Economic Zone in Latest Black Sea Drone Attack
articles.body:
Two commercial ships were hit by drones off the Bulgarian coast on Tuesday, Oct. 6, sinking one and leaving its crew missing.
The origin of the drones has not yet been established. Bulgarian authorities have launched a search operation and convened an emergency government meeting.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Euronews reported that Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev was due to make a statement at the start of the emergency meeting, scheduled for 11:15 a.m. local time.
The crew of the sunken vessel remained missing, while all 18 crew members aboard the second ship were rescued after abandoning the vessel following a fire, Bulgarian public broadcaster BNR reported, citing Rumen Nikolov, head of rescue operations in Varna.
Euronews noted the attack as the first to take place in a NATO member’s economic zone.
Bulgarian shipping outlet Maritime.bg identified the vessels as the Able and the Alfa Watan, the latter of which sank.
The crew of the Able was taken aboard the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria, with some crew members reportedly injured.
According to vessel-tracking website VesselFinder, the Alfa Watan was sailing under the Togo flag toward the Romanian port of Sulina. Its last known location was around 70 nautical miles off Bulgaria’s coast shortly after 2 a.m. local time on Tuesday.
The ships were the latest casualties in an escalating drone war in the Black Sea between Kyiv and Moscow, with the Kremlin targeting commercial vessels in retaliation for Kyiv’s attacks on its oil infrastructure and tankers.
Ukraine Targets Major Russian Oil Hub During Massive Drone Attack on Moscow Region
Black Sea’s drone war
The strikes came just a day after a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying grain was attacked by at least one drone in the Black Sea and later sank after catching fire.
A separate attack on commercial shipping was reported by Ukrainian authorities on Oct. 6.
Oleh Kiper, head of Ukraine’s Odesa Regional Military Administration (OVA), said a Russian drone struck a commercial vessel carrying rapeseed oil in the Black Sea.
“A commercial vessel flying the flag of the Marshall Islands and loaded with rapeseed oil was damaged by a Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) strike,” Kiper said on Telegram.
The vessel’s superstructure was damaged and caught fire. One person was killed and seven others were injured, according to Kiper.
Bulgaria’s new government
Bulgaria, a former Eastern Bloc country that joined NATO in 2004, elected a pro-Russian government in April 2026 after years of political turmoil, having undergone seven national elections within four years.
Radev, the country’s pro-Russian former president, won April’s parliamentary election in a landslide, with his government subsequently announcing plans to halt all weapon deliveries to Kyiv after being a major supplier of Soviet-standard artillery shells to Ukraine.
Sofia also reportedly vetoed EU sanctions on Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church and a confidant of Russian President Vladimir Putin, from the EU sanctions list.

articles.title: Lithuania takes 1st step to lift nuclear weapons ban amid Russian threat
articles.body:
Lithuania's parliament voted on Oct. 6 to advance a constitutional change that would remove the country's ban on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory.
The move comes as Vilnius seeks to strengthen its deterrence amid growing security concerns in the region because of Russia's aggressive posture.
The parliament approved the proposal in its first reading by 106 votes to 18, with six lawmakers abstaining. The measure would repeal Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory.
The proposal comes as Lithuania expands its defense cooperation with NATO allies, including the permanent deployment of a German military brigade, and as France considers expanding its nuclear deterrence role in Europe.
The amendment now faces a second and final vote, which cannot take place for at least three months. It would require the support of at least 94 of the 141 lawmakers to pass.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said before the vote that removing the constitutional ban would strengthen Lithuania's resilience and deterrence.
"This would mean that we secure the strongest possible support," he said.
Olekas said the final vote could take place on Jan. 12.
Lithuania has significantly increased its defense spending in recent years. The country also hosts a NATO multinational force, with Germany permanently expanding its military presence there.
Lithuania's security concerns are also shaped by its location between Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast and Belarus. Both countries host Russian military capabilities, while Kaliningrad borders NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
The proposed repeal would remove the constitutional provision itself rather than directly authorize a specific nuclear deployment.

articles.title: Honcharenko's expulsion from parliamentary group elicites mixed reactions from politicians and experts, ranging from accusations to predictions about formation of new party
articles.body:
As of Tuesday morning, a significant number of MPs from the European Solidarity parliamentary group reposted the party's statement regarding the expulsion of MP Oleksiy Honcharenko, prompted by his recent remarks on ending the Russia-Ukraine war, yet almost no one commented on the decision itself.
Before reposting the statement, European Solidarity MP Volodymyr Ariev explained that the delay in reaching this decision was due to the need for a measured response. "Everyone had been waiting a long time for a decision from European Solidarity. But decisions are not made without internal dialogue or democratic discussion within a party—this isn't the CPSU. And when decisions are made, they are made in a measured way, not hysterically," he wrote on Facebook.
Of all the European Solidarity MPs, only Volodymyr Viatrovych, a member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy, published a personal post after reposting the statement about Honcharenko; he emphasized that the narrative "finally, someone has said what the majority is thinking" is being used to promote capitulatory initiatives within Ukrainian society.
"Its goal is to create an illusion of mass support. That is precisely why bots on social media are so actively spreading this narrative. At the same time, this tactic attempts to cast the actual proponents of such initiatives as courageous truth-seekers and defenders of the interests of the majority of Ukrainians. This is how unity is destroyed and divisions deepened, by pitting the 'party of peace' (portrayed as rational and responsible) against the 'party of war'—that is, those allegedly profiting from the continuation of the conflict," Viatrovych wrote on Facebook.
According to him, to counter this tactic, one must not remain silent but publicly declare that "capitulation disguised as peace is unacceptable." "And you will see how many like-minded people are around you. And what wonderful people they are," Viatrovych added.
Arsen Zhumadilov, former director of the defense procurement agency State Logistics Operator (2025–2026) and former head of the Biliayivka District State Administration in Odesa region (2015–2017), expressed the view that Honcharenko, "through his opposition activities (more likely) or due to treasonous motives (less likely), has lost touch with the pro-state efforts the country has been engaged in since the start of the full-scale war."
"I realized that the person is following a specific agenda. I hope, at least, it is his own—even though it increasingly echoes the Russian one," Zhumadilov wrote on Facebook.
Viktor Ukolov, a former MP of the Verkhovna Rada (6th convocation, 2007–2012) and a veteran of the Russia-Ukraine war, noted that Honcharenko and the European Solidarity faction had "diverged significantly in their statements and actions." However, he expressed regret over the expulsion, remarking that "losing such a prominent MP as Honcharenko is a loss."
Businessman and blogger Karl Volokh suggested that for Honcharenko, "everything is going according to plan, including his expulsion from the faction." "As a result, in the public eye, he is not only the only politician openly advocating for negotiations and an end to the war, but he has also become a martyr for the cause. Since the war will inevitably end at the negotiating table one way or another, a segment of the electorate will inevitably form the impression that he was the only one who possessed the 'foresight and courage' [to take this stance]," he explained on Facebook.
Volokh doubts that Honcharenko will "burst into the top tier of presidential rankings anytime soon," but suggests he might launch a new party of his own—one that could soon begin appearing in opinion polls.
Honcharenko himself has not yet commented on the faction's decision; however, on Monday, hours before the announcement, he posted a lengthy list of 50 achievements dating back to 2014 on social media to refute allegations of pro-Russian activity. Specifically, he highlighted his opposition to the occupation of Crimea, the sanctions imposed on him by Russia (including his designation as an "extremist"), the creation of volunteer hubs within his Honcharenko Centers, fundraising for equipment for the Defense Forces, participation in security forums, his own legislative initiatives (particularly those supporting the military), his work at PACE, and his efforts to prevent the undermining of the independence of the NABU and SAPO.
As earlier reported, the European Solidarity party issued a statement on Monday evening announcing Honcharenko’s expulsion from its parliamentary faction following his recent remarks. "Oleksiy Honcharenko’s public stances regarding the end of the war and Ukraine’s future security architecture diverge from the position of European Solidarity and its ideological principles. For this reason, the European Solidarity faction has decided that we can no longer continue our shared political journey due to ideological differences. This decision does not negate years of working together. However, party unity cannot be a mere formality masking fundamentally different answers to questions about the state's future," the statement reads.
The political group emphasized that their team "is not just a parliamentary faction but also tens of thousands of party members; the most respected among them are our colleagues currently serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, whose opinions and stance regarding the defense of the country are of fundamental importance to us."
Earlier, on October 2, Honcharenko published a series of posts on Telegram calling for the start of negotiations with the Russian Federation to reach agreements on halting strikes against ports, industrial facilities, schools, hospitals, residential buildings, and bridges. He suggested that, following this, discussions could move on to more complex issues, specifically the status of Donbas and Ukraine's neutral status.
Honcharenko is not a member of the European Solidarity party itself, though he is part of the parliamentary faction of the same name. He serves at the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budget Issues and the permanent delegation to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, and participates in numerous inter-parliamentary friendship groups. He also chairs the Verkhovna Rada’s temporary inquiry commission investigating potential violations of Ukrainian defense and anti-corruption laws and the observance of human rights and freedoms during martial law, and serves at other such commissions.
During the previous (8th) convocation of the Verkhovna Rada (2014–2019), he was a member of the Petro Poroshenko Bloc faction and party; however, he did not join the party after its reorganization into the revamped European Solidarity party (led by Petro Poroshenko). In the last parliamentary elections, he ran as an independent, non-partisan candidate in electoral district No. 137 (Odesa region).

articles.title: Russia burned 628,000 new school textbooks in Kharkiv at the peak of back-to-school season
articles.body:
Russian missiles and drones destroyed 13 million Ukrainian books this summer, The Guardian reported. That is about a third of all books printed in Ukraine this year, the government estimates.
Russia is striking civilian warehouses, including those where publishers store their books. The uncertainty is pushing publishers toward safe international bestsellers, Publishers Weekly reported. "We'll all end up fed up with safe, non-risky books—if there are still publishers around to publish them," said Iryna Baturevych, co-founder of the publishing news outlet Chytomo.
Millions of Ukrainian books on fire
Ranok is one of Ukraine's largest publishing houses and a leader in children's literature and school textbooks. On one day in August, Russia destroyed more than 85% of its stock, The Guardian reported.
Viktor Kruhlov, the publisher's co-founder and chief executive, was on the warehouse floor at its headquarters in Kharkiv. The facility, built on the site of a former bread factory, covered about 10,000 m².
Together with five senior colleagues, he was discussing plans for the upcoming school year, the peak of the distribution season. Moments after the meeting began, a strike hit about 30 meters from where the staff had gathered. Kruhlov heard an explosion and almost at once saw a huge fire. As colleagues tried to put out the flames, a second strike came, and he realized there could be a third and a fourth, so the staff evacuated. Fifty people were on shift that day, and no one was injured, Kruhlov told The Guardian.
Eight million books, including 628,000 new school textbooks, were in the warehouse at the time. None could be saved. Firefighters battled the blaze for a week.
Several editorial staff members who saw the remains of the warehouse for the first time looked shaken as they recognized fragments of books they had helped create.
"When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it's an awful feeling," Kruhlov said.
He predicted shortages at Ranok's stores this fall, when the books in stock run out and there is nothing to replace them.
Literature is part of Ukrainian identity
Kruhlov is convinced that Russia deliberately targeted the book warehouse, but Bohdana Laiuk, Ukraine's deputy culture minister, sees the strikes as part of Russia's broader campaign against warehouses, The Guardian wrote.
"They cannot occupy Kyiv. So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us—and books are part of everyday life," she said.
Books also matter to Russia's occupiers, Laiuk said.
"When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do—and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions—is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them," Laiuk said.
Before 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market consisted of Russian-language titles, most of them imported from Russia.
Russian dominance in Ukrainian publishing developed over centuries, from tsarist bans on publishing in Ukrainian in the 19th century to Soviet Russification. Ukrainian writers were purged, and Ukrainian literature stayed in the shadow of Russian literature, the article notes.
Laiuk calls the dominance of Russian books a form of colonialism. Russia deliberately built its own information space in Ukraine through books, media, and television, she argues, so that everything would be ready for it once its tanks arrived.
Even after independence, a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel was long seen as unlikely. But at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukrainian bookstores stopped selling Russian imports, and interest in Ukrainian literature grew, from 1920s classics and poetry to contemporary authors and translations.
"So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are," Laiuk told The Guardian in 2023.
The future of Ukrainian literature is uncertain
Ranok is now rushing to reprint textbooks and bestsellers: schools need the former, while sales of popular titles will help the publisher make up for lost revenue.
For debut authors and writers of less commercial or experimental books, the situation is particularly difficult. Even before the strike on Ranok's warehouse, some publications had been delayed by attacks on printing infrastructure.
Ksenia Shpak's debut novel, an urban fantasy about a girl displaced from eastern Ukraine to the Carpathians, was due out in February 2025 but was published only that November, the article says. Half of the print run was in Ranok's Kharkiv warehouse when it was attacked.
It was her first published book, and Shpak fears the publisher will now focus on bestsellers and reprint her novel only if money allows. The Ukrainian book market is also feeling demand level off and the cost of living rise, she said.
Despite the loss of 8 million books, Kruhlov remained optimistic. Looking over the ruined warehouse in Kharkiv, he said he planned to rebuild everything—and to do it better.

articles.title: Zelenskyy and Dutch PM discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defence
articles.body:
Zelenskyy and Dutch PM discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defence
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has discussed air defence and military support with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten.

Zelenskyy also briefed Jetten on a potential trilateral Ukraine-US-Russia meeting. The US side has proposed the UAE as a possible venue for the meeting.

articles.title: Lithuanian parliament advances bid to remove ban on nuclear weapons
articles.body:
Ilayda Cakirtekin
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
Lithuania's parliament on Tuesday passed the first reading of an amendment seeking to remove the constitutional ban on nuclear weapons, according to broadcaster LRT.
The parliament backed the amendment, which aims to remove the ban on weapons of mass destruction from the country's constitution, with 106 lawmakers voting in favor, 18 against and six abstaining.
The passage of the amendment potentially paves the way for the stationing of allied nuclear weapons in Lithuania.
A final vote is scheduled for Jan. 12 and the amendment will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of parliament to pass.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said before the vote that repeal of the ban could strengthen Lithuania’s resilience and deterrence capabilities.
“By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal," Olekas also said.
Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas reportedly underscored the significance of deterrence, urging lawmakers to make use of all available options to strengthen Lithuania’s security.
“If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions we are having today," Kaunas also said.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade accusations over overnight drone strikes, killing 2
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
06 October 2026•Update: 06 October 2026
- Kyiv authorities say rescuers extinguished fire that broke out on roof of an educational institution in Obolonskyi district of Ukraine’s capital
 
Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes, which have killed at least two people in the region surrounding Moscow, according to local authorities.
 
In a statement on Telegram, Andrey Vorobyov, governor of the Moscow region, claimed that 185 drones were downed across 16 municipalities in the region as it was subjected to a drone attack overnight.
 
“Preliminary reports indicate six injuries. … Tragically, there was a fatality. A 20-year-old man died in the settlement of Radumlya (Solnechnogorsky District) as a result of the attack,” Vorobyov said.
 
He later updated the death toll in the region to two and the number of those injured to nine, noting that “one of the largest drone attacks” also damaged 47 private houses across seven municipalities.
 
Separately, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that 650 drones flew toward the Moscow region between 8.30 pm (1730GMT) Monday and 5 am (0200GMT) Tuesday, with 105 of them destroyed as they approached the capital.
 
He later reported that 29 more drones were shot down as they were heading toward Moscow.
 
Local authorities also reported that one person was injured in the Smolensk region, while two others were injured in the Russian border region of Bryansk due to overnight strikes.
 
The Russian Defense Ministry claimed in a statement that air defense systems shot down 868 Ukrainian drones overnight across 11 regions, as well as over the Sea of Azov and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
 
It further claimed that Russian overnight strikes in Ukraine hit a warehouse in Ukraine's southern Odesa region, as well as a dry cargo vessel in the port of Chornomorsk and berthing infrastructure in the port of Izmail.
 
In Ukraine, Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, said that at least five people were injured due to an overnight strike on a residential building in the regional capital.
 
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said 11 others were rescued from the apartment building in Zaporizhzhia, noting that search and rescue operations have been completed.
 
The service said that search and rescue personnel extinguished a fire that broke out on the roof of an educational institution in the Obolonskyi district of Ukraine’s capital Kyiv following a morning Russian strike, but that no one was injured.
 
Separately, Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said a building belonging to a private enterprise was damaged in the regional capital during an overnight Russian attack, indicating that a fire broke out but was promptly extinguished by emergency responders.
 
“There were no casualties. Cleanup operations are currently underway at the site,” Kiper added.
 
Elsewhere, Dnipropetrovsk Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that four people were injured in the city of Kryvyi Rih following a morning strike.
 
Ukraine's Air Force claimed in a statement that its air defenses downed 114 out of 137 drones launched by Russia overnight.
 
Moscow and Kyiv have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports and energy infrastructure.
 
They deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that the strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Two ships sunk and a third set ablaze off NATO coasts in two days, and neither Bucharest nor Sofia will say “Russia”
articles.body:
Drones sank two merchant ships and set a third on fire in the Black Sea economic zones of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria on 5 and 6 October, killing at least two seafarers, Romanian and Bulgarian authorities reported. Ukraine blamed Russia for the first attack. Neither Bucharest nor Sofia has said who launched the drones.
Russia has spent months striking ships bound to and from Ukrainian ports while denying responsibility or staying silent. Now merchant vessels are sinking inside NATO members' economic zones without either government naming the attacker, so Moscow pays no political price for hitting allied waters.
Grain ship sinks off Romania
The Royad Mammadov, a Turkish-owned ship carrying grain from Ukraine's port of Izmail to Italy, sank on 5 October near Romania's Pescăruș offshore platform, 20 nautical miles from the Romanian coast, Digi24 reported. The Romanian Naval Authority described the incident as a fire on board. Romania's Interior Ministry said 11 crew members were rescued and two people died.
Three injured sailors aged 22 to 50 were taken to the Constanța county hospital, conscious and stable, with multiple injuries. Adrian Mihălcioiu, the leader of Romania's Free Seafarers' Union, said the ship was attacked by Russian sea and aerial drones in waters Romanians consider safe.
"It is a commercial ship, a ship that is not part of the war… people who have nothing to do with the war, it is not their war," he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed the attack on "two Russian drones" and said the ship was in neutral waters carrying corn. Citizens of Azerbaijan and India were on board, and the captain was killed, he said. Romanian authorities have not attributed the sinking to Russia.
Two more ships hit in Bulgaria's zone
A day later, drones struck two merchant ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone east of the town of Byala, the first known attack on ships there, Maritime.bg reported. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan, sailing from Al-Arish, Egypt, to Sulina, Romania, suffered critical hull damage and sank, Militarnyi said. The Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria found only an overturned lifeboat and life jackets at the scene, and the search for the crew continues, Euronews reported.
The Palau-flagged Able, sailing from Galați, Romania, to Istanbul, caught fire, and the Dioscuria rescued its 18 crew members. Both ships are Turkish-owned, Türkiye Today reported. Two sailors with severe injuries were flown to a hospital in Varna, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said, according to AP. Sea and aerial drones hit the ships at about 3 a.m., he said, calling the attack "a blatant violation of international law and maritime law."
Radev called an emergency meeting of four ministries, the presidency, and the security services. No one from the Alfa Watan has been found, he said, warning that if the war is not ended in time, it "will continue to expand its spatial scope." The origin of the drones is still being clarified, Maritime.bg said. Several Bulgarian media outlets cited sources as saying the drones were Russian, Sofia Globe reported.
Russia's war on Black Sea shipping
Russia had already killed the captain of a Tanzanian-flagged ship in September, and days later it struck another civilian vessel, killing its captain too. Ukraine says that route carries 90% of its farm exports.
Romania has destroyed a sea drone near its Neptun Deep gas project and found Russian drones floating in its economic zone. In September, ISW linked drone crashes in Romania and Moldova to a wider Russian pattern of pressure on NATO.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called for a moratorium on Black Sea attacks. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said Ankara was stepping up diplomacy to restore grain exports. Türkiye and the UN are organizing new Black Sea truce talks between Russia and Ukraine, Bloomberg reported, citing a diplomat. Russia earlier dismissed Kyiv's offer of a Black Sea ceasefire.

articles.title: State of Corruption: Zelensky crosses tipping point in new poll
articles.body:
State of Corruption: Zelensky crosses tipping point in new poll
Ukrainians are increasingly disappointed with serving officials and ashamed of their actions, a recent opinion poll indicates. A majority now insists that Vladimir Zelensky must not seek a second term as president, as he once pledged.
Mounting disillusionment with the government, which was highlighted on Monday by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology’s (KIIS) latest omnibus survey, comes on the back of multiple corruption scandals in Kiev involving people close to Zelensky.
Kiev relies heavily on Western financial and military support to pursue its conflict with Russia. Even its staunchest supporters acknowledge that the Zelensky government’s assurances that it is actively tackling corruption are not necessarily sincere.
No second term for Zelensky
The KIIS phone survey, conducted among over 1,000 adults in September, indicates a stark shortage of positive emotions among Ukrainians for public servants. The pollster offered respondents a list of 12 options to indicate their feelings, from which they could pick up to three. The most popular was “disappointment,” chosen by 44%, followed by “shame,” picked by 33%.
More respondents reported negative emotions towards the authorities compared to a similar poll conducted in December 2025, while the share of positive options remained stable. In both surveys, 23% said they were hopeful regarding the authorities and 16% said they sympathized with them.
Asked whether Zelensky should take part in the next presidential election, 53% told KIIS he should not, compared to 46% last year.
Zelensky pledged to be a single-term president during his election campaign in 2019, but has since suggested he may run again. His mandate expired in 2024, but he has retained power under martial law, which critics say violates the Ukrainian Constitution.
Other polls have consistently suggested that in a hypothetical presidential contest, Zelensky would lose in the second round to any of as many as three more popular possible candidates.
Zelensky sinking in graft bog
The Ukrainian leader’s domestic popularity has dropped amid a series of corruption scandals triggered by investigations conducted by Western-backed anti-graft agencies.
The latest major development came in September, when the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) exposed a suspected protection racket run by a senior officer in the Prosecutor General’s Office. The chief suspect was fired, while his boss, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, fled the country before being removed from his position by the Ukrainian parliament.
Previously, Zelensky fired a deputy head of his office after NABU accused her of laundering millions in cash to pay the bail for a former energy minister who is a suspect in a separate anti-graft investigation linked to the Ukrainian leader.
NABU’s reputation in Ukraine is so strong that some crooks are trying to profit off of it. This week, the agency reported helping the police arrest a swindler who had posed as one of its detectives to extort $280,000 from a local businessman, saying the money would allow him to sink a criminal case “commissioned” by competition.
KIIS previously reported that half of respondents in a survey named government corruption as their biggest concern – more than Russian long-range strikes – while 72% said Zelensky personally was responsible for the problem.
German minister admits Kiev has a graft problem
Political opponents of Zelensky, such as his former spokesperson turned vocal critic Yulia Mendel, claim he personally protects corruption networks entrenched in his government. NABU has stressed he is not a suspect in any of his cases, referring to immunity from prosecution that Zelensky retains as long as he claims presidential authority.
The Ukrainian government largely operates on donations and credit provided by foreign sponsors, primarily the European Union. Brussels recently reacted skeptically when asked by Kiev to cover a $27 billion hole in the Ukrainian military budget.
A joint statement by the European Commission and Ukraine last week said they had “identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defence needs for 2026.” The vaguely worded press release was broadly interpreted as a refusal of Zelensky’s request to send “more money, much more.”
Corruption in Kiev is a major concern for foreign donors too, even if they rarely admitted this publicly.
“We want to be sure that this money is used precisely for that [weapons and infrastructure buildup] purpose,” German Economics Minister Katherina Reiche told Bild TV on Monday, when asked about aid sent by Berlin. She stressed that Kiev needs to prove it is actually tackling corruption.
There is an assurance that work will continue. However, we will also have to ensure that this does not remain just an assurance, but that we have measurable results.
EU officials who are not bound to demonstrate support for Kiev by their political allegiances have used more direct language.
“Ukraine is so corrupt. We have no idea how much money is really spent on the functioning of the state or on defense purposes. We don’t know how much is just disappearing,” MEP Fernand Kartheiser told RT’s Rick Sanchez in a recent interview.
Kartheiser, a conservative lawmaker from Luxembourg, said the leaked photo of a golden toilet allegedly owned by Zelensky’s long-time associate Timur Mindich was the turning point for many Europeans who no longer accept the pro-Kiev narrative pushed by their governments. NABU last year accused Mindich of running a $100 million extortion scheme at a state-owned energy company, just after he narrowly escaped pending arrest.

articles.title: Yemen rivals marshal forces for new ‘war of resources’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Yemen rivals marshal forces for new ‘war of resources’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
Yemen’s internationally recognized government has vowed to retake territory held by the Houthis, raising the prospect of a new phase in a conflict that has ravaged the country for more than a decade.
The Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) has ordered its armed forces and security formations to begin implementing plans “until the country is liberated from the grip of terrorist militias,” while also calling for a general mobilization.
But the balance of power is more complicated than the lines on the map suggest, RT’s Oumaima Ichchar reports.
“The government may control more of Yemen on the map, but it is the Houthis who control most of its people,” she said. The PLC is estimated to hold around 60.4% of Yemen’s territory, while the Houthis control about 22.8%, including the capital Sanaa and some of the country’s most densely populated areas.
The Houthis are estimated to have around 350,000 fighters, while estimates for the fragmented PLC forces range from 40,000 to 250,000. But, as Ichchar notes, “even hundreds of thousands of fighters mean little if you can’t properly arm or supply them.”
The Houthis have spent years developing long-range missiles and drones, as well as domestic weapons production, while PLC forces remain closely tied to Saudi military and financial support.
The Houthis have also built a “parallel economy” in the territory they control, collecting taxes, customs duties, religious levies and other revenues estimated at around $2.5 billion a year. The PLC, meanwhile, remains heavily dependent on outside financial support, particularly from Saudi Arabia.
With manpower, weapons, money and foreign backing all potentially determining what comes next, Ichchar examines the comparative strength of the warring sides and what she describes as the “ultimate war of resources.”

articles.title: American rocket artillery opens fire in joint drill
articles.body:
US Army rocket artillery has opened fire during a joint live-fire exercise with the Singapore Armed Forces, with M270 Multiple Launch Rocket Systems used during Exercise Daring Warrior 2026 at Fort Sill in Oklahoma, according to the US Army.
Soldiers from Bravo Battery, 3rd Battalion, 13th Field Artillery Regiment, 75th Field Artillery Brigade conducted the firing on 21 September alongside Singaporean personnel as part of the bilateral training event.
Imagery released by the US military shows an M270 launching rockets across the Fort Sill training area, with American and Singaporean troops also working together around artillery equipment and command systems during the exercise.
The US Army said the live-fire was designed to synchronise American and Singaporean launch crews, allowing the two forces to practise delivering coordinated precision fires while testing their ability to operate together on the range. Exercise Daring Warrior brings together artillery personnel from the two countries for training involving weapons operation, command and control and the coordination required to employ long-range fires as part of a combined force.
The M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System is a tracked rocket artillery platform operated by the US Army and several allied militaries. Its launcher carries interchangeable rocket and missile pods, allowing it to employ different types of ammunition depending on the mission.
Unlike conventional tube artillery, multiple launch rocket systems are intended to deliver fires over greater distances and can engage targets using guided munitions. The M270 shares ammunition with the wheeled M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, better known as HIMARS, although the tracked M270 carries two launch pods rather than one.
The system has also gained renewed prominence during the war in Ukraine, where M270 and HIMARS launchers supplied by Western countries have been used extensively by Ukrainian forces for long-range precision strikes.
For the American and Singaporean troops at Fort Sill, the emphasis was on operating the systems as part of a combined artillery force rather than simply conducting individual launcher firings.
Photographs from the exercise show personnel from both armies working together during equipment familiarisation and planning activity, as well as operating observation and targeting equipment in the field. Other imagery shows American and Singaporean troops positioned around command posts and tactical vehicles before the live-fire phase, reflecting the wider chain of activity required to identify targets, pass firing information and coordinate launch crews.
The Singapore Armed Forces operates its own M142 HIMARS rocket artillery systems, giving its personnel experience with a weapons family that shares ammunition and elements of fire-control architecture with the M270.
Fort Sill is the US Army’s principal artillery training centre and home to the Field Artillery School, making the Oklahoma installation a regular location for both domestic and multinational artillery exercises. The 75th Field Artillery Brigade is also based at Fort Sill and provides long-range precision fires capabilities to US forces, with subordinate units operating rocket and missile artillery systems.

articles.title: US warns foreign financial institutions over business with Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US warns foreign financial institutions not to do business with Iran
The United States on Monday warned foreign financial institutions that if they do business with Iran or its banking sector, Washington could sanction them.
"Foreign financial institutions continuing to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification and should take immediate action to terminate such activity and relationships," the US Treasury said in an "alert" statement.
The United States launched its war on Iran in late February, killing the country's leadership and demanding it cease any nuclear-related activities.
The war has plunged the Middle East into violence, with Tehran's retaliatory action targeting Washington's Gulf allies and sending global energy and fertiliser prices skyrocketing after it virtually shut a key trading route.
Since late August, Washington has stepped up its campaign to isolate Tehran economically, warning its allies that secondary sanctions would hit them if they continued to conduct transactions with the country's government.
The US Treasury has also announced a slew of new sanctions as part of that push, targeting Iran's financial, cryptocurrency, rail, automotive and manufacturing sectors.
It has also taken action against two banks, one in the United Arab Emirates and another in Turkey, over their alleged aid to the authorities in Tehran.
In Monday's statement, the Treasury said Iran's government operated so-called "shadow banking" channels to circumvent US sanctions, and that foreign financial institutions should aim to identify and avoid any such activities.

articles.title: Ukraine demines over 1,300 hectares in September. Now, it has new plan to tackle 132,000 km²
articles.body:
Ukraine continues to demine its 132,000 square kilometers of potentially hazardous territory. During the last month, Defense Ministry demining units cleared 1,347 hectares of that liberated territory, the ministry said.
In September, Tymur Pistryuha, head of the Board of the Ukrainian Deminers Association, said that Ukraine is the most heavily mined country in the world — a fact recognized by the international community. The contaminated area continues to grow with every day of the war, Suspilne reports.
Ukraine clears 483,366 explosive devices overall
During the month, Ukraine surveyed and cleared 339.84 hectares of agricultural land, 21.31 kilometers of roads, 40.4 kilometers of railway tracks of mines and explosive remnants of war.
In total, in September, demining specialists detected and destroyed 364 explosive devices. Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, 483,366 such devices have been detected and destroyed.
Such missions are conducted by several structures at once. Among them are the Main Directorate for Mine Action, Civil Protection and Environmental Safety, and the Defense Ministry, which engages demining units of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the State Special Transport Service in clearing liberated territories of explosive remnants of war.
Explosive ordnance disposal units of the National Police of Ukraine and pyrotechnic units of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine are also involved in demining operations.
Those deminers now fly drones fitted with special magnetometers that register changes in the Earth's magnetic field, picking out hidden metal from the air and keeping sappers off ground that may be sown with mines.
New plan for mass demining
To make the process more effective, the government has approved a procedure under which the Ministry of Defense’s Mine Action Center will prepare a single national humanitarian demining plan every year, while the National Mine Action Authority will approve it.
The plan will be prepared according to a clear timetable for everyone involved in the process, including government authorities, demining operators, and local communities. The Mine Action Center will collect data on contaminated areas, local communities' needs, and demining operators' capacities, and use this information to develop humanitarian demining plans.

articles.title: U.S. Army’s newest Bradley arrives with active protection
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army's 1st Cavalry Division is fielding the M2A4E1 Bradley, equipped with the Iron Fist active protection system, to its 6th Squadron, 9th Cavalry Regiment.
- The division's 2nd Battalion, 82nd Field Artillery Regiment, is also fielding the M7A4E1 Bradley Fire Support Team Vehicle with improved mobility, power and digital systems.
The U.S. Army’s 1st Cavalry Division has started fielding the M2A4E1 Bradley Fighting Vehicle, the first Bradley version fitted with an active protection system designed to destroy incoming anti-tank missiles, rockets and drones before they hit the vehicle.
The division said in a social media post that its 6th Squadron, 9th Cavalry Regiment, is receiving the new infantry fighting vehicles. The M2A4E1 carries Elbit Systems’ Iron Fist active protection system, along with more electrical power generation and an upgraded digital architecture. The division did not say how many vehicles the squadron is receiving or when fielding will be complete.
A second unit, the 2nd Battalion, 82nd Field Artillery Regiment, is fielding the M7A4E1 Bradley Fire Support Team Vehicle. That version carries the forward observers who find targets and call in artillery and air strikes. The division said the M7A4E1 brings improved mobility, power and digital systems to those teams. The post did not mention an active protection system on the M7A4E1.
The 1st Cavalry Division is based at Fort Hood, Texas, and is one of the U.S. Army’s main armored formations.
Iron Fist is a hard-kill system. Radar and infrared sensors mounted around the turret detect an incoming threat, and launchers fire an interceptor that detonates close to it, knocking it off course or destroying it before impact. Elbit says the system can counter anti-tank guided missiles, rocket-propelled grenades, loitering munitions and drones, and that its interceptor uses a combustible casing to reduce fragmentation risk to nearby infantry.
Drones and anti-tank missiles have destroyed large numbers of armored vehicles in Ukraine, including Bradleys supplied by the United States. The U.S. Army has looked at adding an active protection system to the Bradley for years and tested earlier Iron Fist configurations on the vehicle before settling on the current design.
The Army first showed the M2A4E1 publicly in April 2024 at a ceremony in Saco, Maine. At the time, the Program Executive Office for Ground Combat Systems said the Army had received funding to buy an M2A4E1 for every Bradley it had sent to Ukraine. Besides Iron Fist, that version includes an improved high-definition thermal gunner’s sight and a new environmental control unit for the crew and passengers.
Elbit has since received several contracts for Bradley protection systems. A $37 million order in 2024 was followed in January 2026 by a $228 million follow-on contract to supply Iron Fist systems for Bradley upgrades under a program led by General Dynamics, as the U.S. Army moved from testing and limited fielding toward wider use across its Bradley fleet.
The Bradley is built by BAE Systems and has been in U.S. Army service since the early 1980s. The M2A4E1 is the latest step in upgrades that have kept the vehicle in service while the Army develops its successor, the XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle.

articles.title: US Senator Murphy says Pentagon denied him access to US base in Qatar
articles.body:
US Senator Murphy says Pentagon denied him access to US base in Qatar
RIYADH, Oct 6 - US Democratic Senator Chris Murphy said the US Department of Defense denied him access to a key US military base in Qatar during a visit to the Middle East, describing it as part of a US government effort to conceal the impact of the Iran war.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Al Udeid Air Base is the largest US base in the region and has repeatedly been attacked by Iran during the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
"This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people," Murphy told a small group of journalists in Riyadh, the second stop on his trip.
He also said that the Pentagon refused to set up a briefing for him on the war while he was in the region.
"I've never encountered anything like this in my time in the Senate and it's part of a deliberate campaign of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an end to," he said.
Murphy made clear, however, that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had facilitated his visit, including arranging meetings with diplomats, a stance he contrasted with that of the Pentagon.
During his trip, Murphy met with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani and with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as well as other senior Gulf officials. REUTERS

articles.title: Significant share of jet-powered drones shot down by F-16s – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten how to provide greater protection for lives against Russian escalation involving jet-powered Shahed drones.
“A significant share of these drones are shot down specifically by the F-16s that the Netherlands transferred to Ukraine, and there are opportunities to support their operation with the necessary means. We also discussed other ideas for protecting critical infrastructure and bolstering air defense. I am grateful for the readiness to help,” Zelenskyy said on X following the talk.
He also informed Jetten about contacts with the American team and potential trilateral meetings at the technical level between Ukraine, the United States, and Russia. “Realistic proposals that can bring peace closer are important. But Russia must take the negotiations seriously and not try to find more and more pretexts to drag the war out further,” Zelenskyy said.
The President of Ukraine thanked the Prime Minister and the Netherlands for their consistently strong support.

articles.title: Former German intelligence head arrested on suspicion of espionage had traveled to Russia at least seven times
articles.body:
Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office has reported the arrest of August Hanning, the former president of the country’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND), on suspicion of espionage and treason. Along with Hanning, the agency detained Manfred D., the former head of his office.
Hanning headed the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. According to prosecutors, in 2010 Hanning made an arrangement with Manfred D. to receive information from the BND in exchange for payment.
Hanning intended to use the documents he received in his private consulting business. From 2010 to 2022, he obtained approximately 2,000 documents this way, many of them classified.
These materials were intended solely for the BND’s internal use and included, among other things, data from situational briefings. According to information from the German outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR, the documents included materials from foreign partner agencies, documents on Iran’s nuclear program, and documents on the Russian military.
In at least one instance, Hanning is known to have prepared a security report for an unnamed foreign intelligence service (not a Russian one, according to media reports).
Meanwhile, after leaving the BND, Hanning made at least seven trips to Russia, The Insider found — all of them within the period from 2015 to 2019.
Often, Hanning would fly into Moscow in the evening and fly out the next day. In the summer of 2016 he flew from Munich to Moscow on the evening of July 6 and flew out to Berlin on the afternoon of July 7. A similar trip between Berlin and Moscow took place in May 2019.
The investigation into Hanning has continued for several months. He came to the attention of law enforcement last year in connection with his possible involvement in the abduction of the children of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block. As part of that case, Hanning’s home was searched in September 2025; some of the BND documents were found during those searches.
